**ADOPT:**
- Nothing from the group package itself. packages/group/src/index.ts is a 3-line re-export and its only change is the import rename — there is no behavior there to adopt, adopt, or improve upon.
- Unregister-before-teardown as a discipline (upstream group.ts:44 deletes the store key before group.ts:45 disposes the fiber). Not as code — as a review invariant. omp already honors it in mnemopi's PluginManager.unloadPlugin (packages/mnemopi/src/core/plugins.ts:287-292 deletes from the instance map before calling shutdown()), so the value is in codifying it as a check, not in changing behavior.
- The unlink-order of the package.json `files` array: narrow it to the emitted JS plus the .d.ts/.d.ts.map set rather than shipping an entire lib tree, and pair it with an `exports` map. omp already uses `exports` maps, so only the `files` narrowing is arguably new — and it is marginal.

**REJECT:**
- The EntryGroup.remove() adoption guard (upstream group.ts:40, `entry.parent !== this`). Rejecting for omp: it guards a cross-group entry-move path that only exists inside cordis's config-file-driven entry tree. omp has no nested groups, no `:`-separated entry ids, and no entry tree at all. Adopting it would be importing cordis's data model to defend a bug that cannot occur in omp.
- The store-identity case split in the internal/plugin dispose handler (upstream index.ts:121-123). Rejecting: this is the other half of the same coupling as the guard above, and it only pays off once a fiber-disposal handler reads the registry to distinguish loader-initiated removal from self-disposal. omp has no such handler.
- The transactional commit({ id, group, options, legacy, from }) config-tree model (upstream tree.ts:94-129, 157 lines vs 133). Rejecting: 24 net lines of diff for a persistence model omp does not use. omp's settings persistence is a separate, simpler layer; retrofitting legacy-delta commits onto it would be a rewrite with no user-visible benefit.
- equalExceptVolatile / config/diff.ts (vendored-only, 45 lines). Rejecting for omp: it requires a schemastery schema to walk and a plugin remount path to elide. omp has zero schemastery usage in packages/coding-agent/src and no remount-on-config-change path, so there is nothing for the function to compare. It is a good idea in a vacuum; it is inert here.
- Disabling noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noImplicitOverride, noUnusedLocals, and noUnusedParameters in the vendored tsconfig. Rejecting outright: this is fork-local friction removal, not a pattern. omp's rules mandate `bun check` and strictness.

**UNVERIFIED:**

Treat the direction as strongly evidenced but not proven.
- The runtime consequence of the remove() ordering in the vendored fork is reasoned, NOT executed. I did not run a repro. The code is explicit that upstream's `internal/plugin` handler reads the store during disposal (index.ts:121-123, plus the group.ts:41-43 comment), and the fork's handler has no such case — so a fork-side `remove()` would appear to let the dispose handler fall through to `fiber.entry.options.disabled = true; fiber.entry.parent.tree.write()` (vendored index.ts:164-165), persisting a `disabled: true` the user never set. I confirmed the fork's create() DOES carry the same cross-group adoption support (vendored group.ts:23-25 has the identical 'Entry may be moved from another group' comment and `entry.parent = this` as upstream), so create() and remove() are asymmetric within the fork. ## [diff:schemastery]

**VERDICT:** The vendored core is upstream schemastery plus ONE real feature — a DeepSeek-authored "volatile config reference" system (3f7016a422, #4579) — and nothing else. Of the 155 insertions, 66 are doc comments (60 of those are upstream's own, merely absent from the older shigma checkout), and the real code delta is 89 added / 34 removed lines, concentrated in 16 hunks. Everything outside the volatile system is import rescoping (`cosmokit` -> `@deepseek-ai/cosmokit`) and an ESM export flip — both machine-generated and both to be discarded.

**omp should adopt none of it.** omp does not reference schemastery at all (`grep -rn "schemastery" packages/` = 0 hits) and validates config with its own `@oh-my-pi/omptype` (`packages/coding-agent/src/config/models-config-schema-bundle.ts:1`). More decisively, omp already solves the exact problem volatile exists to solve, by a better-fitting mechanism: `packages/coding-agent/src/config/registry.ts:258-278` memoizes derived settings against a `revision` counter plus a per-entry declared `inputs[]` array, and explicitly preserves value identity across recomputation — "Keep identity stable across equal recomputations so downstream derivations and listeners comparing by identity don't churn on unrelated layer rebuilds" (registry.ts:270-271). That is the same guarantee `Volatile<T>` + `createVolatile` provide, obtained without threading a third type parameter through 18 builder methods or adding a schema flag that a static path constraint must police.

The root reason is architectural. Volatile exists because Cordis captures config values at plugin *construction* time, so changing one forces a remount of a live service; `Schema.prototype.volatile()` turns the value into a stable reference whose `.get()` reads through to the new one. omp's `Settings` (packages/coding-agent/src/config/settings.ts:517) is a live facade — consumers read `settings.foo` through handles and subscribe via `onEffectiveChange(sources, listener)` (settings.ts:947) — so the problem never arises and the whole Mode/Volatile apparatus would be dead weight. DeepSeek's actual consumers confirm this reading: every `.volatile()` call site in the harness is a UI preference field (locale, transcript view, busy indicator, link opening) that must not tear down a web app. omp is a CLI/TUI where the equivalent teardown is a re-render.

The one genuinely portable idea is `validateVolatileSchema` (vendored index.ts:488-513): the invariant that a volatile field requires a fixed object path with no enclosing volatile field, enforced with a cycle-safe `seen: Map<Schema, Set<boolean>>` memo. That is a subtle, easy-to-get-wrong rule and the memo shape is a good pattern — but it only has meaning under constructor-captured config, which omp does not have.

### Write-coalescing model: pull-with-debounce vs push-with-single-flight-drain
 class: 
 upstream: Push-driven, single-flight. The loader calls `commit(change)` synchronously on every tree mutation (index.ts:186-192), which records the journal and sets `dirtyWrite`. `_drain()` (index.ts:194-199) starts at most ONE `_loop()`. `_loop()` (index.ts:201-226) runs a two-flag state machine (`dirtyRead` / `dirtyWrite`) and only ever holds one read and one write in flight. Both `flush()` (index.ts:171-176) and `refresh()` (index.ts:179-183) are public and return promises that settle when the tree reflects the outcome — `flush()` waits for writes, `refresh()` does not.
 dsh: Pull-driven, debounced. `writeFile()` (index.ts:310-316) coalesces via `setTimeout(..., 0)` — later calls within the same tick overwrite `pendingWrite`, last-one-wins. `flushWrite()` (index.ts:318-334) chains `_writeFile` onto a `writeQueue` promise so writes serialize, and swallows rejections into a logger warning. The only public entry is `write()` (index.ts:337-340), which must be called explicitly; nothing in the loader's change path calls it. There is no `flush()` and no read/write interleaving state machine — `refresh()` (index.ts:279-287) is a standalone try/catch that logs and keeps the last good tree.

    private _drain() {
      if (this._draining) return
      this._draining = this._loop().finally(() => {
        this._draining = undefined
      })
    }
upstream src/index.ts:202:
    while (this.dirtyRead || this.dirtyWrite) {
vendor src/index.ts:310-316:
    private writeFile(config: EntryOptions[]) {
      clearTimeout(this.writeTask)
      this.pendingWrite = config
      this.writeTask = setTimeout(() => { void this.flushWrite() }, 0)

vendor src/index.ts:324-328 (serialization):

**ADOPT:**
- Single-owner export of the config format (vendor src/index.ts:23 `export const entryListSchema`, :57 `export function applyEntryPatches`). This is the one item in the entire package that is portable to a host that does not use cordis, and DeepSeek's own note records it as a local change to re-apply on upstream sync. omp has no composed-config dump today (only printConfigHelp at packages/coding-agent/src/cli/config-cli.ts:405), so there is no consumer to wire it to yet — but the rule it encodes, that an offline tool must reuse the runtime's own parser and compositor rather than reimplementing them, is the thing worth adopting whenever omp grows one. Upstream actively resists this by keeping both private (index.ts:21, patch.ts:47).
- Stable synthetic identity for config rows that lack one, matched on (parent + deep-equal) so editing a neighbour does not re-identify the row (upstream src/index.ts:386-424 `_assignIds`, src/patch.ts:29-41 `ensureIds`/`ensureInsertIds`). Not applicable to omp's key/value settings map today. It becomes live the moment omp persists a user-editable LIST with durable identity (saved prompt sets, tool allowlists, scheduled jobs). Upstream already solved it and the recipe is 40 lines.
- User-facing conflict REASONS on a skipped external-edit merge. Upstream reports per-entry reasons ('key "x" modified both in file and at runtime', 'moved both in file and at runtime') at src/journal.ts:210-230. omp logs only 'Settings: skipped stale change after external config edit' with path and setting name (settings.ts:3389-3392) — the user cannot tell WHY their edit lost. Cheap to add, and omp's per-setting granularity makes the messages more precise than upstream's.

**REJECT:**
- The transactional journal itself (upstream src/journal.ts, 242 lines): record/merge/reconcile/applyJournal. Rejected because its substrate — a fiber-based entry tree where the loader reports mutations — does not exist in omp. Substituting it for omp's existing generation guard would be a downgrade, not an upgrade.
- PatchIndex ownership routing (upstream src/patch.ts:141-261, 121 lines). Rejected as a mechanism: omp already answers the same question at the storage layer, writing each setting to the layer that owns it (settings.ts:3454, :3589 each pass a distinct `writePath`). Copying a PatchIndex would be a second, redundant ownership model.
- Whole-file compare-and-swap on write (upstream StaleWriteError, index.ts:44-47 + :351-372). Rejected because omp's per-setting `yamlGenerationsMatch` guard (settings.ts:3379-3393) is strictly finer-grained: it drops only the setting that actually lost, where a whole-file CAS would cancel the entire write.
- The dead dynamic-import branch (vendor src/index.ts:221-224) and the `readonly` flag it drags in (index.ts:187, :205, :290). Rejected on both sides: it is unreachable given the constructor guard at index.ts:183-185, and AGENTS.md in this repo explicitly bans `await import()`.
- ConfigFileError staged-error type (upstream index.ts:36-42). Rejected because omp's `YamlLoadResult` discriminated union (switch at settings.ts:2113) plus `#quarantineInvalidYamlLocked` (settings.ts:2093-2109) is the better shape — it not only classifies the failure but refuses to overwrite the file and moves it aside.
- The debounced pull-write model (vendor index.ts:310-340) as a replacement for anything in omp. Rejected — omp's `#exclusive` serialization (settings.ts:144) plus `CONFIG_WATCH_DEBOUNCE_MS = 200` (settings.ts:147) already covers it, and omp's writes are awaited at their call sites rather than deferred behind a timer.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- Whether omp's settings/config contracts are actually covered by tests. settings.ts is ~3600 lines and I did not enumerate packages/coding-agent/src/config/*.spec.ts. I am NOT claiming omp has weaker test coverage than the vendored include — the vendored include has none, so any nonzero omp coverage wins. Stated as unverified rather than assumed either way.
- Whether upstream's journal behaviour is correct or merely present. I read the implementation and the test NAMES, and read the 503 deleted lines in full, but I did not run upstream's suite (`bun test` in packages/include) or any of the 809 test LOC. All claims about what the journal defends are inferred from implementation plus test titles, not from observed passes.
- Whether the DeepSeek revert of #932 was a considered decision or a workaround for a specific breakage. The commit message for 2abb542a22 mentions "without restoring generic Loader rollback" and consumer/packaging incompatibilities, but the actual reason the transactional model was abandoned is not stated in the message or in the note I read (2026-09-09-nontransactional-loader.md was referenced but not opened). If the revert was forced by a Cordis Loader limitation, upstream's journal may be unshippable as-is and the case for adopting it weaker than the line count suggests.
- Whether the two vendor-side additions (entryListSchema/applyEntryPatches exports, EntryGroup marker) have been upstreamed or are still pending. DeepSeek's note (2026-07-30-dsh-dump-config.md:32) says they are 'to re-apply on upstream sync', but I did not check the upstream tree at a newer commit for them, and the upstream checkout I measured is a single squashed commit (f8ea3cd 'chore: bump versions') with no useful history to inspect.
- Behavioural impact of the two aliasing holes (vendor index.ts:62 shallow early return, :91/:93 by-reference insert push) in DeepSeek's actual runtime. Both are real and both contradict the function's documented invariant, but whether any live code path mutates a returned entry object in place is not established — I traced the four call sites in app-boot but not the loader's treatment of `EntryOptions` after `root.update()`.
- omp's equivalence for the `checkAccess` / read-only-config path. Upstream checks `access(filename, W_OK)` immediately before writing and keeps pending changes in memory if it fails (index.ts:322-328), defended by tests 'keeps runtime changes in memory when the file is read-only' (sync.spec.ts:230). I located no corresponding read-only-config branch in omp's settings write path but did not exhaustively search for one.



## [diff:core-fiber]

**VERDICT:** The vendored copy is NOT "DeepSeek's improved Cordis" — it is upstream 4.0.0-rc.7 (commit 56b3d4f7) plus 22 ledgered local patches, and the "upstream" tree here is rc.10. So the diff is two-way: DeepSeek's genuine additions AND ~3 releases of upstream drift the fork never took. Direction of every divergence is provable, not guessed: `deepseek-harness/vendor/README.md` is an exhaustive 22-entry divergence ledger, and `git log -S` on each marker shows it was introduced by the single import commit 72688a3888 and never touched — i.e. everything NOT in the ledger is plain rc.7→rc.10 drift.

The headline number is misleading and I measured it apart: +822 net lines is 70% JSDoc. Only 252 added lines are real code, and ~180 of those are DeepSeek's fiber lifecycle hardening.

The most important finding is a set of verified REGRESSIONS in the vendored copy that DeepSeek's own ledger does not record — they are upstream fixes the fork is missing. I confirmed each by running both trees: `on('toString')` and `on('constructor')` throw TypeError; `on(Symbol())` throws; a `waterfall` listener calling `next()` twice re-runs the entire downstream chain (2x) instead of throwing; `_hooks` keys leak; and `logger.buffer` silently goes stale for any consumer holding a reference. The second most important: the `update()` divergence is NOT drift, it is a deliberate `Revert #932 transactional Cordis reload changes` (e07f41d5fd) — DeepSeek consciously chose non-transactional reload.

For omp: there is no cordis dependency anywhere, and M4 has already decided to port discipline rather than code. The capability layer already has priority but has zero dependency-gating, zero teardown, and zero reload — so the fiber lifecycle is precisely the gap, and the novel reentrant-disposal invariants are the part worth stealing.

**SCALE:** 9 files changed, 1013 insertions / 191 deletions, 1874 -> 2696 lines (+822 net, vendored is larger).

Per-file (upstream -> vendored): context.ts 78->146, events.ts 188->352, fiber.ts 496->754, index.ts 7->16, logger.ts 246->271, reflect.ts 283->418, registry.ts 214->337, service.ts 80->115, utils.ts 282->287.

Additions decomposed (measured with `git diff --no-index -U0 | grep '^+'`): 1013 added lines = 712 JSDoc/comment + 12 blank + 37 import-specifier churn + **252 real code lines**. Per HARD RULE 5 the import churn and the JSDoc collapse to one line each in the report below; the real signal is 252 lines, of which ~180 are the vendored fiber.ts lifecycle hardening.

Version/direction: UPSTREAM = `cordis@4.0.0-rc.10` (packages/core/package.json, shallow clone, 1 commit). VENDORED = `@deepseek-ai/cordis@4.0.4` (vendor/cordis/package.json), forked from upstream `4.0.0-rc.7` @ `56b3d4f7` per `vendor/README.md` manifest table. Both trees carry identical file lists (context/events/fiber/index/logger/reflect/registry/service/utils.ts) and no test directory.

**ADOPT:**
- Owner-scoped effect registration BEFORE setup() runs, with a barrier that makes a reentrant unload await setup and every collected cleanup (fiber.ts:520 + :459-480). This is the single most valuable invariant in the diff: it is DeepSeek-authored, absent upstream, and is a correctness property (no leaked registrations) rather than a style preference. If M4's 'reloading có nối' ever introduces teardown, this ordering must be specified up front.
- Rejecting new work while the owner is UNLOADING, while keeping PENDING and LOADING legal (fiber.ts:419-421). A fail-loud registration rule — one of the three things MILESTONE_4_EXECUTION_PLAN.md:73 nominates as worth borrowing.
- Per-observer error containment on teardown notification (fiber.ts:120 emitPluginDisposed): a throwing observer must not starve peers nor interrupt ownership cleanup. General robustness law for any broadcast path.
- Cleanup is owned once but joinable by multiple observers (fiber.ts:112 effectInertia + :116 runDisposable). Adopt the invariant, not the WeakMap.
- Store config raw and resolve it at activation, not at parse time, so config expressions may reference services that do not exist until then (fiber.ts:641 _resolveConfig, new 'internal/config' waterfall). omp has `!!js`-style interpolation in its own config path, so this is a live bug class, not a hypothetical.
- Disposer removes exactly what it registered, by identity — never by position or by list reference (ledger #21). Pairs with the joinable-cleanup rule.
- UPSTREAM's event-bus discipline, which the fork is missing and which is worth copying if omp ever builds a hook table: null-prototype `_hooks` (events.ts:46), delete the key when a listener list empties (events.ts:149), tolerate symbol event names (events.ts:74-75), and guard against double-`next()` in waterfall (events.ts:125). All four are verified to be broken in the fork.

**REJECT:**
- The fork's non-transactional `Fiber.update()`. This is a deliberate `Revert #932`, not drift, and it is the exact behaviour M4 is trying to move away from: a reload you cannot await cannot be linked to anything. Upstream's awaitable-update-with-suppressed-rejection (fiber.ts:478-494) is the shape omp wants.

I did not construct a scenario that discriminates. Do not act on this without a targeted repro.

I confirmed the code delta but did not build a probe where def-site and use-site resolve to different services, so I cannot say whether the fork silently changes which scope a cross-boundary service call resolves against.

**VERDICT:** The vendored fork is a thin, well-scoped patch on upstream 1.8.1, not a rewrite. Of 200 added src lines, 92 are JSDoc, 3 are `.ts` import specifiers, and 86 are one new file (`volatile.ts`). Only ~9 net lines are non-volatile code, and they carry four real bug fixes to upstream `deepEqual` (sparse-array holes, a dropped `strict` flag in array recursion, URL-by-href, and a stack overflow on cycles) plus one documented semantic tightening. array.ts/misc.ts/string.ts/time.ts are provably comment-only. omp needs none of the `Volatile` feature — its config is pull-based through typed handles with subscribe/identity-preserving recompute, whereas Volatile exists to serve Cordis's opposite model (a plugin fiber holding a mutable `this.config`). omp already carries a better array-hole walk. The single thing worth porting is the cycle guard: omp's own `settingValuesEqual` throws RangeError on cyclic structures, the same bug DSH fixed upstream, and it sits on the settings hot path. Adoption of Cordis would import the whole Volatile protocol (cosmokit + schemastery + cordis + loader, 368/65 across 15 files) for a capability omp already provides by a different and better-fitted design.

### No ancestor tracking anywhere in deepEqual, so a cyclic object graph recursed until the stack blew. deepEqual on two structurally identical but distinct cyclic objects threw RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. The rewrite threads an `ancestors` Set through the recursion, adds on entry and deletes in a finally, and short-circuits to false when `a` is already on the stack. The stated contract is that DISTINCT cyclic structures are unequal — the identity check `a === b` at the top still makes a self-referential object equal to itself, and non-cyclic DAGs (the same node referenced twice as siblings) are still compared field-by-field because the finally deletes on unwind.

## [diff:loader]

**VERDICT:** Direction is the headline, and it is the opposite of what the brief assumed: the DeepSeek tree is NOT ahead of upstream. It is an OLDER cordis fork with in-house patches layered on top, and upstream has since moved past it in two places. Proof: vendored still declares `abstract write(): void`, while upstream replaced that entire persistence contract with `abstract commit(change: EntryChange)`; vendored has no `src/resolve.ts` at all, while upstream added a 69-line project-scoped resolver plus a 115-line spec for it; and upstream's `group.ts`/`index.ts` contain a *coupled pair* of later fixes (adoption guard + the "case 6" store check) that the fork demonstrably predates. "Merge upstream in" is therefore not the operation — these are two different cordis generations.

The fork is not merely behind, though. It contributes one genuine bugfix upstream lacks (`unparse` invoked with its schema receiver — upstream's unbound `unparse(config)` is a real TypeError on any runtime config write, with zero test coverage), one portable hardening (`FiberState.UNLOADING` guard before persisting), and one substantial feature (volatile config hot-patch: ~230 lines spanning loader + core + cosmokit, entirely untested in-tree). It pays for that feature with a whole-package TSDoc pass, a relaxed tsconfig, and a cross-package `internal/config` waterfall that rewrites `loader/patch-context` from async to sync — a core-level divergence the loader merely inherits, not a local choice.

On the question that matters — would omp need this? Almost none of it. omp has no cordis dependency at all (zero hits across every package.json), no EntryTree, no nested groups, and no service-DI realms, so the package is adopt-or-nothing. More importantly, the two ideas that actually generalize are ones omp already has, better: omp's `local-module-loader.ts` solves cordis's `resolve.ts` problem synchronously via `createRequire` with no filesystem write and no `.cordis/` litter, and omp's `config/registry.ts` reactive setting graph is a finer-grained superset of cordis's volatile-refresh, with last-known-good rollback on a bad edit that cordis does not have. ## [kernel:fiber-effects]

**VERDICT:** omp does NOT have this problem, because omp cannot do the thing that creates it. Cordis's fiber machinery exists to make *in-process unload* safe; omp has no in-process extension unload at all. Do not adopt the machinery. Adopt one 3-line contract, and fix one 1-line real bug in omp's own teardown.

CONFIRMED: `ExtensionAPI.on()` returns `void` (types.ts:1302) and `registerTool()` returns `void` (types.ts:1372) — an extension is never handed a disposer. `Extension` (types.ts:1827-1842) is a flat bag of Maps with no ownership tree. A grep for `fiber|Fiber|epoch|LIFO|onDispose|addDisposable` across `packages/coding-agent/src/extensibility/` returns exactly one unrelated hit (legacy-typebox.ts:96, a word in a comment). `setSuspendedExtensions` (runner.ts:976-998) is a *visibility gate*, not a teardown — its own doc says "A suspended extension keeps its module state" — and the only supported way to add an extension is a process restart: "Restart omp to load newly enabled extensions" (sdk.ts:4626). With no unload, there is no LIFO to enforce, no reentrant disposer to survive, and no epoch to invalidate.

omp has ALREADY SOLVED, independently, the one sub-problem that transfers: teardown-notification containment. `emitSessionShutdownEvent` puts `disposeFileFallbacks()` + `clearManagedTimers()` in a `finally` (runner.ts:413-417) and dispatches handlers through `Promise.all(#runHandlerWithTimeout)` (runner.ts:1501-1511), which is per-handler try/catch + timeout. That is the same shape as dsh's `emitPluginDisposed` (fiber.ts:120-137), reached without a fork.

THE ONE REAL BUG on the omp side, and it is small: `disposeFileFallbacks()` (runner.ts:1376) is `for (const dispose of this.#fileFallbackDisposers.splice(0)) dispose()` — FIFO, not LIFO, and no try/catch, so one throwing disposer silently orphans every remaining fallback in the *process-wide* registry. It is bounded: only 2 push sites (runner.ts:781, :800), both host-owned trampolines installed in `initialize()`, not extension-owned state. `ManagedTimers.clearAll()` has the identical shape. Fix: iterate a copy in reverse inside a try/catch, log, continue.

On the dsh fork itself: the manifest's "three reentrant disposal gaps" is a CATEGORY count, not a behavior count. dsh's own `vendor/README.md` #6 headline says three and its own body enumerates nine. Verified by execution, not reading.

**ADOPT:**
- Make omp's `disposeFileFallbacks()` (runner.ts:1376) reverse-order and failure-isolated — it is currently `for (const dispose of this.#fileFallbackDisposers.splice(0)) dispose()`: FIFO, no try/catch, and the registry it clears is PROCESS-WIDE, so one throw orphans the rest. Iterate a copy in reverse, wrap each call in try/catch, log, continue. Same one-line shape for `ManagedTimers.clearAll()` (managed-timers.ts:58-64). This is the only place in omp where the cordis bug class is actually present.
- If omp ever gives extensions a disposer (`on()` returning `() => void` is a one-line change to types.ts:1302), take the SINGLE rule dsh's fork encodes: a disposer must be single-shot for the caller who received it, and simultaneously joinable by whoever is tearing the owning scope down. dsh spent 6 lines of WeakMap (`effectInertia`, fiber.ts:112-117) plus an `inFlight` slot and a `.finally` wrapper (`finalizeDisposal`, fiber.ts:485-502) to get that. It is the single hardest-won idea in the fork and it is 3 lines of prose to state.
- Adopt the CONTAINMENT contract, not the code: teardown notifications must be per-observer isolated so one throwing observer cannot starve peers or interrupt ownership cleanup. omp already satisfies this for session_shutdown (Promise.all of per-handler try/catch, runner.ts:1501-1511) — record it as an invariant so a future refactor does not quietly serialize the loop.
- Adopt the DIAGNOSTIC surface if omp ever adds scopes: the EffectMeta label tree (`getEffects()`), which cordis exposes at fiber.ts:342-346 and which both repos use in tests to assert ownership. omp currently has no equivalent way to ask 'what is still registered on this scope'. The label-as-evidence pattern is what makes ownership testable.
- Adopt dsh's testing discipline for any scope work: 11 adversarial tests in a single focused file (packages/extensions/tool-cordis/tests/cordis-lifecycle.spec.ts), each named for the observable failure it prevents ('makes an effect visible to a reentrant owner restart...', 'lets parent disposal during internal/plugin await the unpublished child to quiescence'). Upstream's 87 tests cover the happy paths; dsh's 11 cover exactly the paths that break.

**REJECT:**
- DO NOT adopt the Fiber/epoch machinery. The load-bearing premise is 'unloading a plugin cleanly is hard', and that difficulty is CONDITIONAL on in-process unload existing. omp has no unload: sdk.ts:4626 tells users 'Restart omp to load newly enabled extensions'. Adopting a load-epoch state machine to manage a lifecycle that cannot occur is the exact over-engineering failure mode.
- DO NOT adopt the UNLOADING registration rejection (dsh fiber.ts:420-422). It is correct for cordis and wrong for omp: omp extensions are designed to register handlers/tools/renderers at arbitrary times, and there is no window in which a registration could escape a snapshot.
- DO NOT adopt the `internal/plugin` publication-ordering work (dsh fiber.ts:265-319). It is loader-shape coupling — it exists because dsh mounts plugin trees from cordis.yml where a loader mutates `inject` during a notification. omp discovers extensions by filesystem path (discovery/omp-plugins.ts, omp-extension-roots.ts) with no dynamic inject.
- DO NOT adopt the PENDING-drain / stale-epoch-skip work (dsh fiber.ts:281-286, :651-658). PENDING is a cordis-specific state meaning 'waiting on injected services'. omp extensions are all-or-nothing loaded.
- DO NOT treat the dsh fork as a model to imitate wholesale. It regresses three upstream behaviors that upstream has tests for: the failed-fiber-reentry guard, the duplicate-next() waterfall guard (TWO tests), and the null-prototype `_hooks` map. Executed proof for all three is in the divergences array. The fork's own `vendor/README.md` re-application procedure (item 6) exists precisely because these are a patch stack over a moving upstream, not a maintained fork.
- DO NOT adopt dsh's JSDoc density (~600 added lines, 712 of 1,189 total changed lines across 9 files). omp's AGENTS.md has an explicit anti-slop-comment rule and a why-comment discipline; dsh's @param/@returns-everywhere style would violate omp's house style and its own rule about not adding tests/ceremony for low-risk changes.
- DO NOT port cordis's `def-site/use-site` traceable proxy. Note that dsh REMOVED it (symbols.caller) — if omp ever needs a context proxy, start from the simpler single-site model rather than reconstructing the pair.

All upstream behavior claims are from reading packages/core/tests/ plus the vitest specs; all dsh behavior claims are from executing standalone bun probes I wrote against vendor/cordis/src/index.ts. ## [kernel:adopt-cost]

**VERDICT:** REJECT for adoption; the only thing omp would actually gain is scoped DI (Service/Reflect), and omp has no demonstrated pain that it would fix. Cordis is 5.6% of omp's size (4,991 src LOC vs omp's 114,016), so this is not a size decision — it is a "does omp need scoped, hot-swappable dependency injection" decision, and the answer is no. Every other cordis component maps onto something omp already has and, in three cases, has already hardened better: omptype (10,642 LOC) replaces cosmokit+schemastery (1,553 LOC) with an ArkType-compatible JIT; managed-timers.ts (83 LOC) replaces cordis-plugin-timer (147 src/318 test) and adds hardening cordis lacks (issue #5664 — a throw in a raw setInterval becomes a fatal uncaughtException; omp unrefs every handle and routes callbacks through onError); omp's extensibility layer (21,376 LOC incl. a 1,297-LOC plugin manager, marketplace, per-plugin feature gating) is a superset of cordis's loader. Two hard blockers make adoption actively costly: (1) cordis-plugin-logger-console writes console.log at shared.ts:66, which omp's AGENTS.md bans outright in TUI/RPC/SDK/worker paths and mandates ~/.omp/logs rotation for; (2) npm `latest` for cordis is 4.0.0-rc.10 — ten release candidates, no stable 4.0 — so a plain `npm i cordis` pins omp to an RC. The DeepSeek vendored copy is not a model to copy either: it carries 1,388 direct-import files and 32 loader-composition spec files, meaning they didn't "adopt cordis," they rebuilt their entire application substrate on it — a bet already made and paid for at a scale omp has no reason to match. The decisive fact for the adopt/vendor tradeoff: the fiber.ts lifecycle hardening is the ONLY substantive code change in the entire vendored copy (+176/-57 code lines, comments stripped), it is 100% absent from upstream rc.10, and every other divergence is JSDoc, renames, or version skew. That is ~119 net lines of real work protecting reentrant disposal — cheap to adopt upstream-style as a pattern, not worth a framework dependency.

## [final]

## 1. what_cordis_is

Cordis is a **DI container with a fiber lifecycle**, and that second half is the only reason this comparison is interesting.

Measured: 4,991 src LOC / 6,497 test LOC across 9 packages (upstream shallow clone `f8ea3cd`, 2026-09-08). Core is 1,874. The kernel is `Fiber` — a state machine (`PENDING/LOADING/ACTIVE/FAILED/DISPOSED/UNLOADING`) that owns a `_disposables` list, and `effect()` is the only way to register a disposer. Everything else (`Service`, `Reflect`, `Events`) hangs off that.

The DeepSeek copy is **not** a fork-forward. It is upstream `4.0.0-rc.7` @ `56b3d4f7` (vendor/README.md manifest table) + 22 ledgered patches, and the tree you compare against is rc.10. So every difference is two-way, and direction is provable per marker: `git log -S` on each shows it landed in the single import commit `72688a3888` and was never touched → anything *not* in the ledger is plain rc.7→rc.10 drift the fork never took.

**The headline +822 net lines is 70% JSDoc.** Measured on the 9 core files: 1,013 added lines = 712 comment + 12 blank + 37 import churn + **252 real code**, of which ~180 are one file.

## 2. the_unload_answer

**No. Upstream rc.10 alone does not deliver clean unload, and I confirmed the hardening is 100% DeepSeek-authored, not drift.** Verified myself:

```
grep -c 'effectInertia|setupBarrier|emitPluginDisposed' upstream/core/src/fiber.ts  →  0
```

What DeepSeek had to add, in `deepseek-harness/vendor/cordis/src/fiber.ts`:

| line | invariant | upstream state |
|---|---|---|
| `:515` | `effectInertia.set(wrapper, () => inFlight)` — an effect is on its owner's list **before** `setup()` runs, so an unload begun *from inside* setup still sees it | `fiber.ts:338` registers the wrapper *after* `this._execute(runner)` |
| `:462,:467,:475` | `setupBarrier` / `waitForSetup` / `disposeAfter` — a reentrant unload awaits setup **and** every cleanup setup then collected | absent |
| `:421` | `throw new CordisError('INACTIVE_EFFECT')` while the owner is `UNLOADING` — cleanup-time registrations cannot escape the in-flight snapshot | only `assertActive()`; uid is still non-null during UNLOADING |
| `:112,:114` | `effectInertia` WeakMap + `runDisposable()` — cleanup is **owned once, joinable by N observers** | second caller gets `undefined` and proceeds as if teardown were done |
| `:120` | `emitPluginDisposed` — per-observer try/catch so one throwing callback cannot starve peers or interrupt ownership cleanup | bare `context.emit(...)`; upstream `EventsService.emit` has no per-callback containment |
| `:511` | `if (executing) return disposeAfter(waitForSetup())` | absent |

That is the entire substantive delta. Everything else in the vendored core is JSDoc, `@deepseek-ai` renames, or rc.7 drift.

**And the fork is not safe to copy — it regressed upstream in three places, all executed:**

```
vendored events.ts:132  _hooks: ... = {}            | upstream :46  Object.create(null)
  → on('constructor') / on('toString') THROW TypeError
vendored events.ts      grep -c 'called multiple times' = 0
  | upstream :125 if (called) throw new Error('next() called multiple times')
  → a listener calling next() twice re-runs the whole downstream chain, silently
vendored cordis        0 test files  |  upstream 6,497 test LOC
```

`vendor/timer/` additionally replaces upstream's waiter **queue** with a single slot — a second concurrent `next()` overwrites the first promise, which never settles. Nobody diffed that package.

## 3. the_three_ideas — ranked, worth stealing regardless

**#1 — A disposer is single-shot for its caller, joinable by whoever owns the teardown.** `fiber.ts:112,:515` cost 6 lines of WeakMap plus an `inFlight` slot. Three lines of prose: *"the disposer I handed you fires once; the owner tearing the scope down may join a run already in flight."* This is the hardest-won invariant in the fork and the one omp has no equivalent of. Ranked first because it is the part of a fiber you can have without a fiber

## [dsh:workflow-orchestration]

**VERDICT:** This is not a workflow engine. It is a JavaScript fan-out script runner with a very well-built kill button, wrapped in ~85,000 lines of unusually disciplined TypeScript. The prompt's framing (DAG? state machine? queue?) has the wrong answer: the model writes a JS string, it is compiled into a `node:vm` context inside a separate sandboxed process, and the only combinators are `parallel()` and `pipeline()` — both `Promise.all` over an array. The `meta.phases` field is the closest thing to a graph and the source comment says outright it "imposes no execution structure" (workflow/src/types.ts:26-27). There is no task DAG, no dependency edge, no critical path anywhere in the 11 packages.

What is genuinely good — and it is a real list: the fatal-vs-per-item-null error discipline with unforgeable host-realm `instanceof` fatality; the double parse so a syntax error is a correctable tool result; `materializeFromRealm` as a total, path-tagging JSON boundary; the monotone durable depth floor that stops a resumed agent laundering its recursion budget; capability declaration as a fail-loud contract; the runtime invariant companion; and above all Ralph (tool-ralph), which runs the SAME engine with the trust model inverted — a deployment-owned constant script the model cannot edit, where the workspace is the memory and only a 16KB validated report crosses rounds. That contrast is the most transferable idea in the entire area.

Where it is bad, bluntly: NOTHING RESUMES. A crash loses the run, its queue, and its partial results. The session log writes run-start/agent-start/agent-end/run-end, but nothing ever reads them back — that is an audit trail, not a resume capability. `jobs-local` has zero persistence, so even `run_in_background: true` dies with the process. Second: there is NO TIMEOUT. `timeoutMs: null` at workflow-ptc/src/host.ts:281 maps to "no wall timer" in ptc-runtime-node/src/index.ts:163; the 5s `syncTimeoutMs` bounds only the synchronous prefix of an async IIFE, so one hung child hangs the run forever. Third: no cost or token budget for a fan-out — `maxTotalAgents: 1000` bounds calls, not spend. Fourth: the one-shot subagent path has NO concurrency cap; the `maxActiveSubagents: 8` pool is reached from exactly one call site and guards only continuable children.

Three things in scope are not orchestration and should not be counted as such. `plan` is a boolean mode flag plus a review gate (its projection type is literally `{active, pending}`). `todo` is 47 lines of types: a whole-list snapshot with three statuses, no ids, no deps, no priority — and the source comment says the omission of ids is deliberate. `deliverables/` is a file-attachment tool plus a git diff viewer; nothing in 11 packages judges whether work was completed. The only completion check that exists anywhere is a shape check on the model's own self-report in the Ralph loop (`evidence.length > 0 && nextSteps.length === 0 && blocker === ''`) — that validates the report's structure, not its truth.

Two organizational cautions. Skill "selection" is exact-name lookup against a name+description catalog: rule-driven, zero semantic retrieval, so routing quality is 100% prompt quality — conventional and fine, but do not describe it as an engine. And the ratio is 85,022 lines to ~2,196 lines of actual orchestration; the test density (1,880 it/test blocks, 718 in subagent alone) and comment quality are real, but the line count badly overstates the mechanism.

Net for omp: take the error discipline, the Ralph inversion, the monotone depth floor, the capability contract, and the JSON materialization boundary. Do not take the null timeout, the in-memory-only job registry, the hardcoded `stop_hook_active: false`, parse-and-drop hook fields, or the package-per-concern layout at this volume.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- Runtime behavior of the PTC workflow path — `bun test packages/workflow/workflow-ptc/tests/integration.spec.ts` fails on this machine with `SyntaxError: Export named 'stripTypeScriptTypes' not found in module 'node:module'` (Bun 1.4.2). Every workflow claim here is from code reading, not execution.
- That `timeoutMs: null` really means unbounded end-to-end. The chain (workflow host → ptc-runtime resolve → node runtime wallTimer) is read from source; I did not observe a hanging run.
- Whether the shipped composition actually wires tool-workflow, tool-ralph, tool-subagent, tool-skill, hooks, and the subagent providers together. I read packages in scope, not the composition/preset graph that assembles them.
- Cancellation latency under real load. The code path is correct by reading (the abort race at host.ts:222-238 is the right shape), but I did not measure time-to-quiescence.
- Whether `maxConcurrentAgents` auto-resolving to `min(16, availableParallelism() - 2)` behaves correctly inside a cgroup-limited sandbox where availableParallelism may report host cores.
- Whether the 10 subagent providers are all exercised in a shipped composition or several are aspirational. packages/subagent has 9 sub-packages; which are mounted is a composition question outside the read scope.
- Real-world skill routing accuracy. The mechanism is rule-driven exact-name lookup, so quality is a function of the descriptions, which I did not evaluate against real traffic.
- Whether `subagent-dsh-sdk`, `subagent-codex`, and `subagent-fork-in-process` are production-ready — each has a large test file and an `.e2e.ts`, but I did not run them (same Bun/`stripTypeScriptTypes` blocker).



## [dsh:safety-sandbox-guard]

**VERDICT:** The kernel-level sandbox is real and unusually well built — genuinely OS-level on all three platforms, fail-closed by contract, with an honest 'full'/'partial' enforcement grade. That part is better than most agent sandboxes and worth mining. Three of the brief's premises turned out to be wrong in ways that matter: (1) `guard/` is 321 lines of advisory loop-hygiene with NO security semantics and no veto power; (2) `identity/` is 100 lines containing one anonymous telemetry UUID; (3) there is NO declarative exec policy at all — the brief asked about "rules carrying match examples and justifications", and that feature does not exist in this repo. I verified its absence three ways (repo-wide rule-file extension sweep returning only 2 pyproject.toml hits; a field-level grep for matchExample/rationale-as-rule returning zero; and the in-tree `TODO(permissions)` at packages/shell/tool-bash/src/index.ts:11-12 that admits it is unbuilt). The only rule language is a bridge that imports Claude Code and Codex hook configs, where bad matchers ARE rejected at config-load time. The licensing claim from the prior audit is CORRECT and I confirmed it by reading the file: BSD 3-Clause, 'Copyright (c) 2026, node-addon-landlock-run contributors', all 5 LICENSE files byte-identical (sha256 fed2134d...). The refinement the prior audit missed is PROVENANCE — the root repo is MIT (c) 2026 DeepSeek, so native/system is a vendored third-party project, not DeepSeek code. The 'no Windows build' claim is also technically true but badly misleading: it is true of native/system (whose CI matrix has exactly 4 platforms, none Windows), yet Windows sandboxing exists and is the LARGEST backend in the tree — 2,122 lines of TypeScript over koffi FFI with 26 Win32 API bindings, MIT-licensed, no prebuilt binary, and entirely independent of native/system. The real gap is not platform coverage but scope: this sandbox confines WRITES ONLY. Reads pass through under every mode (stated verbatim at fs-sandbox/src/index.ts:6-7), and there is no network confinement on any platform — the bwrap profile omits --unshare-net and the Seatbelt profile is `(allow default)(deny file-write*)`. Given the agent runs as the operator's own UID, `cat ~/.dsh/.credentials.yaml` succeeds inside a 'read-only' sandbox. Their own README admits this ('That is discretion, not a boundary'), which is more honesty than most projects manage. The single most transferable idea is the `ConfinedArgv` envelope: carrying `enforcement: 'full'|'partial'` plus per-backend `denialSignatures` and `runnerFailureRules` on every wrap, so a consumer can never mistake 'the runner failed' for 'confinement blocked it', and can never read a denial a given backend never produces. Second is the credential seam's value-free view types.

The refinement the prior audit missed is PROVENANCE: the root repo is MIT (c) 2026 DeepSeek, so native/system is a vendored third-party project, not DeepSeek-authored code. MIT-compatible, notice preserved — legally fine, but not 'their' code.
- The prior audit's 'no Windows build' is TRUE for native/system (github-matrix.mjs RUNNERS has exactly linux-x64, linux-arm64, darwin-x64, darwin-arm64) but MISLEADING as a sandbox-coverage statement. ## [dsh:thinking-reasoning-loop]

**VERDICT:** dsh's thinking loop is the most carefully engineered one I have measured, and its central bet is the one I would most want to copy: **the loop owns almost no state — it owns an event log, and every request is a pure derivation of that log** (`session.deriveMessages()` at agent.ts:671, incremental O(new-nodes) via `derivedGeneration`/`derivedNodes` at session/src/index.ts:860-873). Compaction, tool scheduling, retry, crash repair, cache-state, and migrations are all layered on top of that one append-only stream rather than bolted beside it. Concretely, three nested loops (kick 254 -> turn 313 -> step 407) totaling 978 lines of actual loop code in agent.ts + tool-calls.ts, and the surrounding packages (compaction 3,189 / spill 1,209 / session 17,863 src LOC) are almost entirely non-invasive policies that hook `agent/pre-step`, `agent/request-error`, and `tools/post-execute`. The two best ideas are both about honesty toward the model rather than cleverness: the compaction gate that **throws if the new summary is not smaller than what it replaces** (region.ts:418-422), and the crash-recovery text that tells the model an interrupted tool's outcome is unknown and must not be retried blindly if it may have side effects (repair.ts:31-43). I refute one prior claim outright: **dsh has a full on-disk session-format migration system** — v0->v1 through v3->v4, 6,614 lines, adjacency- and completeness-enforced, streaming, with verified atomic write-back (chain.ts:30-75, generation.ts:891-911); the "bidirectional exact-version gate" that prior audit found is real but belongs to the *projection cache* (`stateVersion`, projection/src/index.ts:412-429), a different subsystem. Two honest gaps: there is **no step or turn cap anywhere in the loop core** (grep for maxSteps/maxTurns/maxIterations across agent-loop/src returns nothing) — context pressure is the only bound — and there is **no memory system at all**; I searched the concept under a dozen alternate names before concluding that, and what ships is a disposable lexical FTS index over transcripts exposed as opt-in tools, which is a transcript reader, not memory.

**UNVERIFIED:**

- The key-gated live cache test (tests/request-cache.e2e.ts) requires a real API key. I read its stated contract but could not verify it passes, nor measure the actual cache hit rate.
- I did not open packages/llm/**/*, packages/api/**/*, or packages/interaction/**/* line by line beyond the greps and the two files cited. The llm package at 13,548 src LOC contains the adapter layer, streaming, and error taxonomy, and the api package at 20,525 src LOC is a surface/transport layer I did not audit. Anything about provider quirks, token accounting, or the API surface is unexamined.

- The claim that no semantic memory exists rests on negative search. I searched for mnemopi/mnemorical, embeddings, vector stores, FTS outside session-query, and eleven alternate namings (consolidat, distill, episod, semantic, long-term, decay, recall, recollect, digest, learn, note-store, scratchpad, knowledge) with no semantic-retrieval hit. I did not audit packages/experimental/**/*, which is where an unbuilt or experimental memory layer would most plausibly live and which I excluded from scope.

## [dsh:persistence-settings-config]

**VERDICT:** dsh HAS a real layering model, and on the specific claim the brief asked me to check, the prior audit was CORRECT in every particular: the refusal exists at packages/boot/config-editor/src/index.ts:128, it fires BEFORE the first write (:130), and it is covered by a contract test that asserts the patch file is byte-identical afterward (settings/tests/configuration.spec.ts:39-46). dsh is NOT better than what omp's M4-6 wants, though, and the reason is specific: dsh's layering model is a *composition* model, not a *provenance* model. It knows the winning value and can refuse a write that something shadows, but it cannot tell you which file won or which field it won. "provenance" appears zero times in any .ts file in the repo. The best reporting surface is `--dump-config` (apps/cli/src/dump-config.ts:51-75), and it attributes at *row* granularity via whole-entry JSON.stringify diffs (app-boot/src/index.ts:484-489) — a filename, not a field path. That is exactly the gap M4-6 exists to fill, so dsh is a strong REFERENCE and a weak BORROW here. Where dsh genuinely beats a naive design, and where I would copy: the shadow-refusal is a *functional* check (re-render, recompose through the real patch algorithm, diff the effective value) rather than a hand-maintained priority table, so it catches layers the author never enumerated. The two lock mechanisms are both better than what most projects have. The storage layer's shared cross-implementation conformance suite and the session lease's deliberate no-expiry design are the two things here I would most want in omp. The one thing to avoid: the config editor will serialize `!!js` eval nodes into persisted config, safe today only because it has exactly one production caller, with no sanitization in the persistence layer itself.

## [dsh:mcp-lsp-tools]

**VERDICT:** dsh solves omp's M2 WI-12 gap by REMOVING it, not by solving it. MCP is client-only, and MCP server instances can only come from an operator-authored cordis.yml — there is no model-facing verb that mounts one, and the node:vm sandbox façade for model-written plugins explicitly withholds ctx.plugin ("Framework internals (root, fiber, registry, extend, plugin, …) are withheld by design", guard.ts:733). The model can write tools and register them; it cannot contribute a server. That is a legitimate, cheap answer, but it is an answer to a question dsh never had to ask, and it comes with a real hole next door: the approval gate covers only the CLIENT (browser) half of a model-authored plugin. A host-only package activates immediately with no approval (index.ts:275-280), and the sandbox module itself states it is "not containment: host-realm helper functions remain an escape route" (sandbox.ts:6-7). So if omp's WI-12 is about plugin-contributed MCP servers, dsh supplies a strong structural precedent (make the capability unreachable) but NOT a trust model it would be safe to copy wholesale.

The tool registry is the strongest part of the audit and the most directly portable. The MCP naming scheme answers omp's long/duplicate-name question completely: mcp__<server>__<raw>, with a 12-hex SHA-256 of (serverName\0rawName) appended on ANY lossy normalization, and the invariant that the public name is never parsed back to recover the raw name (tools.ts:8-10, 81-87). Tool generation swap is two-phase with all-or-nothing rollback — the model sees the full generation or none, never a partial set (tools.ts:113-162). The registry itself, however, does zero name-shape validation (index.ts:1062-1086), so the 64-char budget survives only because one bridge happens to enforce it.

LSP is deliberately tiny and I like it: exactly 4 operations (types.ts:17), zero built-in languages, exactly one provider implementation in the entire repo, and a closed union with no JSON-RPC escape hatch. Its answer to "does it survive edits" is the best idea here: it never holds a document open. Each query re-reads the file from disk through ctx.fs, sends a transient didOpen at version 1, queries, then didClose (index.ts:279, instance.ts:159-177). Staleness after an edit is structurally impossible rather than a sync-correctness problem. Cost: no incremental sync, full re-index per query, and zero out-of-box language coverage — a first-run user gets nothing until they author the server table.

On the render question omp flagged: dsh does NOT have omp's bug class, and the reason is architectural, not vigilance. There is one event-sourced conversation projection — a single ConversationNodeDefinition whose match() handles the live assistant/live-chunk stream, the durable tool/call and tool/result, and nested ptc dispatches in the same state machine (tool.ts:247-298). There is no second renderer to drift. omp buys richer UX (partial-args preview) and pays for it with two code paths; dsh buys the invariant by dropping the feature — during `preparing` the tool card deliberately has no argsRaw (tool.ts:44-49). That is a real trade, not a free win, and omp's AGENTS.md shows the cost is already visible as a documented class of bug with a per-path verification ritual.

The typed render contract is mandatory and enforced at registration (register() throws a TypeError if output.render is not a function, index.ts:1065-1070), and presentCall/presentResult are typed as pure fn(args) with doc comments stating a UI may call them during live streaming AND a session-log replay (index.ts:279-297). That is the contract-level version of the fix. One more mechanism worth stealing outright: the projectContent staged-projection pattern in MCP tools (tools.ts:237-245) — an async side effect computed during execute is applied only if the result still deep-equals what was staged, which structurally prevents "prepared content doesn't match the real result".

Scale honesty: 1,024,738 TS LOC across 4,805 files in 61 packages. The five in-scope packages total ~95,987 TS LOC, but that number is misleading twice over — packages/api (57,085) is a gRPC/remote-transport layer with almost no bearing on MCP/LSP/tools beyond one 40-line event-declaration file, and 12,364 of packages/extensions' 25,888 is two GENERATED catalog files, leaving ~13.5k hand-written. The real subject of this audit — MCP + LSP + the tool registry — is roughly 1,426 (mcp src) + 2,406 (lsp src) + 14,679 (core/tools) = ~18.5k LOC of source, against 3,906 + 3,153 = 7,059 LOC of tests in mcp+lsp alone (2.7x and 1.3x test-to-src). A final integrity note: the `rg` on this machine is a shell function that pipes through claude.exe and silently rewrites tokens (it reported @deepseek-ai/dsh-n for dsh-mcp-client and 'n' for 'tool-call-delta'). Every exact-text claim above was re-verified with plain grep.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- I did not run any test suite. All test claims are FILE and LINE COUNTS (mcp 3,906 test LOC across 11 files; lsp 3,153 across 14; extensions 18 .spec.ts; feedback 4 .spec.ts) and the existence of a reconnect.spec.ts at 617 lines. I make no claim that any of them pass.
- I never executed the MCP client against a live server. The reconnect/backoff/stability-window logic and the image-admission path (tools.ts:352-440) are read, not observed.
- @modelcontextprotocol/client@2.0.0's own behavior — negotiation, pagination, cacheMode:'refresh' semantics — is out of scope. I audited dsh's usage of it, not the SDK.
- I did not read the .agents/notes/ design notes. The repo marks them 'Frozen Agent Notes are historical snapshots, not current search authority' (.rgignore), so the vendor's own rationale for the naming contract and the sandbox boundary is UNVERIFIED against the code. I derived both from source and doc comments only.
- The 'no second render path' finding is verified for the TOOL node specifically (tool.ts, raw-tool-call.ts, tool-call-model.ts, ToolRow.tsx). I did not audit every other conversation node in ui-chat, nor ui-trajectory. Other surfaces may have their own live/replay split.
- packages/feedback: I read types.ts, the export list, and the group README. I did not read MessageFeedbackService or the /feedback command implementation, so their correctness is unassessed. All feedback statements beyond the type shapes are THEIR CLAIM from packages/feedback/README.md.
- packages/api: I measured sizes and read remote-events.ts. I did not audit session-controller (25,677 LOC) or gateway (14,486 LOC).
- The claim that model-written packages cannot mount an MCP server rests on the sandbox ctx façade withholding ctx.plugin and harness being limited to {defineTool, registerTool, handle} (guard.ts:636, :718-780; sandbox.ts:105). I verified those allowlists by reading them. I did not attempt an actual escape, so 'cannot' is a code-reading conclusion, not a demonstrated one.
- The api-catalog 'cannot diverge' property is THEIR CLAIM (api-catalog.ts:9-10). I verified the generator exists (scripts/gen-cordis-catalog.ts:42) and the file carries the generated header, but I did not run gen-cordis-api and diff, so I did not confirm the freshness gate currently passes.

## [dsh:kernel-everything-is-plugin]

**VERDICT:** "Everything is a plugin" is real, but only for the in-tree tier, and the slogan is wrong in a specific way: dsh does not have a core/plugin boundary, it has a TRUST-TIER boundary. Three mechanisms are genuinely enforced (I executed the kernel, I did not take the docs' word): dependency-gated activation with automatic revival, hard-fail service ownership, and effect-owned reversible teardown. Against that, the specific claim at docs/architecture.md:13 is overstated in one respect I could reproduce — a plugin can register an effect on the public `ctx.root` and it will NOT unwind when the plugin unloads, because the root fiber is not the plugin's fiber and the kernel has no capability check. That is the real boundary: not "no privileged core" but "the kernel does not stop you stepping outside your own scope, and the tier that IS fenced (node:vm dynamic plugins) is fenced by an entirely different mechanism." The prior audit's "three places" is false — the phrase appears exactly once in all shipped markdown. Its "no priority system" is also false: 132 `priority` hits in packages/*/src plus a full fail-loud priority/shadowing system in packages/client/ui-slots; the grep hit the kernel, where 0 is correct but says nothing about dsh. Sibling-effect teardown is reverse-order initiation with concurrent completion, not LIFO (nested effects are). The vendored fork is mostly packaging noise; the 8 load-bearing divergences are #6, #22, #15, #18, #8, #19, #11, #14.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- THE PRIOR AUDIT'S 'THREE PLACES' CLAIM IS FALSE AS STATED, not merely unverified. 'no privileged core' appears in exactly ONE place in all shipped markdown: docs/architecture.md:13. I grepped every .md in the repo — 14 total hits for 'privileged', of which 13 are unrelated (security/UX prose in .agents/notes/*, one in packages/client/ui-settings-general/README.md:48). The two other slogan phrasings are docs/i18n/style-samples.md:9 ('everything is a plugin') and README.md:65 (the page title). No file contains three instances.
- I could not run the repository's own test suite. node_modules is not installed (`ls node_modules` exits 2) and installing a 13,946-file pnpm workspace was out of scope. All kernel findings come from executing the vendored cordis source directly under Node v24.14.1 with --experimental-transform-types, after rewriting the bare `@deepseek-ai/cosmokit` specifier to a relative path and stubbing the type-only `@standard-schema/spec` (confirmed type-only: the only non-`import type` matches for 'standard-schema' in vendor/ are two comment lines). No logic was altered, but this is not the repo's own harness and does not exercise loader, include, schemastery or HMR at all.
- The dsh-specific forks in vendor/loader, vendor/include and vendor/schemastery were read and their divergence list checked against code, but not executed. The volatile-config path (#22) and the lazy-config-resolution path (#15) are verified by code reading and by production consumers (product-analytics, speech-to-text), not by running them.
- Whether ui-slots' priority system is reachable from the host half or only from the client half. I read the client-side register path and the browser-side facade (which auto-assigns a priority LOWER than every shipped entry so dynamic plugins win). I did not trace the host-to-client boundary.
- HMR's 58 tests are counted from the spec files; I did not run them, so 'the contract is enforced' rests on the test titles plus code reading, not on a green run.
- packages/boot/plugin-manager, packages/boot/app-boot profile resolution, and the desktop host were read only at directory/grep granularity. The 367-row and 177-plugin figures are counted from shipped YAML patch files, not from a booted tree — a row could in principle be disabled at runtime by its own `disabled: !!js` expression.
- PROCESS NOTE: while staging the runnable copy of the kernel, a stray `> package.json` redirect from a failed directory-creation attempt executed in the repo root and clobbered deepseek-harness/package.json. I detected it via `git status`, restored it with `git checkout -- package.json`, and verified the working tree is clean and the file is back to its committed 260 lines. This happened after all measurements were taken and no measurement depended on it, but the repo was briefly modified and the fix is worth stating rather than hiding.

## [dsh:client-ui-interaction]

**VERDICT:** There is no TUI. What looks like a "TUI + web" product is a web/desktop product whose UI happens to be enormous: packages/client is 294K lines across 66 workspace packages, 70% of the entire in-scope surface, while apps/web is 67 source lines. The product is one React UI mounted by a 40-line entry that serves both browser and embedded-Electron from the same code path.

The "no privileged core" claim is the strongest thing here, and it survived adversarial checking — I tried to break it and could not. Zero value imports of the kernel exist in client source (dsh-agent and dsh-fs appear only as `import type`; dsh-fs-local's LocalFileSystem only in tests), and it is not merely convention: a rolldown resolveId plugin throws on any unapproved @deepseek-ai/* value import, with 475 lines of tests pinning that dsh-agent itself is a build error. The reverse direction is also clean — the apparent kernel→client dependency in packages/api/* turned out to be a module-table injection declaration, not an import, which I confirmed by grepping for real import statements and getting zero hits.

The standout idea is the test infrastructure, not the architecture. Web goldens are accessibility-tree snapshots (role, accessible name, state) rather than pixels or DOM, captured with a poll-until-two-consecutive-captures-are-equal loop to defeat React commit races, and normalized through locale-aware volatility harvesters that even cover zh-CN date shapes. That is a genuinely better answer to "how do you test a UI" than anything in the surrounding architecture, and it is directly portable.

Where it is thin is exactly where the brief expected: attention. The state model is better than the opencode `focus:"unknown"` idea — tri-state `running` with a real `undefined` for "no baseline yet", unread gated on an observed true→false transition so a never-observed session never falsely lights up, and focus modelled as a per-session retain count rather than a global window flag. But every one of those facts only ever drives a passive sidebar icon. There is no sound, no OS notification, no badge, and no tab-visibility signal anywhere; the sole `new Notification` in the repo is wired to mandatory app updates, not agent attention. The repo has built a correct attention *state machine* and then declines to act on it. The irony is that apps/desktop/src/update-attention.ts already contains exactly the right notification discipline — silent, skipped when focused, auto-cleared on focus, never stealing focus — just not attached to anything the user cares about.

ACP is competent and honestly scoped: 12 methods over the official SDK, capability advertisement derived from the live system with every unknown resolving negative, realpath canonicalization on client-supplied paths, and byte-exact wire goldens. It deliberately omits the human-interaction half rather than stubbing it. I could not compute spec completeness because the SDK is not in node_modules.

One scope caveat worth surfacing: the user-visible request was to clone and read oh-my-openagent, but the computed task assigned this deepseek-harness audit. I completed the audit as assigned; the clone was not performed.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- Whether a TUI ships outside this repository. apps/cli/tests/expected/launcher-help.txt documents `dsh tui` as a profile, and profiles live under $DSH_HOME/profiles (user-supplied), but no tui profile template exists in-repo (`rg -i "'tui'|\"tui\""` across all yml/yaml/kdl = 0 hits) and git history is squashed to a single commit, so I could not determine whether a TUI was removed, lives in a separate repo, or never existed. My finding is scoped precisely: no TUI code exists in this repo.
- ACP percentage-complete against the @agentclientprotocol/sdk 1.4.0 specification. The package is declared in package.json but not present in node_modules, so I could not read its method table. I verified the 12 methods the bridge registers and the client-side methods it omits — not what the SDK offers in total.
- Whether all 206 scenarios currently pass. I counted 206 dirs containing snapshot.yml (210 scenario dirs total) but did not execute the snapshot suite; it requires a prior build for lib mode.
- Runtime behavior of the attention system. Every attention claim is read from source and from unit tests, not observed in a running app. Specifically unverified: whether a backgrounded session's unread badge surfaces anywhere other than the sidebar row, and whether any Electron-side path surfaces agent attention.
- The large majority of packages/client source. I sampled the biggest and most architecturally significant subpackages (ui-chat, ui-conversation, ui-primitives, ui-session, ui-workspace, ui-trajectory, ui-schedule) and every file relevant to the specific questions asked, but did not audit 294K lines exhaustively.
- Process note: the user-visible request relayed into this run was to clone and read code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent, while the computed task assigned an audit of deepseek-harness area "client-ui-interaction". I completed the assigned audit against deepseek-harness at HEAD 21638c56, which is what this output describes. The oh-my-openagent clone was not performed.



## [dsh:prov-refutations]

**VERDICT:** Of the seven claims, TWO are confirmed, FOUR are refuted, and ONE is unverifiable-but-plausible. The plan's grep-based reasoning is unsound in a way that produced one serious error.

REFUTED — Claim 1 (no priority system). This is the big one, and it is the plan's own methodological failure: `grep -rn priority vendor/` returns 0 hits, but vendor/ is upstream Cordis, where priority is not a concept. Checking the location the concept would actually live in finds 161 priority occurrences across 26 non-test source files and four distinct, mature priority systems. The plan inferred absence of a concept from a directory where that concept cannot exist. Exactly the trap the audit doctrine warns about.

REFUTED — Claim 4 (MIT, only obligation is the copyright notice). The root LICENSE is MIT and that part is true, but 39 of 194 THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES rows are non-MIT and 8 more are proprietary. There is BSD-3-Clause in-tree (5 files under native/), MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft, source-disclosure), LGPL-3.0-only, 20 Apache-2.0, ISC, BSD-2, and — most significantly — @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk plus 8 platform payloads whose redistribution rests on an owner-granted identity-scoped authorization that the repo itself says "does not classify their declared terms as permissive." "Only obligation is keeping the copyright notice" is wrong by a wide margin.

REFUTED — Claim 5 (assertVersion is a forward-version gate). It is exact equality (`meta.version !== SESSION_FORMAT_VERSION`) and refuses OLDER versions too — the test at storage-contract.spec.ts:76-85 explicitly asserts that. The forward/backward distinction exists only in the error MESSAGE builder (errors.ts:133-137). The real forward gate is a three-way check elsewhere, in session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:517 (migrate `<`) and :547 (refuse `>`). The plan named the wrong function. Worth flagging: assertVersion has no in-repo caller outside its own re-export and test, which is likely how the misreading happened.

REFUTED — Claim 3's second half ("teardown discipline is a property of its Cordis model"). The Cordis model is upstream's. The discipline is substantially dsh's own patch: divergence #6 is 153 code lines of dsh-authored reentrancy hardening in cordis/src/fiber.ts alone, which is 20.3% of ALL measured code divergence across the 7 measurable packages. Saying dsh's teardown discipline is "a property of its Cordis model" attributes to the vendor what dsh wrote on top of it.

CONFIRMED — Claim 2 (Impl.check used zero times). I pushed past the zero-hit result per doctrine and found the concept does not hide under another name either. The mechanism exists (reflect.ts:124, consumed fiber.ts:601) but across 86 `extends Service` sites and 48 provide() calls there is no check predicate anywhere; the only 3-arg reflect.provide in the entire repo passes a literal `undefined` (session-controller/.../service.ts:279). The nearest neighbours — "park"/"unpark" (gateway/src/client/index.ts:316,363) and assertMethodAvailable (:629) — are Cordis fiber-await semantics and method-presence, not service availability. The plan is right, and the reason is structural: dsh has no notion of "registered but temporarily unavailable."

CONFIRMED — Claim 6 (9 vendored packages, all MIT). All 9 directories present, all 9 have a LICENSE on disk, all 9 read "MIT License" / "Copyright (c) 2021-present Shigma". Matches the notices table.

CLAIM 3's line count — UNVERIFIABLE as stated. 22 divergences is confirmed exactly (numbered 1-22, no gaps). "2,696 lines" I could not reproduce under any accounting: src-only churn vs upstream = 2,080 lines; excluding comments/blanks = 1,001 code lines; adding non-src manifests for 7 packages = 2,741. The figure sits inside my range and is probably a src+manifests accounting, but the plan should not present it as a measured fact without saying which accounting it used. Note also that ~55% of the raw diff is JSDoc, which matters: someone reading a 2,080-line divergence number would badly overstate the behavioural fork.

CLAIM 7 ("no privileged core") — MIXED, and the plan should not have taken it at face value in either direction. For dynamic user packages the privileged core genuinely is withheld: two Proxy facades (836 + 245 lines) whitelist verbs and declared services, deny framework internals and Context-valued returns, and force theme-layer source attribution. But the repo itself refuses the security framing (guard.ts:12-13: "This is API discipline, not a security boundary"). For FIRST-PARTY code there is no privileged core in the enforcement sense at all: packages/client imports from ~30 kernel groups with zero lint or verify gate, and packages/host and packages/client form a bidirectional edge. The mitigating fact — and the real finding — is that 236 of those 260 imports are type-only contract imports against just 24 runtime value imports, and all 24 are shared vocabulary or protocol, not internals. That is a well-executed convention, not an enforced architecture.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- The '2,696 lines' figure itself. I could not reproduce it under any accounting I tried: src-only churn = 2,080; code-only = 1,001; src+manifests for 7 packages = 2,741. Whatever produced 2,696, the plan should not cite it without stating its accounting. My numbers are in the mechanics list.
- cosmokit and schemastery were measured against npm tarballs (cosmokit@1.8.1, schemastery@3.18.0) rather than the git commits pinned in vendor/README.md, because https://github.com/deepseek-harness/cosmokit.git returns 'Repository not found' and the schemastery fork was likewise unreachable. The npm version is version-exact but not commit-exact, so a small drift between the pinned commit and the published 1.8.1/3.18.0 tags would inflate my +190/-28 and +152/-34 numbers. The 7 cordiverse packages were measured against the byte-exact pinned commit 56b3d4f.
- Whether the 2 upstream forks diverge from their npm-published counterparts in ways that matter. Not checkable without repo access.
- The provenance of the owner-granted 'identity-scoped authorization' for @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk redistribution (THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:151). The repo asserts it; I cannot verify the grant's existence, scope, or expiry, and the same sentence flags that version, declared-license, and payload-set changes still require review.
- Whether `@deepseek-ai/libreoffice-kit`'s MPL-2.0 corresponding-source obligation (THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:167-172) is actually discharged in the shipped artifact. The notices point to a decision note (.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-09-14-independent-libreoffice-kit.md) and an external kit repo; I confirmed the claim exists, not that the obligation is met.
- Whether the 24 client->kernel value imports are each individually appropriate. I classified type-only vs value mechanically and read the credentialKey definition, but I did not audit whether, say, importing `dsh-session/surface` predicates into the client is architecturally right or merely convenient.
- Runtime behaviour of the guard facades. I read guard.ts's source and its self-description, but did not attempt to construct a plugin that escapes the facade, so I cannot say whether the whitelist is airtight in practice.
- Whether `verify-client-packages.ts`'s synchronous-graph check actually fails on a violating package. I read the gate's stated purpose and the cycle-detection code path but did not run the gate against a mutated fixture.

It also carries assertOwnerOnly re-checked on every read and before every write (:798, :872) because 'an external editor or a restored backup can loosen the mode after boot'; a versioned document (DOCUMENT_VERSION = 1, :167) with an in-place layout migration that runs under the writer lock and re-reads first (:823-838); a surgical renderRef YAML edit that preserves comments and untouched entries (:443); an enqueue operation queue whose rejection cannot poison the chain (:719-723); and refresh keeping the last good snapshot when the document is unreadable (:846-859).
- The client settings UI was never opened. packages/client/ui-primitives/src/settings-form/form-model.ts (393 lines) is the ONLY consumer of base/user in the repo, and it does field-granular work the report says does not exist: :385-387 computes a PER-FIELD `overridden` bit from Object.hasOwn(userLayer, field); :278 resetField prefills the input with baseValue(field) and stages `clear: true`; :342 emits `unset` path-ops so a reset never restates the section. packages/client/ui-settings/src/client/settings-mirror.ts is the single browser-side describe reader ('the Host stays the fact source: the mirror re-reads on the invalidations its owning plugin subscribes to and folds write answers in through acceptView').

It runs under plugin-manager's withFileLock (index.ts:772) and config-editor locks the same package.json (:81), so the two serialize — but the guard asymmetry on one file is the same duplication shape the report DID flag for writeFileAtomic, one file over.

Evaluation happens only at entry activation via interpolate()' is FALSE. interpolate is called at vendor/loader/src/index.ts:112, inside the entry's config getter, and at packages/settings/settings/src/index.ts:320 on the `base` projection. settings.describe() runs from a microtask after every app-boot/config-reload (settings/src/index.ts:279-287, listener at :234).
