- 'Optimistic-concurrency revision on every form' overstates the guarantee. The revision is always COMPUTED, but enforcement is conditional: `if (expected !== undefined && descriptor.revision !== expected)` (settings/src/index.ts:393), and every wire method documents 'undefined writes unconditionally' (settings-controller/src/index.ts:111, :127, :146). The concurrent-write test also passes because config-editor serializes in-process via hmr.runExclusive + withFileLock and the revision is re-read inside the lock — not because a compare-and-swap rejected the loser.
- 'The only guard is settings' validatePaths ... a field-name check with no expression-content check' undercounts the defense. There are three: cloneJsonShaped (settings/src/index.ts:134-166) rejects non-plain objects, cycles, and non-finite numbers before anything else; validatePaths (:399-408); and resolveConfig(fiber.runtime, resolved) at config-editor/src/index.ts:92 validates the candidate against the plugin's OWN schema before the write. I traced the injection concretely — {list:[{__jsExpr:'...'}]} passes validatePaths (a volatile path hits `continue` at :402, so the whole subtree is unchecked) and skips the visit() tagging (a 2-key map fails node.items.length !== 1 at :118), but is then refused by resolveConfig because the element schema requires `name` (tests/live-config.ts:37). All 69 production .volatile() fields are scalars, enums, or arrays of typed objects; none is z.any/z.record/catchall. The tier is right; the stated reason is not.
- 'settings describe() shows only 3 of the 5 layers' is directionally right but materially understated. `base` is composed from loaded.layers + loaded.patches only (config-editor/src/index.ts:60-68), i.e. layers 1-2. The home patch, the --patch overlays, and the telemetry row appear in `value` (the live composed config) and in NEITHER `base` nor `user`. They are observable only as a refusal.
- Small citation drift, no material effect: lease.ts docstring is 1-28 (report said 1-22) and LEASE_FILENAME is at :37 (report said :38); the session ladder is 4 migration steps across 5 versions (v0-to-v1 .. v3-to-v4 confirmed), not 'a 5-step ladder'.
- CONFIRMED CORRECT, no change: scale numbers are exact. I re-measured all seven scoped directories — 343 .ts files, and every per-package file/line count (session 208/47890, fs 53/14222, attachment 28/4436, storage 25/4132, workspace 8/2926, document 10/1772, settings 11/1413) matches to the line. Total repo .ts excluding node_modules/dist is 4587, so the brief's '13,946 files' is a different denominator than any .ts count. The shadow-refusal line citations are exact: throw at config-editor/src/index.ts:128, first write at :130, rollback at :131-137, and configuration.spec.ts:39-46 asserts byte-identical file plus 'overridden' plus the live consumer still reading 'home'. The two-writeFileAtomic duplication is real and both are used (fs-local/src/index.ts:40,236,280 vs. 12 atomic-write call sites). The storage conformance suite is exactly as described: 5 shared tests at storage/tests/contract.ts:32-101, adopted by both backends with a reopen()-based harness. Session persistence size claims are exact (index.ts 1725, lease.ts 135, win32.ts 208).
- I re-ran the report's key NEGATIVE claim at the alternate locations it did not check: 'provenance' has zero hits across docs/ and website/ for anything config-related (only SessionTitleModelProvenance in a session-title type), and originOf/sourceFile/whichFile/effectiveSource/attributedTo/configSource/layerLabel have zero relevant hits across every .ts in packages/ and apps/ INCLUDING the client packages the report never opened. The report's central negative finding survives.

**TIER CHANGES:**
- '!!js is an inert marker until activation' BORROW -> REFERENCE. The shape (a plain data object everywhere except one sink) is still right, but the safety claim that anchors it is false as implemented: the expression is evaluated on every read of entry.fiber.config, not once at activation. Borrow the marker shape, not the 'inert until activation' framing.
- do_not_copy bullet 3 ('Do not copy the refusal message's information content ... a user hitting it has no next action beyond guessing which of their config files to edit') must be REWRITTEN, not just softened. The repo already contains the good version at packages/credentials/credentials-local/src/index.ts:780-787, which names the shadowing layer and the fix. The accurate finding is 'dsh has two refusal messages — one that names the cause and one that does not — in the same area', which also makes the good one a BORROW the report wrote a DO-NOT-COPY around.
- do_not_copy bullet 2 ('The eval-node write path as structured') stays DO-NOT-COPY but its argument changes from 'no defense, one field-name guard' to 'no content guard in the persistence layer, protected only by three caller-side accidents (cloneJsonShaped, validatePaths, the plugin's own resolveConfig)'. Lower severity than the report states, same conclusion.
- NEW BORROW the report missed entirely: the allowlist wire projection at packages/api/settings-controller/src/index.ts:41-60 — re-project every field by name before crossing the trust boundary precisely because the provider is profile-supplied code.
- NEW BORROW the report missed entirely: credentials-local's assertOwnerOnly mode re-check on every read and before every write (index.ts:798, :872), which catches permission drift introduced by an external editor or a restored backup.
- writeFileAtomic in packages/util/atomic-write stays REFERENCE, but its stakes are higher than the report implies: 3 of its 12 call sites write credential documents (credentials-local:691, :712, :764, :834) at mode 0o600 with dirMode 0o700, so the self-declared 'fsync out of scope' gap (:74, TODO :84) sits on a secrets file, not just on a config file.
- NEW BORROW the report missed: plugin-manager's per-operation lock timeout (index.ts:181 default 120000, :790) is now joined by a second precedent the report never cited — credentials-local threads DOCUMENT_LOCK_WAIT_MS through every write site, reinforcing that lock timeout is a property of the operation.
- The 'session format chain' REFERENCE tier is unchanged, but the citation should say 4 steps (v0->v1 .. v3-to-v4) rather than 'a 5-step ladder'.



## [critique:mcp-lsp-tools]

**MISSED:**
- `ctx.tools.restrict()` — an entire per-agent tool MASKING layer the report never mentions (packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1097-1122). It rejects a context-global restriction because it 'would mask every agent', rejects empty filters, rejects naming the reserved run_code transport, and rejects unknown names while printing the full sorted list of known global tools. Restrictions COMPOUND across the scope chain (index.ts:1194-1200: a name is visible only if `layers.every(layer => layer.admits(name))`). This qualifies the report's own headline invariant: 'the model sees either the full generation or none' is true of REGISTRATION, but a scope can still mask those tools. The report treated the registry as a single flat namespace.
- Cross-session tool isolation in packages/experimental/browser-use-runtime/src/mcp.ts:135-141: a `tools/execute` interceptor that throws '<name>: browser tool belongs to another Session' when a tool definition is invoked from a different agent than the one that opened it. This is a per-tool ownership guard directly relevant to omp's tool-identity concerns, and the report only found the guard.ts tools façade.
- `packages/sandbox/` — 3,608 LOC, 21 source files, 5 subpackages (sandbox, sandbox-local, sandbox-policy, sandbox-windows-acl) — the actual approval/escalation machinery. Never opened despite being the answer to the report's own central question. `approveEscalation` (packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/escalation.ts:171) is documented as 'the ordered fail-closed sequence that resolves a sandbox_permissions request through a user-approval channel BEFORE anything executes'.
- `packages/experimental/` — 28 packages, containing the other two MCP mount paths plus three `*-mcp` packages (browser-use-playwright-mcp, browser-use-chrome-devtools-mcp, computer-use-cua-driver-mcp) and the session-scoped MCP lifecycle. Entirely outside the declared scope with no justification.
- `packages/boot/plugin-manager/` — the model-facing bundle/profile tool. Contains the single most relevant approval precedent in the repo (see tier change), and was never read.
- The shipped model-facing SKILL at packages/preset/agent-preset/skills/cordis-plugin-development/ (SKILL.md + references/ + templates/mcp/cordis.patch.yml), which is written as direct model instruction ('Read templates/mcp/ ... write its files into your bundle directory ... then call mcp__demo__ping ... to verify the connection'). The report audited the code the model runs but not the instructions the model is given.
- A fourth instance of the all-or-nothing rollback idiom at packages/lsp/lsp-stdio/src/index.ts:170-177 (register providers in a loop, `disposers.reverse()` on throw, then a drain-order disposer). Same pattern as MCP's tools.ts:152-160, in a package the report treated as unrelated.

**UNSUPPORTED:**
- CENTRAL CLAIM IS FALSE: 'there is no model-facing verb that mounts [an MCP server]'. `plugin_manager` (packages/boot/plugin-manager/src/tools.ts:20) has an `install_bundle` action (tools.ts:78), and the shipped skill packages/preset/agent-preset/skills/cordis-plugin-development/references/mcp-bundle.md instructs the model to write a bundle whose cordis.patch.yml inserts '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client' with serverName/transport/url, install it via plugin_manager, then 'call mcp__demo__ping ... to verify the connection'. That is a documented, model-facing MCP-server mounting procedure. The skill even teaches the stdio form with arbitrary `command`, `args`, `env`, `cwd`. The whole honest_verdict premise collapses.
- 'MCP server instances can only come from an operator-authored cordis.yml' — FALSE, two other mount paths exist, both programmatic `ctx.plugin(...)` calls, not YAML loads: (1) packages/acp/acp/src/mcp.ts:32 `agentCtx.plugin(McpClient, config)` driven by an ACP `session/new` request's mcpServers array (acp/src/session.ts:135,159), where the external client supplies command/args/env/url/headers; (2) packages/experimental/browser-use-runtime/src/mcp.ts:144 `scope.ctx.plugin(McpClient, ...)` mounted per-Agent-session, lazily, under an exclusive browser reservation. I searched for a fourth (.mcp.json / mcpServers config loader) and found none, so cordis.yml is one of three, not the only one.
- The approval analysis is materially incomplete, which understates its own strongest finding. There IS a second, earlier gate the report never found: plugin_manager calls `approveEscalation({ requestedMode: 'danger-full-access', ... })` with justification 'Profile changes persist across sessions; installed Host code runs outside the workspace sandbox' (tools.ts:38-45). `approveEscalation` gates exactly five tool families repo-wide (plugin-manager, core/tools/ptc, tool-fs, tool-bash, tool-pwsh) — and cordis-host-runner is NOT among them (0 hits for approveEscalation/sandboxPolicy/user-approval in its src). So the asymmetry is real and sharper than reported, but the report described the wrong gate as the only one.
- Severity inversion on the DO-NOT-COPY: the skill's documented MCP path is a CONFIG-ONLY bundle with 'no Host/Client entry files', which lands exactly on the ungated `clientCode === undefined` branch (index.ts:275). So the shipped model-facing MCP-mounting workflow is the one that skips the cordis approval gate — reaching it only via the plugin_manager escalation. The report reached 'ungated host half is bad' without finding that the flagship documented workflow is the ungated one.
- 'packages/extensions: 12,364 of that is GENERATED' — measured 8,228 + 4,133 = 12,361. Trivial, but it is the one number in an otherwise exactly-correct set that does not reproduce.
- Not wrong, but asserted without the check that would have caught the above: the report never opened packages/sandbox/, packages/boot/, packages/experimental/, or the preset skills, yet declared a capability absent. Rule 3 of its own brief was applied to the wrong repo region.

**TIER CHANGES:**
- 'Approval gate that covers only the browser half' stays DO-NOT-COPY but must be REWRITTEN. The correct statement is that dsh has TWO independent gates and neither is sufficient on its own: the bundle-install route is gated by a sandbox-escalation approval (plugin_manager/tools.ts:38-45) while the cordis_run route has none (cordis-host-runner has zero sandbox imports). For omp the borrowable object is that escalation pattern — an approval whose justification string names the concrete capability being granted ('installed Host code runs outside the workspace sandbox'), rather than a generic approve/deny. The report missed the one approval precedent in the repo that is actually doing the security work.
- NEW finding the report should have had, and it is BORROW-grade: the plugin_manager escalation contract (packages/boot/plugin-manager/src/tools.ts:38-45) plus its description's own threat model ('Package installation can execute allowed build scripts', 'Version exemptions risk crashes and data loss: warn the user and obtain explicit permission for the exact plugin and runtime versions'). The `acceptRisk` parameter requiring a prior explicit warning for a specific version pair is a stronger pattern than anything the report credited from guard.ts.
- NEW BORROW finding: `ctx.tools.restrict()` per-agent masking with compounding restrictions and four distinct fail-loud guards (core/tools/src/index.ts:1097-1122, 1194-1200). Directly portable to omp, and it is the piece that makes the MCP generation-swap invariant actually hold end to end rather than only at the registration layer.
- 'Two-phase tool generation swap with all-or-nothing rollback' remains BORROW and remains correct, but loses its distinctiveness: packages/lsp/lsp-stdio/src/index.ts:170-177 has the same dispose-in-reverse rollback idiom. It is a house pattern, not a local MCP invention — omp should adopt it as a convention, not as a borrowed trick.
- 'Server namespace reservation as a load-time effect' remains BORROW but is overstated as a single mechanism: packages/acp/acp/src/mcp.ts:9 and :40-41 independently re-declare the same /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,32}$/ pattern and run their own duplicate-normalized-name check. The WeakMap is belt, the ACP check is braces.
- The 'model-authored host code is trusted by default' weakness should be promoted from a weakness to the report's top finding, and restated around the config-only-bundle path rather than the cordis_run path.



## [critique:client-ui-interaction]

**MISSED:**
- `.agents/notes/` — a first-class, git-tracked decision corpus (3,675 files; 1,214 English Agent Notes = 518 implemented / 642 archived / 40 proposed / 14 rejected) that the audit never once mentions. The evidence base was code-only. The repo documents its own architecture decisions at a higher level than the code, and the report's biggest claims live there.
- THE TUI EXISTED AND WAS DELETED 8 WEEKS BEFORE HEAD. `.agents/notes/archived/simplification/2026-08-04-remove-tui-package.md` is a full decision record: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tui` / `packages/ui/tui` (terminal renderer, interactive command + question adapters, extension overlays, snapshot fixtures, a patched `pi-tui` dependency) was deleted 2026-08-04, note archived 2026-09-04, HEAD is 2026-09-27. Reason on record: the implicit `dsh` terminal app was removed first, leaving the package with no shipped composition and only the SDK project generator as a consumer. The report's honest_verdict opens 'There is no TUI' with no mention that one shipped and was deliberately killed.
- 39 archived TUI design notes (1,513 lines of English prose) the report never read — the most portable thing in this repo for omp, which HAS packages/tui. Contents include: `paletteSpec(scheme)` as one SGR table with branded color/attribute types and no component emitting its own escapes; tool card = one colored `Tool / <name>` status header over one dim body; `Ctrl+O` tri-state fold (collapsed -> expanded -> hidden) where hidden also drops card-owned leading gaps; cross-workspace resume with a Tab scope toggle that refuses records without a cwd; and an explicit rule that a future XML fallback must use a real parser, not regex.
- The remove-tui note states a reusable bar: 'Reintroducing a terminal frontend requires a named product or deployment, an explicit package boundary, a concrete interaction provider, and assembled lifecycle and transcript acceptance for that frontend.' Nobody quoted this.
- `packages/experimental/` — 459 files / 75,448 lines across 22 sub-packages, absent from the scale section. Contains directly in-scope client UI: `client-ui-agent-team` (9 files / 1,219 lines) and `client-ui-voice-input` (21 / 1,989). The report's 'Total in-scope: ~418K TS lines' is understated by ~75K (~18%) if experimental is in scope, and the scope boundary was never stated either way.
- `apps/desktop/src/tray.ts` and `background-notice.ts` — never opened, and they are the most likely attention channels on Windows. Reading them CONFIRMS the report's gap rather than refuting it, and sharpens it: the tray is the always-present surface (comment at tray.ts:1) but its tooltip is a fixed `messages.aboutProduct` with no per-session or per-job state (tray.ts:30-31), and `background-notice.ts` is a one-shot Windows confirm-before-hiding dialog, not attention. A session count in that existing tray tooltip was the natural channel and is absent.
- `packages/client/ui-settings-account/src/client/AccountNotice.tsx:83-101` — a BORROW the report missed and, ironically, one its own falsified grep was looking for. It gates an account notice on `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`, defers the paint, and re-attempts on every `visibilitychange`, so a notice the user was not looking at is not marked seen. That is visibility-gated attention deferral, already shipped.
- The report never listed `apps/desktop/src`, so its attention sweep never covered the main-process surface where Electron attention lives. I swept it: `setAppBadge`/`navigator.setAppBadge`/`setBadge(` = 0 hits repo-wide; `showNotification` (web push) = 0; `speechSynthesis`/`new Audio(`/`navigator.vibrate` = 0 outside voice-input's own `AudioContext`; tray tooltip static. The DO-NOT-COPY verdict holds — it just was not earned.

**UNSUPPORTED:**
- FALSIFIED — 'Verified negative: rg "document.hidden|visibilitychange|hasFocus" packages/client --glob "src/**" = 0 hits.' The glob `src/**` can never match `packages/client/**/src/**` when rg is rooted at `packages/client`, so it returned 0 by construction, not by absence. Correct glob `-g '**/src/**'` returns 3 real hits: `ui-directory-picker-browse/src/client/DirectoryBrowser.tsx:806` (`if (!document.hasFocus()) return`) and `ui-settings-account/src/client/AccountNotice.tsx:87,91,97,99` (`document.visibilityState === 'hidden'` plus a `visibilitychange` listener). This is exactly the report's own hard rule 3, and it takes down weakness #2 ('No window/tab visibility signal in the client').
- FALSIFIED — 'Reverse: rg "from \"@deepseek-ai/dsh-client" packages/api --glob "src/**/*.ts" = 0 hits' and the do_not_copy line 'I verified zero value imports from packages/api/**/src'. Same broken-glob bug. Correct glob returns 30 hits, ~14 of them genuine VALUE imports: `packages/api/remotes/src/client/index.ts:4,16,21` (product-analytics/remote, ui-plugin-manager/remote, file-upload/remote) and `notifySubscribers`/`createSnapshotStore`/`ObservableSnapshot` from `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-store` at `api/workspace-controller/src/client/model.ts:3`, `api/job-controller/src/client/model.ts:9`, `api/session-controller/src/client/contract/events.ts:2`, `.../sessions/notifier.ts:1`, `.../sessions/projection-store.ts:17`, `.../sessions/service.ts:11`, `api/terminal-controller/src/client/{index,model}.ts`.
- MISLEADING — the report's own interpretation of that reverse direction survives, but its stated verification does not. I confirmed the mitigation independently: `packages/api/job-controller/package.json` keeps client packages in `devDependencies` + `dsh.client.inject`, and `dependencies` holds only `dsh-typert-protocol`/`schemastery`/`zod`. All 30 imports sit under `src/client/`. So the finding should read 'the host half is one-way; each API package ships a browser-half facade that imports client runtime through the client module table', not 'zero imports'.
- FALSIFIED — 'Toasts are error-only (ui-conversation/src/client/skeleton/InputBar.tsx:92).' `packages/client/ui-workspace/src/client/session-actions/RowActionToast.tsx:34` renders `tone="success"` with undo actions for `archived` / `stoppedAndArchived`; `packages/client/ui-schedule/src/client/DeleteToast.tsx:21` types outcomes `'deleted' | 'deleteFailed'`. A whole toast family exists (DeleteToast, RowActionToast, open-failure-toast, CatalogFeedback) and the report cited one file.
- OVERSTATED — '`new Notification` appears EXACTLY ONCE repo-wide.' There are 2 raw matches; the second (`packages/sdk/client/src/client.ts:354`, `new NotificationSubscriptionImpl`) is a substring artifact. The substance (only real DOM notification is the update path) holds, but 'EXACTLY ONCE' is stated as a verified fact without the artifact excluded.
- UNDERSTATED — '`from "@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent"` = 2 sites, both `import type`.' 16 sites reference dsh-agent or dsh-agent-preset-registry in client src: 13 `import type` (mostly `/types`), 3 VALUE imports of the allow-listed `@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset-registry/display` (`ui-agent-preset/src/client/locales.ts:114`, `ui-settings-plugin-inventory/src/client/index.ts:12`). The 'zero value imports of the kernel' conclusion survives — but only because `/display` sits in INLINE_SAFE, i.e. the narrower count hid the very escape hatch the report then praised.
- WRONG NUMBERS — snapshot per-area counts. Report: session 120, web 55, sdk 25, acp 10 (summing to 210, while claiming 206 total). Measured: `find snapshots/<area> -name snapshot.yml` gives session 118, web 55, sdk 24, acp 9 = 206. The area root was counted as a scenario. Totals 206 / 338 goldens / 440 jsonl are correct.
- WRONG — '759 *.spec.ts(x) files + 156 *.e2e.ts in apps/web alone.' Repo-wide spec count is 1,865. The 156 e2e is apps/web-only, the 759 is not; stated adjacently they read as the same scope.

Those four stand.

**TIER CHANGES:**
- 'No TUI exists' REFERENCE/'definitive' -> must be rewritten and promoted in importance. The five negative checks are all valid CODE checks and the conclusion (no TUI code at HEAD) is true, but the framing is misleading: a TUI shipped and was deliberately deleted ~8 weeks earlier, with the full rationale in-repo. For omp — which has packages/tui — the 39-note archived TUI design corpus and the remove-tui decision record are the highest-value thing in this repo, and the report missed all of it. All are confined to `src/client/` and resolved through the client module table with client packages in devDependencies — so the underlying pattern is still BORROW, arguably better than a hard one-way rule, but 'zero value imports' and 'I verified' must both go.
- 'Attention is passive badge-only' DO-NOT-COPY -> verdict CONFIRMED and independently strengthened (0 hits for setAppBadge/showNotification/speechSynthesis/new Audio(/navigator.vibrate; static tray tooltip; background-notice is a one-shot hide-confirm). Two edits: strike 'Toasts are error-only' (RowActionToast.tsx:34 is `tone="success"` with undo), and drop weakness #2 as written — a visibility signal EXISTS and is used (AccountNotice.tsx:87-101). Add AccountNotice's defer-until-visible pattern to BORROW.
- New DO-NOT-COPY the report missed: a Windows system tray that is present for the entire run (tray.ts:1, :22) carrying a static product-name tooltip and no per-session state (tray.ts:30-31). The cheapest possible attention channel was already built and left unused — a concrete missed opportunity, not a stylistic absence.
- packages/experimental (459 files / 75,448 lines, incl. client-ui-agent-team and client-ui-voice-input) must be added to scope or explicitly excluded. At 18% of the reported 418K total, omitting it silently is the difference between 'comprehensive for packages/client' and a scoped claim.
- Two independent 'verified negative' greps (hasFocus/visibilitychange, and api->client imports) share one root cause: rg globs written as `src/**` against a search path already rooted above `src`. Any other '= 0 hits' in the report using that glob shape should be re-run before being trusted.

Direction is otherwise 39+ client packages -> host and 0 host -> client. The conclusion inverts the actual shape.

'This is API discipline, not a security boundary: a dynamic package's code is as trusted as the host process that accepted its definition' is at packages/extensions/cordis-client-runner/src/client/guard.ts:12 — the CLIENT guard. The mechanics entry and the verdict both cite it as 'guard.ts:12-13' adjacent to packages/extensions/cordis-host-runner/src/guard.ts:718/:808/:816 citations; the host guard's :12-13 is inside its @module JSDoc block. The hijacked impl occupies a real store slot under a fresh isolation symbol, and its disposer calls notify(['events']) (reflect.ts:299-304), which runs _checkImpl + _refresh() on every fiber that injects events. It is a read no-op with a lifecycle side effect, which is worse than the report says, not better.

This also weakens the report's central 'dsh has a trust-tier boundary' thesis, which rests on this tier.

Two facts the report did not check: (a) the Context interface marks `root` `@experimental` (vendor/cordis/src/context.ts:20); (b) the one fenced tier already withholds it by name — packages/extensions/cordis-host-runner/src/guard.ts:729-733 denyRead: 'Framework internals (root, fiber, registry, extend, plugin, …) are withheld by design', over a Proxy({}) whose set trap rejects every write (:769-771). So the escape is real for in-tree plugins (which already have full ctx) and already closed for the tier the report calls the boundary. The proposed remedy (make root non-writable / refuse effect() on a context you do not own) is still right; the honest_verdict's 'the kernel does not stop you stepping outside your own scope' is too strong.
- Silent core-service hijack: stays DO-NOT-COPY, but the stated failure mode is wrong in the direction that matters. But it is not inert: the impl occupies a store slot under a fresh isolation symbol and its disposer runs notify(['events']) -> _checkImpl + _refresh() on every fiber injecting events (reflect.ts:299-304, :594-612). Read no-op, lifecycle side effect.

The named contracts (dependency-scoped non-replacement, replacement-import failure keeps the old plugin, volatile references replaced after in-place config update, self-disposal without deadlock) are the right ones, and fork entries #9/#19 hang off them. It should not sit below the config-patch item, which the report rates REFERENCE with no execution at all.
- NEW BORROW the report missed: the symbols.shadow / noShadow caller-scope rebinding (vendor/cordis/src/utils.ts:150-215; noShadow registered at reflect.ts:216, registry.ts:202, events.ts:137, logger.ts:206, loader/src/index.ts:99). A service method invoked through a child context resolves against that child — the kernel's answer to 'how do you scope a shared singleton per caller', and the precondition for the sandbox facade being able to Proxy a live service at all. Ranks above the config-patch item.
- NEW BORROW the report missed: deferred activation and deferred *call* off one primitive — `ctx.inject(deps, callback)` (vendor/cordis/src/registry.ts:300-302) and the method-level `@Inject()` decorator (registry.ts:47-56), which queues an initializer that awaits the declared services before invoking. The report described activation as epoch-driven only, which is half the mechanism.

With zero numeric priority and no load order, a live effect/dependency dump is the only way to debug the self-solving tree — the missing half of the 'no explicit ordering lever' weakness.
- NEW BORROW the report missed: packages/preset/agent-preset/skills/cordis-plugin-development/ (12 files, 166 lines of prose + two complete working plugin templates). A shipped, LLM-executable plugin-authoring contract is a stronger artifact for 'everything is a plugin' than any of the vendor mechanics, and it is the one place the framework states its own rules in the form a plugin author will actually follow.



## [omo:omo-license-hygiene]

**VERDICT:** The prior audit's "MESSY" label was directionally right but imprecise in both directions, and the task's own framing was wrong on two counts. Correcting both matters for triage.

The real finding: this is not untidiness, it is a live contradiction between LICENSE.md and npm metadata. The root is SUL-1.0 (non-commercial, internal-use only, and explicitly forbids altering or obscuring the licensor's notices). Yet 24 published npm packages — 12 platforms x 2 name families — declare MIT. I verified this against the live registry, not just in-tree: oh-my-opencode-linux-x64@5.0.1 -> license=MIT, oh-my-openagent-linux-x64@5.0.1 -> license=MIT, against oh-my-opencode@5.0.1 -> license=SUL-1.0. The mechanism is mechanical: publish-platform.yml:641-650 republishes each arch package under a second name using a jq filter that rewrites .name and .description but not .license, propagating the stale field 24 times with no review step.

But the task's hypothesis that these were "prebuilt binaries of the SUL project relabelled MIT" is wrong, and the correction changes the severity. script/build-binaries.ts:168-176 writes a ~160-line Node launcher stub, not a compiled payload. It requires OMO_WRAPPER_PACKAGE_ROOT and execs dist/cli/index.js from the SUL root package. The SUL code never enters these tarballs. So the exposure is a licensing metadata defect on a small first-party shim — not redistribution of SUL binaries under a false MIT. Anyone acting on the original premise would over-escalate badly; anyone dismissing the finding on those grounds would ship an incorrect license. Both errors are avoidable by reading build-binaries.ts, which takes two minutes.

The second stated hypothesis — that insane-search might be non-commercial or source-available — is also wrong. It is MIT upstream (GitHub API verified). The actual defect is that its 28 files / 4448 lines ship with no reproduced MIT notice; the repo's own ATTRIBUTION.md:24-26 admits this outright. Credit where due: that disclosure is honest and is the kind of thing most audits never surface. It is still a gap, and the fix is to paste upstream's license text, which they evidently could have done.

The clean part, stated plainly because the task's framing obscured it: there is zero AGPL, zero non-commercial, zero source-available third-party code. Zero MuPDF hits repo-wide. Every grep hit for those terms is the repo's own SUL text, a CLA rule, unrelated prose, a React hook name, or a footer string. All four submodules are permissive (MIT x3, Apache-2.0 x1), and all 16 production dependencies are enumerated in the notices file — which even catches that posthog-node declares MIT in metadata while shipping Apache-2.0 text. That is real diligence.

The "43 packages declare nothing" figure is the most misleading number in the prior audit. I measured it: 42 of the 43 are private:true and never published. Exactly one public package is affected — omo-ai, which is on the registry right now with license=NONE. That is simultaneously the smallest count and the sharpest consequence, since an undeclared license defaults to all-rights-reserved. One line to fix.

Net: the repo's license hygiene is worse in one specific, serious, live way (24 packages) and dramatically better in the way the framing suggested it was bad (43 undeclared). Two DO-NOT-COPY items are worth omp actively avoiding — relabeling sub-packages away from a source-available root, and a compliance gate whose coverage is a hand-maintained subset of the shipped manifest, which passes green while never examining the 1.1 MB of vendored third-party content that actually ships. The genuinely good parts — the executable notice gate, the per-component upstream pinning, and the refusal to infer a license from a missing file — are worth taking, provided the gate's path list is derived from files[] rather than hand-written.

**UNVERIFIED:**
- Whether the vendored insane-search snapshot's specific pre-0.7.0 baseline (commit a4e4ed797, 2026-06-21) was MIT-licensed at that date. I verified only that insane-search is MIT at its current HEAD via the GitHub API. The task flagged insane-search as a possible non-commercial/source-available component; I found no evidence for that, but I did not check the upstream repository's license history or any earlier commit.
- Transitive dependency licenses. node_modules is absent in this checkout, so I could not audit the full dependency graph. THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md's 16 direct production dependencies are all covered and all permissively licensed per the file's own claims, but those claims are the repo's, and I could not independently confirm any of them against installed packages.
- The license of @code-yeongyu/senpi, the external npm package that publish-platform.yml:358,744 pins the built senpi-desktop-engine artifact against. It is out of tree. If that package ships the MIT-labeled Rust binary, the Cargo.toml inconsistency becomes live; I could not check it.
- License history. The checkout is shallow (git log shows only bc67110, the merge commit), so I could not determine when any license field changed, whether the arch packages were ever SUL, or whether Cargo.toml was ever consistent with the root. Every git log I ran returned only the single HEAD commit.
- Whether the other 10 arch packages (beyond linux-x64 and the two oh-my-openagent ones I spot-checked) carry identical license metadata. I confirmed all 12 in-tree package.json files declare MIT with files:["bin"] and the build script treats them uniformly, and I registry-verified 3 of 24 published packages. I did not registry-verify all 24.
- Whether the ~160-line launcher stub in each arch package would be considered covered by SUL or separable from it. That is a legal determination, not a code fact. I report only that the stub's source lives in the SUL-licensed repository and that SUL-1.0 forbids altering or obscuring the licensor's notices.
- Whether the insane-search engine's 4448 lines still meaningfully resemble the MIT upstream, which would affect how much notice is owed. ATTRIBUTION.md documents substantial modification (de-personalization, surrogate retrieval stage, module split, added test suite) in both directions from the baseline.



## [omo:omo-ideas]

**VERDICT:** The prior audit is roughly right but mislabels two of its seven and misses the single sharpest piece of evidence against their model layer. VERDICT BY CLAIM: (1) width allocation — CONFIRMED, the best-verified borrow, and the DAG row independently re-derives the same budget which shows the pattern is deliberate rather than accidental; (2) token bag — MISLABELED and only half real. The stats are a bag, but the ORDER is a hardcoded array literal in each renderer, and status-row-format.ts:102-104 claims a no-drift guarantee that the code does not provide. Present, not good; REFERENCE only; (3) motion — the LABEL is wrong, the IDEA is right and stronger than described. There is no scale. What exists is a three-part claim/no-claim/freeze contract, and it is well tested. BORROW the contract, not this repo's task widget, which violates the contract in the same string it renders; (4) negative contracts — CONFIRMED and strong, including the high-value absence-vs-zero pair; (5) delivery ack boundary — CONFIRMED but the framing "instead of a toast queue" is false, the toast manager is still there serving a different consumer. reason: REFUTATION ATTEMPTED ON LEGAL/PROVENANCE GROUNDS AND FAILED. The claim survives both the factual check and the provenance check. It is not idea-only — the code is legally clean to copy into an MIT-licensed public project.

1) The cited lines are exact, not approximate. vendor/cordis/src/fiber.ts:418-422 reads: 418 `effect(execute: () => Effect, label = 'anonymous'): any {` / 419 `this.assertActive()` / 420 `if (this.state === FiberState.UNLOADING) {` / 421 `throw new CordisError('INACTIVE_EFFECT')` / 422 `}`. `INACTIVE_EFFECT` is a genuinely registered machine code (CordisError.Code, fiber.ts:170-173, message 'cannot create effect on inactive context'), and `FiberState.UNLOADING` is a real enum member (fiber.ts:147-154). The "VERIFIED: throws CordisError INACTIVE_EFFECT" annotation is correct.

2) The guard is a real dsh-authored modification, not upstream code and not a README-only claim. I fetched upstream cordis master directly (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cordiverse/cordis/master/packages/core/src/fiber.ts, 496 lines): its `effect()` has `this.assertActive()` and NO UNLOADING check. The error code, `assertActive()`, and the `UNLOADING` enum member all exist upstream; the 3-line state guard is DeepSeek's delta. That independently corroborates vendor/README.md item #6 rather than taking the vendor README's word for it (THEIR CLAIM, UNVERIFIED -> now verified against upstream).

3) The mechanism is a genuine leak-closer, not a decorative guard. `assertActive()` (fiber.ts:351-354) only tests `uid !== null`. `_unload()` (fiber.ts:673) opens with `this._disposables.clear()`, but a fiber enters `FiberState.UNLOADING` (fiber.ts:284, 636, 670) while `this.uid = null` is only set later, inside the disposer body (fiber.ts:268). So a real window exists where state === UNLOADING and uid !== null: a cleanup-time `ctx.effect(...)` would be accepted into a snapshot `_unload` had already cleared, and the disposer would never run. The guard closes exactly that window, which is what makes "registrations are effects that unwind" true rather than aspirational. Claim's rationale is technically correct.

4) License chain is MIT end to end, with no CLA, no copyleft, and no non-commercial rider. Base: vendor/cordis/LICENSE = "MIT License, Copyright (c) 2021-present Shigma"; upstream LICENSE fetched live says the identical thing, so the base is genuinely MIT. Delta: the dsh root LICENSE is "MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 DeepSeek" and `git remote -v` shows the public https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git, so DeepSeek's modification is itself MIT. All 9 vendored packages carry a preserved LICENSE file AND `"license": "MIT"` in package.json AND an MIT row in the generated THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md table. `ls | grep -i cla` returns only CLAUDE.md (agent instructions, not a contributor agreement) — there is no CLA in dsh. MIT expressly permits copy, modify, sublicense and redistribute, so the composed file is freely copyable; the only obligation is retaining the copyright notice, and 5 lines is far below "substantial portions" anyway.

5) One residual constraint, and it is a naming constraint, not a code constraint: MIT conveys no trademark rights. A copier may not brand the result "Cordis" or imply endorsement by Shigma/cordiverse. That does not block taking the code.

6) Integration note for the SUL-1.0 target (oh-my-openagent), not a defect in the claim: omo's own LICENSE.md carves out "All third party components incorporated ... are licensed under the original license provided by the owner," so MIT code may live in omo as an attributed third-party file. But MIT is not sublicensable, so the guard cannot be folded into omo's SUL-licensed body — it must stay a separately attributed file carrying the Shigma/DeepSeek notice. Going the other direction (MIT-licensed public project) is unconditionally clean.

## [v1]

reason: The three line citations are all ACCURATE and the refusals genuinely fire — I executed them against the real vendored code, not just read it. But the claim's load-bearing normative sentence ("a DI container where overwriting someone else's service is a typed error") is factually wrong, and "hard boundary" is overstated on two counts.

1. "TYPED ERROR" IS FALSE. All three refusals throw a plain `Error`. Executed: constructor `Error`, `.name === "Error"`, `.code === undefined`, no subclass, no discriminant — a caller cannot branch on it and must string-match the message. The irony is that the vendored cordis *ships the machinery and does not use it*: `CordisError` (vendor/cordis/src/fiber.ts:157-166) exists precisely to give "a stable machine-readable code", but its `Code` enum has exactly ONE member (`INACTIVE_EFFECT`, fiber.ts:164) and none of the three ownership violations use it. So the specific idiom the claim tells the reader to copy is absent from the very lines it cites. The contrast is not pedantic: the consumer repo has 155 `class …Error extends` sites (e.g. `IsolationExistsError`, `HashlineMismatchError`) — "typed error" is the house idiom there, and cordis is the outlier.

2. THE BOUNDARY IS SCOPE-LOCAL, NOT GLOBAL. `Context.isolate(name, label?)` (vendor/cordis/src/context.ts:121-125) mints a fresh `Symbol(name)` per scope, so `key` differs, so the `this.store[key]` slot at reflect.ts:289 is empty. Executed: a third fiber providing the SAME name `svc` under `isolate('svc')` did NOT throw, and the two implementations coexist — root still resolved `{"owner":"A2"}` while the isolated ctx resolved `{"owner":"C"}`. That is last-write-wins shadowing, by design. "Service-ownership as a hard boundary" holds only within one isolation scope.

3. "DISCIPLINE" IS UNENFORCED BY ANY TEST. Zero behavioral coverage: no `.spec.ts` asserts the double-provide or cross-fiber-mutation refusals (grep for `has been registered at` / `in multiple fibers` across all specs → 0). `scripts/cordis-core-api.spec.ts` (49 lines) only checks doc generation. Deleting the throw at reflect.ts:289-291 would leave the full suite green. An invariant nothing tests is a convention, not a discipline.

TWO SUB-FINDINGS THAT CUT THE OTHER WAY (credit where the claim is stronger than I expected): (a) The cross-fiber ownership check is NOT bypassable — I tried routing the write through the public `internal/set` waterfall with a listener returning a substitute value, and the assignment still threw, because the ownership check lives in the waterfall's finalizer which always runs. So peers can *observe* a write attempt but cannot *defeat* it. (b) The container is genuinely load-bearing: 198 files, 646 `ctx.provide(` call sites — this is real architecture, not a demo.

Also note: the earlier `grep -l` for those error strings across 15 files is a false positive — 14 of 15 hits are coincidental English prose ("without provider credential selection", "archives freely without a write"). Only vendor/cordis/src/reflect.ts contains real throw sites.

TIER: BORROW the *intent* — ownership-as-refusal rather than last-write-wins is the right instinct, and the incumbent-fiber-naming message is a genuinely good diagnostic. DO-NOT-COPY as stated: there is no typed error to copy, and "plugins are peers" does not follow, since `isolate()` is a first-class, documented, in-scope escape hatch that makes peers able to shadow each other silently. REFERENCE only: the `CordisError` code pattern is the one piece genuinely worth lifting into omp.

## [v1]

reason: The citation is exact and the core mechanism is real, but three of the claim's four assertions are inaccurate as stated, and the gap is not academic.

1) "a collision at the exact same cell AND the exact same priority throws" — true for single/keyed/list, FALSE for `chain`. `case 'chain':` (index.ts:1237-1239) has no occupancy check at all; `entriesOfSlot` returns chain entries raw because "shadowing does not apply" (index.ts:1345-1346). I registered 3 chain entries at the same priority with the same `select` — none threw (ledger length 3, winners 3). So the discipline covers 3 of 4 slot kinds, and the kind it excludes is the only one production actually uses `priority` on (see 4).

2) "naming the occupant and the registrant" — overstated twice. `registrant` is OPTIONAL (`registrant?: string`, index.ts:833). With an occupant that supplies none, the message drops it entirely: `single slot "s" already has a registration at priority 0 — register at a different priority to shadow it (lowest renders)`. The cited file — the bare core — guarantees nothing; registrant only appears in production because a DIFFERENT package injects a fallback (`ui-renderer/src/client/registry.ts:481`: `options.registrant ?? fiber?.name`). The code's own doc (index.ts:1139) claims only "throws naming the occupant" — it never claims the registrant. And it names the CELL (slot + key/id), not the occupant: the occupant is identified only by that optional free-text label; the component identity is never named, and a `single` slot has no distinguishing handle beyond the priority.

3) "loud about genuine ambiguity" — not always. It throws when there is NO live ambiguity: after `reportEntryError(..., {abdicate: true})` the crashed entry is skipped by `entriesOfSlot` (cell projects empty) but stays in `rec.entries`, and the collision check searches `rec.entries` unfiltered (1217/1223/1231) — re-registering the visibly-empty cell still throws, naming a dead occupant. Doc 1534-1535 confirms "The registration itself stays on the ledger either way." Conversely the guard is trivially bypassed: the check is strict `===` on the number, so `priority: 0.5` vs `priority: 0` never collide. It is a default-clash tripwire (0 vs 0), not a general ambiguity detector — and the 0-vs-0 case is the one where loudness is least warranted, since two plugins may both legitimately want the default.

4) SCOPE — the "open to extension" half is unexercised. Repo-wide grep for a numeric `priority:` on register options yields exactly two production sites, `ui-subagent/src/client/index.ts:99` (priority: -10) and `ui-approval/src/client/index.ts:93` (priority: 1) — and BOTH target `conversation.composer`, which is `kind: 'chain'` (`slot-catalog.ts:362-363`), i.e. chain election order, not cell shadowing. Zero production registrations use cell-shadowing priority on a single/keyed/list slot. `entriesOfSlot`, the shadowing winner projection, has zero test coverage (no hits in `tests/`). Only the throw side is covered: `core.client.spec.ts:58-62, 196-204`.

Accurate, uncorrupted parts: the line range 1211-1240 is exactly the described code; shadowing is genuinely allowed (different priority on the same cell is accepted, lower number wins, both stay on the ledger); default-0 and explicit-0 correctly collide; and the remedy text is present in all three throws via `occupantHint` (1213-1214) — though "a different priority" underspecifies it, since shadowing requires a LOWER number (probe 3b: pMinus1 beats p0 beats p9).

Verdict: overstated on registrant-naming and on "genuine ambiguity", and narrow on scope — it holds for 3 of 4 slot kinds, with the excluded kind being the only one exercised in production.

TIER: BORROW the cell+priority model and the remedy-in-the-message habit. DO-NOT-COPY (a) the unfiltered `rec.entries` occupancy scan — filter abdicated entries or a crashed plugin permanently bricks its cell; (b) strict numeric `===` as the only conflict key, which a fractional priority walks around. Worth noting for omo: omp's own catalog KDL rule tree already encodes the stronger version of this idea — `AmbiguousOverlapError` at resolve time, with equal-rank overlaps requiring an explicit `priority=` in KDL (see AGENTS.md "Model/Provider Policy Lives in KDL"). That is a compile-time collision check with a remedy, strictly louder than this runtime one.

reason: Split verdict, but the claim as a whole is refuted on its load-bearing framing.

CONFIRMED BY EXECUTION (I ran it, not just read it): the mechanical description is accurate and the line ranges are correct. Copied `vendor/` to a scratch dir, ran the real vendored source under bun 1.4.2. `fiber.ts:611-622` `_refresh()` builds the epoch as `epoch += ':' + impl.fiber.uid` over `Object.keys(this.inject)`, and sets `INACTIVE` if any dep is missing. Measured epoch `":1"` for one dep, `":1:2"` for two deps. Provider `dispose()` drove the consumer ACTIVE(2) -> PENDING(0) with `epoch === "__INACTIVE__"` and `store === undefined`; re-provision drove it back to ACTIVE(2) with the consumer body re-running (bodyRuns 1 -> 2) and picking up the new impl value. So "VERIFIED BY EXECUTION" is honest, and the claim is not overstated on the mechanism itself.

REFUTED — the attribution and the recommendation. "The best idea in the repo and the hardest to build from scratch" credits deepseek-harness for a design it vendored verbatim from a third-party MIT framework. `vendor/cordis` is a source-vendored copy of upstream Cordis (the Koishi-lineage framework by Shigma), pinned in `vendor/README.md`'s manifest table to `cordiverse/cordis` `packages/core` commit `56b3d4f...`, version 4.0.0-rc.7; `vendor/cordis/LICENSE` is MIT, "Copyright (c) 2021-present Shigma". I fetched that exact upstream commit and diffed the cited ranges: lines 611-639 (`_refresh` + `_setEpoch`) — the epoch construction and the whole INACTIVE-transition machinery the claim describes — are BYTE-IDENTICAL to upstream (diff exit 0). Lines 646-673 (`_reload`) differ by exactly one local hunk, the stale-epoch checkpoint guard, and the repo's own local-modification log entry #6 describes precisely that (not the feature). Entry #15 further concedes part of even the local delta is "ports cordiverse/cordis#41".

This inverts the actionable advice. If a BORROW item is upstream MIT code, the correct move is to depend on or copy `cordis`, not to "build it from scratch" — the claim as phrased would send omp into a from-scratch reimplementation of a solved problem, and it credits dsh for third-party architecture. dsh does not own a fiber/DI implementation: `packages/extensions/tool-cordis/src/` is a 231-line *consumer* of the vendored framework, and dsh's own contribution is narrow (JSDoc enrichment, disposal hardening, Node/Windows compat).

One secondary gap: the claim says the epoch is "the concatenated uid" but omits that a single missing dep collapses the whole epoch to INACTIVE (`fiber.ts:616-619`) — that gate is the actual load-bearing part, and it is upstream too.

reason: REFUTED ON PORTABILITY. The claim is faithful to dsh, but it does not survive the trip to omp, and the instruction "default to refuted unless the port is clearly net-positive" resolves against it on three independent grounds.

(1) THE THROW IS A REGRESSION IN omp, NOT AN IMPROVEMENT. This is the decisive finding. dsh's throw is safe because ui-slots registration is a scoped composition step, not a "load this whole module" step. omp's equivalent cell is written during the extension factory, and omp's factory error handler DISCARDS THE ENTIRE EXTENSION on any throw: extensibility/extensions/loader.ts:455-458 returns `{ extension: null, error: "Failed to load extension: <msg>" }`. So a naive port of "throw on exact cell collision" into setWidget/setStatus would mean a cosmetic status-line key collision silently takes down every command, tool, handler, and message renderer the user's extension registered. The dsh failure mode is "your registration failed"; the omp failure mode would be "your plugin vanished, and here is one generic line about it." DO-NOT-COPY.

(2) THE PRIORITY AXIS — the mechanism that makes the dsh discipline possible — DOES NOT EXIST IN omp AND IS NOT PORTABLE. I checked the registration signatures, not just the text: zero `priority` parameters across all 12 register* methods on ExtensionAPI (types.ts:1372-1768) and all 6 ExtensionUIContext cell setters (types.ts:266-281). The only two `priority` hits in extension types are unrelated (LLM request priority at types.ts:529; a reasoning-effort enum at 1267/1269). And omp's shadowing is not a raw priority number — it is three richer, issue-tracked mechanisms that a numeric tier would actively degrade: load-order tiering documented for determinism (loader.ts:483, "last-wins collisions, shared runtime flag defaults stay deterministic"), source-scope shadowing (plugins/loader.ts:222-223, 265; marketplace/types.ts:188-196 `shadowedBy: "project"`), and enablement-aware shadowing (skills.ts:214-215, 350, 365 — each carrying a linked issue, e.g. #7190, plus the subtle "a disabled higher-priority provider must not hide an enabled lower-priority provider" invariant). Collapsing that into "register at a different priority, lowest renders" would be a net loss.

(3) omp ALREADY HAS THE EXACT CELLS, AND ITS DIAGNOSTICS ARE STRICTLY BETTER ON THE CLAIM'S OWN CRITERION. The dsh message is a string-only `throw new Error(...)` (index.ts:1218) — no machine-readable fields. omp's skill collision diagnostic is structured: `interface SkillWarning { skillPath: string; message: string }` (skills.ts:43-46), returned as `warnings: SkillWarning[]` (skills.ts:50), where `skillPath` IS the registrant and the message names the occupant. That is "naming the occupant and the registrant," better than dsh, because it survives serialization. runner.ts:1167-1172 does the same for shortcuts, naming registrant (`extensionPath`) and occupant (`existingExtensionPath`) separately. On "loud about genuine ambiguity," omp's collectable diagnostics beat a string throw.

SCALE (measured, not estimated): dsh ui-slots = 1964 lines / 3 files, of which the cited discipline is 25 lines (index.ts:1210-1234) inside a 1669-line declarative framework. omp extensibility = 68 .ts files, 17,501 lines. But the fix is a WARN, not dsh's THROW, for the reason in (1). REFERENCE — registerComposerStyle (tui/src/components/composer/registry.ts:44-52) is the closest existing prior art: it already throws on both built-in replace and duplicate extension id, with an identity-checked idempotent disposer. DO-NOT-COPY — the throw itself at extension-factory-time, and the numeric-priority tier model, which would regress issue-tracked source-scope and enablement shadowing.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED as a port. The mechanism is real in cordis (I executed the vendored source and saw the throw), but the claim fails portability on two independent grounds, and its stated causal payoff is factually wrong.

(1) THE CAUSAL CLAIM IS WRONG. "Closing the cleanup-time-registration leak is what makes 'registrations are effects that unwind' actually true" — false. I patched the guard out of a throwaway copy of vendor/cordis and ran it. The orphan IS created mid-restart (`getEffects() ["too-late"]`, disposer live), but a subsequent unload REAPS it: after 5 consecutive restarts, live resources went 1 -> 0 -> 0 -> 0 -> 0 and registered effects 1 -> 0 -> 0 -> 0 -> 0; after a full dispose(), `getEffects() []` and the orphan's own cleanup fired (`lateRan 1`). The invariant already holds without the guard. The guard does not make "registrations unwind" true; it makes the VIOLATION loud and immediate instead of silent and deferred. That is a real but much smaller win than claimed, and it is a win only in a framework that restarts fibers in place.

(2) OMP HAS NO EFFECT SYSTEM TO GUARD. `ExtensionFactory = (pi: ExtensionAPI) => void | Promise<void>` (extensions/types.ts:1685) returns void — no disposer, nothing to unwind. `Extension` (types.ts:1827-1842) is a plain record of Maps held for the session. Rule-3 sweep: `grep -rn "createEffect|\.effect(|EffectRunner|SyncEffect|AsyncEffect" src/` -> 0 hits; `grep -rin "fiber" src/` -> only Go-fiber and React-fiber npm/unrelated hits. omp's extension "unload" analog, `setSuspendedExtensions` (runner.ts:976-999), is a pure array filter that runs NO disposers — there is no UNLOADING state to reject registration in.

(3) OMP ALREADY HAS THE SAME GUARANTEE, SOLVED THE OPPOSITE WAY — and throwing would be a regression. `AgentSession.beginDispose()` (agent-session.ts:5102-5104) sets `#isDisposed = true` then `for (const dispose of this.#disposers.splice(0)) dispose();`. `#doDispose` (5268-5269) calls it FIRST, then runs a long await-heavy teardown (5270-5344) that includes `await emitSessionShutdownEvent(this.#extensionRunner)` at 5283 — which runs extension `session_shutdown` handlers inside that window. Line 5346 then sweeps `#disposers` AGAIN, with the comment at 5345: "beginDispose() drained the rest; this catches registrations made during teardown." That IS the identical no-orphan-late-registration contract, delivered by a second sweep instead of a throw, and it is load-bearing: `beginDispose()` is also called standalone at agent-session.ts:10586 and sdk.ts:4716, where no second sweep follows.

(4) `addDisposer` DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CHECK DISPOSED STATE. agent-session.ts:2213-2215 is a bare `this.#disposers.push(dispose)`. Its main consumer is config/registry.ts:323 — `setting.listen(scope, onChange)` wires its unsubscribe through `scope.addDisposer?.(unsubscribe)`. 9 `addDisposer` references total. An INACTIVE_EFFECT throw there would break `setting.listen` for any `session_shutdown` handler and defeat the 5345 contract outright.

(5) OMP'S GUARD CONVENTION IS ON WORK, NOT REGISTRATION — the same protection, zero false positives. `#isDisposed` is checked at ~25 sites (1111, 1364, 1763, 2089, 2335, 2709, 2717, 2758, 4218, 4591, 5045, 7910, 8785, ...). "Don't start new work after dispose" is the idiom; the disposer registry stays open because settings listeners legitimately re-register.

(6) THE ONE EXTENSION-FACING DISPOSER REGISTRY IS ALREADY LEAK-PROOF. `addExtensionTerminalInputListener` (modes/controllers/extension-ui-controller.ts:1201-1208) tracks into `#extensionTerminalInputUnsubscribers`; `clearExtensionTerminalInputListeners` (1222-1227) iterates the Set DIRECTLY (not a splice(0) snapshot) then `.clear()`. Under JS Set semantics entries added during iteration ARE visited, so a re-registration inside the sweep is caught in the same pass. The underlying unsubscribe (packages/tui/src/tui.ts:1790-1794) is a pure `Set.delete` with no extension callback, so no reentrancy window exists at all.

DO-NOT-COPY: the throw-on-UNLOADING guard, into `addDisposer` or any omp disposer registry. It would convert omp's working second-sweep into a hard failure on a live path.

BORROW (small, and it is a test not a guard): the 5345 late-registration sweep is documented only in a comment. I found no test asserting it — test/headless-persistence-shutdown.test.ts:126 stubs `addDisposer: () => {}` and test/modes/session-teardown.test.ts asserts teardown ORDER only. A regression test that a `session_shutdown` handler calling `session.addDisposer(...)` still gets reaped by 5346 would defend a contract that is currently undefended.

REFERENCE: cordis's `getEffects()` meta tree (fiber.ts:568-572) as a diagnostics surface; not worth copying without the effect system.

Scale, honestly: omp extensibility = 68 .ts files / 21,376 lines. cordis src = 2,696 lines total, fiber.ts 754. Vendored cordis ships no tests in the tree.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED as a portable idea. The claim is technically ACCURATE about dsh/cordis — I verified every cited line — but it does not survive contact with omp's architecture. Four independent blockers, each with omp file:line evidence.

WHAT I CONFIRMED IN THE SOURCE (dsh, C:/Users/ADMIN/Projects/deepseek-harness)
The mechanism is real. `reflect.ts:124` declares `check?: () => boolean`; `reflect.ts:277` `provide(name, value, check)` attaches it; `reflect.ts:323` calls `fiber._checkImpl(name)`, which is the cascade trigger. `fiber.ts:597-609` `_checkImpl` deletes the impl from `_store` when `check` returns false; `fiber.ts:611-623` `_refresh` concatenates `':' + impl.fiber.uid` over `Object.keys(this.inject)` and sets INACTIVE if any is missing — that is literally "the fiber epoch is the concatenated uid of the impls behind its declared `inject`"; `fiber.ts:625-639` `_setEpoch` fires `_reload()` on INACTIVE→active; `fiber.ts:646-673` `_reload` re-runs `this._execute(this._runner)`, i.e. the consumer body. The cited line ranges are correct, not paraphrased.

BLOCKER 1 — omp has no `inject` for an epoch to be computed over.
`Provider<T>` (capability/types.ts:69-93) is exactly five fields: id, displayName, description, priority, load. `PluginManifest` (plugins/types.ts:27-49): name, version, description, entry-point paths, features, settings. `ExtensionAPI` (extensions/types.ts:1277+) is a flat registration surface (`on`, `registerTool`, `registerFileWriteFallback`, …) where every method returns `void`. There is no declared dependency edge anywhere in omp's three extension surfaces, so there is nothing to hash into an epoch.

BLOCKER 2 — omp's providers return DATA, not live services, and cannot be unloaded at all.
All 64 `registerProvider` calls across 15 capabilities produce `LoadResult<T> = {items, warnings}` (types.ts:60-65), consumed as a startup snapshot. In cordis, `provide()` hands consumers a live proxy they read through (reflect.ts:144 errors on "cannot get property without inject") — that live handle is what makes "unload → consumer goes PENDING" meaningful. omp has no such handle. And `registerProvider` (capability/index.ts:101-129) is strictly one-way: I grepped the whole package for `unregisterProvider|deregister|removeProvider` in the capability layer and found ZERO hits. A capability provider has no unload path, so the triggering half of the claim has no host in omp.

BLOCKER 3 — where the concern could apply, omp already chose the opposite of PENDING, deliberately.
`loadImpl` (capability/index.ts:154-174) runs every provider in an eager `Promise.all` and converts a provider throw into a warning string — the item is silently absent, and the consumer sees a shorter list with no degraded signal. That is the actual gap (see below), but it is a *reporting* gap, not a lifecycle gap. In the one subsystem where PENDING was genuinely available, omp rejected it on purpose: manager.ts:890-896 documents leaving pending MCP connections in flight rather than gating startup on them, because awaiting "gated the entire UI on the slowest server's per-request timeout (issue #2100: a single unresponsive MCP server blocked startup for the full 30s)". The fiber's core move — hold the consumer PENDING — is the strategy omp explicitly backed out of.

BLOCKER 4 — omp already has a better-shaped version where the concern actually bites, and it is not the fiber's shape.
MCP is the real "provider that dies mid-session" case, and omp solved it with a different, cheaper mechanism: `DeferredMCPTool` (mcp/tool-bridge.ts:760-807) is provisioned from the persistent `MCPToolCache` (mcp/tool-cache.ts, config-hashed, 30-day TTL) even when the server never connected (manager.ts:912-921); execution blocks on `waitForConnection` (tool-bridge.ts:830) and revives through `reconnect` (tool-bridge.ts:861-880, 888-899); staleness is killed by a monotonic `#connectEpoch` bumped on `disconnectAll` (manager.ts:301) plus a reconnect-storm circuit breaker (manager.ts:94-130). That IS dependency-gated activation + automatic revival + the epoch machinery — scoped per-CALL rather than per-FIBER, which is the correct scope for a transport that can die between two calls in one turn. Porting the fiber would replace a working, tuned mechanism with a heavier one at the wrong granularity.

BLOCKER 5 — a tested omp invariant is directly incompatible with fiber re-run semantics.
`bindPreparedExtensions` (loader.ts:416-459) deliberately separates module evaluation from session binding; test/extension-prepared-rebind.test.ts asserts the module body evaluates exactly ONCE (counter === 1) across two independent bindings, and that each session gets a fresh `Extension` and `runtime`. A fiber re-runs the consumer body on revival; that invariant would have to be deliberately broken. Relatedly, extension registration is documented as load-time-only: "Call this during extension load, like the other `register*` methods: handlers are installed when the runner initializes, so an extension that has registered none by then is skipped and a first registration made later never takes effect" (types.ts, registerFileWriteFallback doc). The only arrival-notification mechanism, `toolRegistrationListeners` (runner.ts:1056-1077), is a one-shot PUSH callback with a scoped disposer — not a body that is torn down and re-run.

Also note `ManagedTimers` (extensions/managed-timers.ts:22-63), the closest thing omp has to a fiber effect registry, is session-owned and `clearAll()`-ed at teardown — never revived. Its stated purpose is containment, not lifecycle (issue #5664). And `setEnabled` on a plugin only rewrites the lock file (plugins/manager.ts:874-881) — no live unload at all. My grep for revive/reactivate/PENDING across omp's src returned only collab agent-process parking and DAP debug sessions — unrelated to plugin DI.

WHAT SURVIVES THE PORT (the honest carve-out)
The generic EPOCH primitive is not missing from omp — it exists ad hoc at two sites: `#connectEpoch` (manager.ts:301) and `nextLegacyPiLoadTag()` (legacy-pi-compat.ts:2101-2104, feeding the `?mtime=` cache-bust at legacy-pi-compat.ts:2630 that gives every extension load a fresh module identity, backed by a Bun onLoad graph snapshot). So the idea is already internalized; it is just not centralized. The one genuinely missing piece is narrow: capability/index.ts:172-174 turns a provider throw into a bare warning string. A consumer needing that provider gets a silently shorter list. That is fixed by surfacing a per-capability "degraded: provider X failed" state — a few lines — not by importing 1770 lines of vendored DI.

TIER VERDICT: REFERENCE, not BORROW. Worth reading `_setEpoch`'s re-entrancy guard (fiber.ts:654, 666 — the "a disposer queued before this checkpoint may already have invalidated the load" check) as a pattern for any future invalidation tag. DO-NOT-COPY the fiber itself: dsh had to VENDOR cordis under `vendor/cordis/` (with a `patches/` dir alongside), the DI core is 1770 lines (fiber 754 + reflect 418 + registry 337 + service 115 + context 146) on top of 2696 total, and dropping it into omp means running a second competing dependency-resolution model next to the existing 64-provider capability registry.

ONE HONEST CAVEAT ON THE CLAIM ITSELF: the "VERIFIED BY EXECUTION" tag has no committed artifact behind it. `vendor/cordis/` ships src/, bin.js, package.json, README.md, LICENSE — zero test files — and a repo-wide search of dsh's *.test.ts for `fiber`, `FiberState`, or `provide(` returned nothing. I could not run dsh's suite to check whether an ad-hoc execution happened, so that sub-claim is UNVERIFIED, not refuted. I also could not execute omp's suite: `bun test` fails at import because `pi_natives.win32-x64.node` is not built (0 pass / 1 error), so every omp finding above is static code reading, not a passing test.

## [v2]

reason: The claim is mis-cited, and its mechanism is a substrate feature omp does not have — so the pattern has no port target and, worse, its advice would be false in omp.

WHAT I MEASURED (dsh side, the quoted home repo)

1. The file:line is WRONG. `sandbox.ts:64-100` is the `nodeApiTraps()` factory plus a doc comment. The teaching strings are the `NODE_API_REDIRECTS` table at sandbox.ts:68-80 — exactly 7 traps (require, setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, clearTimeout, clearInterval, fetch), and the `throw` is at sandbox.ts:87. The second half of the claim's quoted message does not exist in this file. It lives at `guard.ts:726-727`, inside `denyRead` (guard.ts:723-735), a different module in the same package.

2. "Every trap names the cordis service" is true of the 7 traps but has a hole the claim misses: `process` — the single most-reached-for Node global — is deliberately withheld with NO trap and NO message. sandbox.ts:62-67 states the reason (a throwing accessor would detonate the common `typeof process` feature probe), and `sed -n '101,117p'` confirms `process` appears 0 times in the `createSandbox` object literal. A model writing `process.env` gets a bare `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. dsh's own most valuable denial teaches nothing.

3. The genuinely good part, which the claim undersells: `denyRead` *discriminates*. guard.ts:724 branches on `ctx.get(prop) !== undefined` to pick between two different messages — "is not injected, declare it" (726) versus "sandbox ctx does not expose, here is what IS available, framework internals are withheld by design" (730). Naming the offender AND the available surface is real teaching.

WHY THE PORT FAILS

The teaching is only *true* because cordis supplies two substrate properties: a declaration array the package author writes and the host reads back (`Object.keys(ctx.fiber.inject)`, guard.ts:710), and fiber parking — cordis's automatic suspend-when-a-declared-hard-dep-is-absent behavior. Port the string without the substrate and "declare it in inject: [...]" points at an `inject` key that does not exist in omp. That is strictly worse than omp's current honest refusal.

omp HAS NO SANDBOX TO DENY IN

- `grep -rn "node:vm"` across all of `src/extensibility`: **0 hits**.
- `grep -rni "sandbox"` across all of `src/extensibility`: **3 hits, all incidental prose** (extensions/types.ts:1381 embedder-in-a-sandbox, types.ts:1415 a boundary that denied an unlink, plugins/loader.ts:74 "a sandbox, restrictive permissions" in a trust comment).
- The load path is a plain host-realm dynamic import: `custom-tools/loader.ts:78` — `await withHostGuard(() => import(resolvedPath))`. Same shape at extensions/loader.ts:419,452 and hooks/loader.ts:151,166. Full Node, real realm, nothing withheld, nothing to teach.
- `runner.ts:1271 createContext()` is a false friend: it returns a hand-built `ExtensionContext` plain object (~30 top-level members), not a vm context.
- No DI anywhere. `grep -rni "inject"` over extensibility returns only TypeBox/omptype/pi-coding-agent *shim objects passed as function arguments* — a different concept entirely, not declared service dependencies.

Per the "0 grep hits is not proof" rule I checked where the concept actually lives in omp: `src/eval/` (14,373 TS lines vs dsh's whole cordis-host-runner src at 3,329). That is omp's model-authored dynamic-code surface, and it is not a sandbox either.

DOES omp ALREADY DO THIS BETTER? — On the trap axis, no; on the teaching axis, yes, at a better layer.

Honest weakness: omp's denials here are thinner. `custom-tools/loader.ts:47` "expected object with string name, string description, parameters, and execute function" restates the spec instead of diagnosing. Eval denials are bare: "Eval-defined tools are unavailable in plan mode." (eval/agent-bridge.ts:178), "agent() needs the session's async job manager; unavailable here" (agent-bridge.ts:206).

But the teaching already happened before the failure, and better:
- `withHostGuard` (utils.ts:118-193) IS the same concern — fencing host process state off from third-party module evaluation — and its error explains the mechanism and cites real incidents: `ExtensionExitError` (utils.ts:57-67) names the offender, states the rule, and rides on documented bugs #5618 (stdin hijack) and #6488 (native-exit escape). Explain-the-mechanism is already omp's house style, with bug numbers the dsh copy has no equivalent for.
- A 632-line `prelude.txt` is injected into the model's execution context, so capabilities are taught proactively. The dsh traps would be redundant with it.

Tiers: the trap-string style and the two-branch `denyRead` discrimination are REFERENCE; the `inject`/parking teaching is DO-NOT-COPY (false advice in omp); dsh's silent `process` withholding is a real defect, and the one thing worth carrying forward.

ENTRY 19 — upstream bug confirmed, symptom named. Upstream `packages/loader/src/internal.ts` does `if (major >= 24) return _cachedLoader = Object.assign(raw, { version: 'v2' })` — every major 24 tagged v2. The local fix at C:/Users/ADMIN/Projects/deepseek-harness/vendor/loader/src/internal.ts:138-140 classifies by API shape instead (`getOrCreateModuleJob` -> v2, `getModuleJobForImport` -> v1). The log names an observable symptom, not just the mechanism: "`dsh web` served an empty client graph (`__DSH_BOOT__.entries: []`) and HMR partial reload resolved no entry URL, both behind swallowed or warn-level errors." `__DSH_BOOT__` is a real shipped symbol (packages/client/web/src/boot.ts, packages/client/modules/src/invariant.ts:32), not invented. Corroborated by the CI pin at .github/workflows/ci.yml:398 (`node: '24.9'`) with the comment "Pinned inside 24.0-24.11.1: those releases carry the v1 internal loader while reporting major 24".

ENTRY 11 — upstream bug confirmed, symptom named. Upstream `packages/include/src/index.ts` calls `buildMap(data)` ONCE before the patch loop and never re-indexes after `insert`, so an inserted row never enters `entryMap` and a later patch targeting it misses. The local fix at vendor/include/src/index.ts:100 adds `buildMap(insert)`. The log names the symptom: "leaving inserted rows silently unpatchable" plus the user-facing consequence "surface-only rows would otherwise be unreachable from user config". The cited regression test really exists at packages/boot/app-boot/tests/config-reload.spec.ts:150 ("lets a later patch configure or disable a row an earlier patch inserted").

THREE CAVEATS, none of which refute the claim as phrased:
1. "silently" is loose. Upstream's miss path is `logger?.('loader').warn('patch: entry %C not found', id)` — a warn, not total silence. "Silently unpatchable" describes the effect on the row (no error, the override just does not apply), not the absence of a log line. The same word is used in the local code comment at vendor/include/src/index.ts:99, so the claim faithfully quotes its source.
2. Entry 11's bolded headline is "patch-semantics export" — a refactor the README itself calls "Behavior-preserving for mounting". The bug fix is one clause within that entry, not its subject. The claim correctly identifies that clause, so it is not overstated, but anyone citing #11 as "the upstream bug fix entry" would be overreaching.
3. The pattern is real but NOT the log's dominant character. Of 22 entries, entries 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 16, 17 are packaging/build/rename/meta work, 13 is type-only, and 15 is a port of an upstream PR. The claim is explicitly scoped to #19 and #11 and both hold; generalizing it to "dsh's vendor log always attaches a failure mode to every divergence" would be overstated.

The anti-drift mechanism is the import itself plus delegation, not a parity test — I looked for a mount-vs-dump equality test and config-dump.spec.ts:118 asserts "exactly like boot()" against the flattened call, not against a live tree. That is a weaker guard than a real parity test, but the shared-symbol structure makes drift structurally impossible rather than merely tested-against.

## [v2]

reason: TRUE IN DSH, BUT THE PORT IS NOT NET-POSITIVE. It does not survive the port, for four measured reasons.

(1) THE TRIGGER DOES NOT EXIST IN OMP. The rule is only needed where a declarative entry list is mounted through a non-trivial *patch algorithm* that an offline tool must reproduce — dsh has id-keyed overrides, `insert`, a `!!js` YAML dialect, and per-layer patch composition. omp has none of that shape. There is no `applyEntryPatches` to extract, and no consumer to extract it for. omp's config is a typed settings registry, not a patchable entry list.

(2) OMP ALREADY SATISFIES THE RULE WHEREVER A RESOLUTION ALGORITHM DOES EXIST — MORE STRONGLY THAN DSH.
- Plugins: `getEnabledPlugins(cwd)` (`extensibility/plugins/loader.ts:229`) is the single exported resolver; all four aggregators delegate to it (`:418, :432, :446, :460`), 7 call sites. `resolvePluginManifestEntries` (`:348`) is shared by the install-time validator (`plugins/manager.ts:397`) and the four runtime path resolvers (`:394-408`).
- Models: `applyModelPatch` (`config/model-patch.ts:268`) is an exported pure function, 5 call sites. `omp models` does not even import the pure function — it constructs the real `ModelRegistry` (`cli/models-cli.ts:392`) and prints whatever the runtime would produce. That is a *stronger* anti-drift guarantee than dsh's: same-class, not same-function.
- Extensions: one exported `loadExtensions` (`extensions/loader.ts:485`), 8 call sites (`sdk.ts:987, :2438`, `main.ts:488`, `plugins/manager.ts:414`, legacy shim, sdk re-export).

(3) OMP'S CONFIG TOOLING ALREADY READS THE SAME DECLARATIONS, SO DRIFT IS STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE. 520 `register({...})` sites across 40+ domain modules all fold into `config/registry.ts` (956 lines) via `config/all-settings.ts` (125 lines). `omp config list/get` (`cli/config-cli.ts`), the TUI settings panel (`modes/settings.ts`, `modes/interactive-mode.ts:359`), and the runtime (`extensibility/settings.ts`, `modes/acp/acp-agent.ts:1192`) all read that one registry. `omp plugin list` renders `plugin.enabled`/`enabledFeatures` straight off `manager.list()` → `#resolvePlugin` (`manager.ts:270-271`) — the same object the install path builds, not a recomputation. The closest analogue to dsh's `--dump-config` in omp is `config-cli.ts:324` "Where the effective value comes from…", which reads the live `Settings` instance rather than reimplementing resolution.

(4) THE ONE REAL DUPLICATION IS A DIFFERENT CONCERN, AND DSH'S MECHANISM DOES NOT REACH IT. `PluginManager.getPlugin` (`manager.ts:737-751`) re-derives project-shadows-user resolution, and its own comment admits the mirror: "Resolution order mirrors getEnabledPlugins" (`:731`). But that mirror exists because the manager needs *mutating* install/uninstall/enable APIs — a pure roster export cannot serve it, which is the opposite of dsh's read-only-dump case. At ~15 lines with a documenting comment, this is REFERENCE-tier at most, and the rule as phrased is not actionable against it.

Net: importing "extract a pure function so tooling cannot drift" would add a rule with no violation to police and no function to extract. omp's configuration model has no artifact of dsh's shape, and the paths where omp *does* have a resolution algorithm already route every consumer through one shared resolver. DO-NOT-COPY as an instruction; at most a one-line note in the plugins area that the `getPlugin` mirror is deliberate and load-bearing.
