## [v1]

reason: Overstated, and one of its three assertions is contradicted by the very file it cites. The mechanism is real and worth borrowing; the description of what it does is wrong.

WHAT CHECKS OUT. Both cited ranges exist and contain exactly the described code. `workflow/src/index.ts:108-148` = the 11-code `WorkflowErrorCode` taxonomy, `WorkflowError.fatal`, and `isFatalWorkflowError` = `error instanceof WorkflowError && error.fatal` (:146-148). `workflow-ptc/src/runtime.ts:296-339` = the `parallel` and `pipeline` catch blocks, each `if (isFatalWorkflowError(error)) throw error; return null`. Scale: the two packages are 1,306 lines of src + 3,006 of tests across 24 files.

FAILS #1 — "only a child failure dissolves to null" is inverted. The predicate is a CLASS test, not a CAUSE test: `if (isFatalWorkflowError(e)) throw; return null` means *everything that is not a fatal WorkflowError* dissolves to null. The repo's own canonical test proves it — `guest.spec.ts:52-59` runs `parallel([() => agent('a'), () => { throw new Error('ordinary') }, () => { throw { fatal: true } }])` and asserts `first: ['a', null, null]`, then `pipeline(...)` with a bare `throw 'skip'` asserting `second: [4, null, 16]`. A plain Error, a bare string, and a forged object all become null. ZERO of those nulls are child failures. The cited file's own header (runtime.ts:3-4) states the accurate rule the claim omits: "ordinary child failures **and stage errors** become per-item nulls," and the inline comment at :333 says "An ordinary stage throw drops the ITEM to null." The claim paraphrases the code worse than the repo's own docstring does.

FAILS #2 — "a typo kills the script loudly" holds only on the host-validated surface. It IS loud for a typo'd `agent()` option key (runtime.ts:252-257 → `UNSUPPORTED_OPTION`, fatal). It is SILENT for an ordinary JS typo — the most common LLM typo class (`paralel(...)`, `results.lenght`, `undefined.map(...)`), which throws ReferenceError/TypeError. Those are not WorkflowError, so they hit `return null` and the run still reports `stopReason: 'completed'` (asserted at guest.spec.ts:58). A silent null where the work should be, reported as success — exactly the failure mode the claim says is prevented. Grep for "ReferenceError"/"is not defined" across both test dirs: no hits, so this path is also untested.

FAILS #3 — the `fatal` flag is dead in production. `fatal: false` is passed nowhere outside tests (repo-wide grep: only workflow.spec.ts:35,41). All 32 `new WorkflowError(...)` sites take the `?? true` default. In the shipped path `isFatalWorkflowError` ≡ `error instanceof WorkflowError`; the flag is a one-way vestigial knob whose only consumer is the test suite. The real discipline is "WorkflowError-vs-everything-else", not "fatal-vs-per-item-null".

SURVIVES — the `instanceof` unforgeability is real, but trivially so: the script realm is handed only `agent/parallel/pipeline/phase/log/args` (runtime.ts:85-98) inside a `vm.createContext`, so it never holds a `WorkflowError` reference at all. `guest.spec.ts:54`'s `{fatal:true}` proves the script cannot forge fatality. The flip side the claim ignores: a script also cannot legitimately escalate anything.

"the single best idea in this repo for LLM-authored orchestration code" is an unfalsifiable superlative I cannot confirm from code — and for the stated purpose it is self-undercutting, since ordinary script errors are precisely the class that gets silenced.

TIER: BORROW the mechanism (error taxonomy, loud cap paths, unforgeable-fatality test), NOT with the claimed semantics. Copied as described, you would build the opposite of the intent.

=== THE ONE THING WORTH TAKING (REFERENCE, not code) ===

reason: Partly true mechanism, materially false framing. But the claim is refuted on three counts. (1) WRONG CITATION: tool-ralph:130-133 is only the 'complete' arm of the status switch. The shape validation is :110-147, and there is a second, stricter 87-line independent host-side validator (readReport/readRunResult, :245-331) that re-checks the exact key set, status coherence, and the char cap. The claim understates by pointing at 4 lines. (2) NOT A SHIPPED DEFAULT: the row is disabled:true in packages/bundle/base/cordis.patch.yml:449, packages/bundle/web-app/cordis.patch.yml:543, and presets standard:127 / ptc:129 / cordis:126; minimal carries no row at all. A default session never sees the ralph tool — .agents/notes/implemented/simplification/2026-09-12-ralph-off-in-shipped-defaults.md records this as a deliberate demotion because completion is unverified worker self-declaration. "Context discipline by construction" describes an opt-in composition, not the product. (3) "THE REPORT IS THE ONLY THING THAT CROSSES" IS FALSE: the objective re-enters every round prompt at :155 and is bounded only by a non-empty check at :441 — no length cap, no model override possible, and the deployment ceiling is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (:36,196). Separately, "THE WORKSPACE IS THE MEMORY" is prompt text at :157, not enforcement: ralph passes no toolFilter (:443 requireFreshProvider checks only outputSchema/inheritsParentContext), so nothing constrains where the child writes. Also note inheritsParentContext is documented as "descriptive, not a service-validated start capability" (subagent/src/types.ts:350-353), so :226 is a declaration check, not a sandbox. Net: accurate as a description of an opt-in tool's handoff discipline; inaccurate as a claim about what ships, and the "only thing that crosses" half is refuted outright.
evidence: MEASURED FACTS (all read from source, not docs):

Bounded handoff — CONFIRMED, with a caveat.
- packages/workflow/tool-ralph/src/index.ts:26,36 — "Maximum serialized characters in one structured handoff (default 16384)"; `maxHandoffChars: z.number().step(1).min(1).max(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER).default(16_384)`.
- :142-145 (in-script, per round) — `const serialized = JSON.stringify(report); if (serialized.length > args.maxHandoffChars) throw new Error('Ralph round report exceeds maxHandoffChars (' + serialized.length + ' > ' + args.maxHandoffChars + ')')`.
- :273-276 (host-side, defensive re-decode) — `const chars = JSON.stringify(report).length; if (chars > maxChars) throw new Error('Ralph workflow returned an oversized handoff ...')`.
- :152 — the ONLY prior-round state passed forward is `JSON.stringify(previous)`.
- CAUTION: 16384 is a DEFAULT, not a hard cap. The ceiling is `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (:36, :196). No shipped yml overrides it (grep for maxHandoffChars in all *.yml returned 0 hits), so 16384 is the effective value in every shipped composition — but it is deployment-tunable and the model cannot set it (RalphCallArgs :73-76 exposes only objective + maxRounds).

Shape validation — CONFIRMED but the CITATION IS WRONG.
- Cited range tool-ralph:130-133 is only the `'complete'` arm of the status switch:
    130  if (report.evidence.length === 0 || report.nextSteps.length !== 0 || report.blocker !== '') {
    131    throw new Error('a complete Ralph report needs evidence, no nextSteps, and an empty blocker')
    132  }
    133  break
- The real shape validation is :110-147 (report is a non-null object, non-empty normalized summary, evidence/nextSteps are arrays of non-empty normalized strings, blocker is a normalized string, then a 3-arm status switch enforcing status/state coherence: 'continue' requires nextSteps AND empty blocker; 'complete' requires evidence AND no nextSteps AND empty blocker; 'blocked' requires a concrete blocker).

"THE REPORT IS THE ONLY THING THAT CROSSES" — REFUTED.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED as a net-positive port — but not because the claim is false. The claim is substantially accurate about dsh (two minor citation corrections below). It fails on portability on four independent grounds, the last of which is decisive: dsh's own maintainers shipped this tool DISABLED in every default composition, and the reason they cite is a defect that shape validation structurally cannot fix.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM ITSELF
1. Citation is off. `tool-ralph:130-133` is only the `complete`/`blocked` branches. The shape validation spans src/index.ts:110-141; the char bound is :142-145. The consumer-boundary re-check is :258-278 and :281-331.
2. "the report is the only thing that crosses" is true of the SCRIPT (`previous` + immutable objective only, :152, :172) but the "workspace is the memory" half is NOT enforced by code — it is a prompt instruction at :157 ("Treat the previous report only as a bounded handoff; confirm it against the workspace"). Nothing checks it.

WHY THE PORT IS NOT NET-POSITIVE

(1) NO SUBSTRATE. dsh's ralph is `inject = ['tools','workflowEngine','subagents','systemPrompt']` (:19) and executes a build-time-fixed script that calls `agent(prompt, {schema})` inside a for-loop (:151-174), with the parent re-decoding the terminal value defensively (:281-331). omp has no workflow engine: `grep -rn workflowEngine packages/` = 0 hits. The entire dsh engine is 4 files / 519 lines in packages/workflow/workflow/. Porting a "handoff bound" here means porting a script-DSL runtime first. That is a subsystem import, not a borrow.

(2) omp ALREADY BOUNDS THE SAME CROSSINGS, AND BETTER.
 - Subagent return: MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES=500_000 + MAX_OUTPUT_LINES=5000 (task/types.ts:29,32), then FULL_OUTPUT_THRESHOLD=5000 inline preview with an `agent://<id>` pointer for the full text (task/result-summary.ts:15,59-60; executor.ts:2578-2600,2727). dsh THROWS the entire multi-round run at 16384 chars (:143-145, re-checked :273-276). A verbose-but-correct round is fatal in dsh, a preview in omp.
 - Main-loop context: token-denominated and window-SCALED — DEFAULT_RESERVE_TOKENS=16384, MAX_SUMMARY_TOKENS=16384, keepRecentTokens:20000, effectiveReserveTokens = max(floor(0.15*window), reserve) (agent/src/compaction/compaction.ts:212, 222, 232, 333-335). dsh's 16384 is a fixed CHAR count (~4K tokens) invariant across a 200K or a 1M window. Adopting it in omp is a ~6x tightening against an adaptive budget. Same numeral, wrong unit, worse policy.
 - Shape validation: omp's is general JSON Schema enforced on BOTH sides — output-schema-validator.ts:1-7 says it is "the single source of truth for that pipeline — keeping the two callsites in lockstep." dsh's is a hand-rolled 5-field record. The double-check idea is NOT novel: dsh already does in-script + consumer-boundary; omp already has the generalized form. The one idea worth keeping is already implemented.

(3) THE "WORKSPACE IS THE MEMORY" HALF IS ALREADY AN omp PRIMITIVE. local:// is documented at internal-urls/local-protocol.ts:191 as "Session-scoped scratch space for large intermediate data, subagent handoffs, and reusable planning artifacts," and copyLocalArtifacts (:253-256) migrates it across session transitions so handoff-carried references stay readable. autoresearch persists per-run state to on-disk run directories (autoresearch/storage.ts 700 lines; ExperimentState in types.ts). The novel half is present; only the cap is left to port — and the cap is the weak part.

(4) DECISIVE — dsh SHIPPED IT OFF. packages/bundle/base/cordis.patch.yml:447-452 sets `disabled: true` with the comment "completion is a worker self-report, not an independent evaluation." Same at web-app/cordis.patch.yml:542-543 and in presets cordis/ptc/standard. The tool's own description restricts it to runs "the direct human explicitly asks for" (:177-182). Shape validation detects MALFORMED reports, not WRONG ones: a worker returning {status:'complete', evidence:['done'], nextSteps:[], blocker:''} without doing any work passes every check at :110-141 and terminates the run at :170. The claim's "context discipline by construction" is real; the reliability it implies is not.

(5) omp ALREADY HAS THE MISSING HALF dsh LACKS. packages/coding-agent/src/judgment/ resolves an independent `judge` model role (judgment/index.ts:1-15; Judge/TextJudge/TypeSafeJudge). That is precisely the capability dsh's demotion note cited as missing. Porting ralph-shaped self-report loops into omp without wiring them through `judge` would import the known defect.

(6) IT ADDS A COMPETING LONG-RUN PRIMITIVE. omp's `goal` tool is the sanctioned long-run path and deliberately keeps ONE context under a token budget (goals/tools/goal-tool.ts:16-20; 715 lines). omp's only bounded multi-round loop is `compress` (668 lines), which keeps ONE session with a nonce-guarded approve/rewrite protocol (compress/index.ts:199-211) — it needs no handoff at all. dsh draws the same line itself: "Ordinary long-running same-session work belongs to goal tools" (:181-182). A ralph port lands a third parallel surface beside two that already exist.

TIERS
- BORROW: the "two callsites in lockstep" invariant for delegation-boundary shape validation — already implemented in omp (output-schema-validator.ts). Nothing to copy; the idea is already held.
- REFERENCE: tool-ralph/src/index.ts (477 lines) as a worked fixed-script fresh-agent loop, only if omp ever builds a workflow engine.
- DO-NOT-COPY: the hardcoded 16384-char cap (window-invariant, wrong unit, ~6x tighter than omp's token budget) and the throw-on-oversize failure mode (kills the run instead of pointing at a persisted artifact).

MEASURED SCALE. dsh ralph: 477 src lines + 696 test lines; prerequisite engine 4 files / 519 lines. omp counterparts: task/ 13,695 lines; compaction/ 6,737; compress/ 668; goals/ 715. omp's 30 builtin + 3 hidden tools (tools/builtin-names.ts) contain no loop/ralph; the three runSubprocess callers are isolation-runner.ts:436, structured-subagent.ts:722, vibe/runtime.ts:1375 — all one-shot or keep-alive, none looping.

1. `SubagentCapabilities` exists exactly where claimed: `packages/subagent/subagent/src/types.ts:130-136` (doc comment 119-129). "Checked before dispatch" is literally true, with line ordering: `index.ts:559-570` — `expectProvider` (560) → `assertCapabilities` (561) → depth/schema validation (562-563) → descriptor resolve (564-568) → `provider.start(resolved)` (570). 3. `NO_START_CAPABILITIES` exists at out-of-process.ts:57-63 (doc 51-56), frozen, all-false. All four out-of-process backends declare all-false start capabilities: codex (index.ts:64), claude-code (index.ts:74), dsh-sdk (spreads it into `SDK_START_CAPABILITIES` at index.ts:110-113, flipping only `agentOptions: true`), and ACP (index.ts:147-153, an inline literal with identical values and the same rationale in its doc comment).

reason: REFUTED from the portability angle. The claim is TRUE in dsh but does not survive the port, on three independent grounds.

(1) THE PRECONDITION IS ABSENT IN omp. The pattern exists to police heterogeneous subagent backends. dsh has 6 real providers (`ls packages/subagent/*/` → subagent-acp, subagent-claude-code, subagent-codex, subagent-dsh-sdk, subagent-fork-in-process, subagent-spawn-in-process); 3 are out-of-process and all three declare `NO_START_CAPABILITIES`. omp has exactly ONE execution backend. `C:/Users/ADMIN/Documents/Projects/ultraworkers/packages/coding-agent/src/task/executor.ts:3446-3447` reads `/** Run a single agent in-process. */ export async function runSubprocess(...)` — despite the name it is in-process. All four `runStructuredSubagent` callers (cleanse/agent.ts:132,166; eval/agent-bridge.ts:217; task/index.ts:1497; task/workpool.ts:380) funnel through structured-subagent.ts:684 → `runSubprocess` (line 722) or `runIsolatedSubprocess` (line 727), and isolation-runner.ts:34,436 also calls the same `runSubprocess`. Every subagent executes in this process. reason: The claim is refuted on three independent grounds, two of them measured by execution rather than reading.

(1) "never-throwing" is false. I ran `materializeFromRealm` against 16 realistic tool-output shapes: 14 threw `MaterializeError`. The file's own docstring says `@throws` (realm.ts:59). dsh's own test suite has 7 tests asserting it *rejects* (realm.spec.ts:65,75,80,88,94). The "is total" test (realm.spec.ts:141) belongs to `renderThrown`, a different function — the claim conflates two exports. dsh's `index.ts:21` exports only `materializeFromRealm` and `MaterializeError`.

(2) The premise does not exist in omp. grep for `node:vm`/`bun:vm`/`new Worker(` across all 68 files in `packages/coding-agent/src/extensibility` returns zero VM hits. omp loads extensions with `await import(resolvedPath)` (custom-tools/loader.ts:78) into the host process with full privileges; `withHostGuard` (extensibility/utils.ts:118) is a cooperative shutdown guard that patches `process.exit`, not a realm. An extension already has process/fs/network, so a value-materialization boundary defends nothing.

(3) "Copy this shape for any sandboxed tool output" is the actively harmful part. It is a *reject* boundary, not a *sanitize* boundary. My probe shows it rejecting Date, Map, Set, Uint8Array, Buffer, Error, class instances, NaN, Infinity, bigint, circular refs, functions, and bare `undefined` fields — the last being ubiquitous in TypeScript tool results. Placed at omp's tool-output boundary it hard-fails the majority of real payloads, because tool output must be *delivered*.

(4) omp already has a strictly better version of this concern. `collab/replication-shrink.ts` is 397 lines with 7 progressive shrink passes, UTF-8 byte measurement instead of UTF-16 (its docstring at lines 29-32 records that a `.length` comparison under-counts CJK payloads by up to 3x — a bug class `materializeFromRealm` has no concept of), a depth cap because `JSON.stringify`/`structuredClone` throw `RangeError` at ~40k levels (lines 70-80), cycle elision, and typed placeholders so the guest replica stays connected rather than hard-failing. Backed by 705 lines / 17 test cases. The decisive design difference: **omp elides, dsh rejects** — and elision is the correct semantics for tool output.

The one genuinely portable idea is the totality of `renderThrown` for thrown values, and omp's `renderError` (tools/tool-errors.ts:37) is measurably less total — it reads `e.message` and calls `String(e)` with no try/catch, so a throwing `message` getter propagates. That is a real but ~3-line gap, fixable inside the existing central helper, not a case for importing a 147-line boundary module. dsh itself declined to apply "central boundary" discipline here: `renderThrown` is not exported from `index.ts` and is re-implemented locally in at least 4 other dsh packages.

2. `packages/coding-agent/src/modes/rpc/rpc-prompt-results.ts:117-135` — correlates `agent_start`→`agent_end` in production via a monotonic counter (`#agentStarts`, snapshotted at `begin()`), strictly more robust than object identity; and `#report()` line 138 is the identical `if (!this.#open.delete(ticket)) return;` guard the claim calls "neat." ## [v1]

reason: NOT REFUTED — the claim is accurate at the cited lines, and it holds for the right reason, but it over-narrows the pattern's scope in two precise ways.

ACCURATE. The code at goal-round-driver/src/index.ts:142-150 does exactly what the claim says: when ctx.sessions.flush() rejects, the driver calls disarm(state) and returns instead of falling through to reserve another round on state that was never persisted. Both premises are the repo's own vocabulary, not my paraphrase: (a) flush is genuinely the durability barrier, not a best-effort append — packages/session/session-persistence/src/index.ts:122 says verbatim "append persists best-effort; flush ... is the durability barrier", and packages/core/session/src/index.ts:1182-1187 calls it "the awaited session/flush durability checkpoint" and explicitly names "goal-round-driver's idle checkpoint" as one of its sanctioned callers; (b) disarm genuinely revokes automatic authority — the driver helper's own doc at line 116 is "Remove automatic authority while preserving the durable phase", the service at goal/src/index.ts:283-284 is "Remove process-local continuation authority without changing durable goal phase or revision", and the driver gates round reservation on goal.activation === 'armed' at line 165 plus a second fence at line 356. The claim is not just plausible reading — it is the asserted contract of two named tests, one of which states the claim's rationale verbatim.

OVERSTATED IN SCOPE, twice:

1. "When the durability barrier fails" means specifically "a REGISTERED session/flush listener rejected" — not "nothing is durable." Sessions.flush returns Promise<boolean> meaning "whether at least one durability listener participated" (core/session/src/index.ts:1194), and the driver discards that boolean at line 145. A session with zero registered durability listeners resolves false, the catch never runs, and the driver proceeds as though the barrier had held. So a total absence of persistence is silently treated as success. This is the one real hole in the pattern, and the claim does not mention it.

2. Revocation is itself best-effort. disarm() (lines 117-124) wraps ctx.goals.disarm in its own try/catch and downgrades a throw to logger.warn. If disarm itself throws, the goal stays 'armed'; only that one drive() pass is skipped, and a later requestDrive can grant a round again. The pattern fails soft one level below where the claim implies it fails hard.

MISFRAMED AS A LOCAL PATTERN. Lines 142-150 are not a bespoke one-off. disarm(state) appears at 12 sites in this single 456-line file (148, 222, 228, 238, 248, 276, 330, 337, 371, 415, 431, 440), covering agent/error, driver throw, task rejection, reservation-check failure on both sides of the pre-step hook, max-tokens turn end, aborted turn, load-time sweep (431) and teardown (440). The checkpoint case is one instance of a file-wide "fail closed: warn and disarm" discipline. That strengthens the pattern rather than weakening it, but the claim's citation implies the checkpoint case is where the idea lives, and it does not.

PATH NOTE: the claim writes "goal-round-driver/src/index.ts"; the real path is packages/goal/goal-round-driver/src/index.ts. It resolves; the prefix is just abbreviated.

TIER: BORROW. The generalizable idea for omp is the fail-closed shape — when a persistence/durability step fails, revoke the automatic-continuation authority rather than proceeding on unrecorded state, and make that revocation one shared helper called from every failure branch. The specific checkpoint trigger is REFERENCE-only. Worth improving on transfer: check flush's boolean return instead of discarding it (fixes hole 1), and let a failing disarm escalate rather than degrade to a warn (fixes hole 2).

A test that hand-builds `new Context()` + `ctx.plugin(InvariantRegistry)` + `ctx.plugin(WorkflowInvariant)` (tests/invariant.spec.ts:14-19) is not "production".

(2) THE CODE IS NOT LIFTABLE. Licensing is NOT the blocker — all three pieces are MIT (root LICENSE "Copyright (c) 2026 DeepSeek"; packages/runtime-diagnostics/invariants/package.json:28 "MIT"; vendor/cordis/LICENSE MIT (c) Shigma), and omp is MIT (Mario Zechner / Can Bölük / Stencil Labs). (3) THE "NEAT" MECHANISM IS INSEPARABLE FROM CORDIS. The staged* WeakSets work only because cordis emits `internal/dispatch` inside dispatch() BEFORE listener resolution and context filtering (vendor/cordis/src/events.ts:165-175 — emit on L169, filter/map on L172-174), so a `{global:true}` observer sees dispatches a scoped listener would not. (4) MECHANISM INACCURACY IN THE CLAIM: the WeakSets are not a de-dup device ("without double-firing"). WeakSet.delete is inherently once-only, so it cannot be double-firing protection in the usual sense. They are a VALIDATED-ADMISSION GATE — trace state is mutated only for objects that passed pre-validation in the same dispatch — which the code's own comments state: `/* v8 ignore next -- internal/dispatch stages the same run-info object */` (L107, L112, L119, L124).

REFERENCE: this file, read for the admission-gate idea. DO-NOT-COPY: the staged* WeakSet idiom in isolation (meaningless without internal/dispatch) and the registry+workspace-* plugin surface. ## [v1]

reason: The claim's literal ingredients all exist, but its causal framing — a deliberate per-population policy choice, documented in the error message — is not supported by any code, comment, or doc I could find. Three specific failures: (1) NO per-population policy pair exists. The queueing pool and the fail-fast pool are in different packages guarding different resources with zero shared code, constants, or cross-referencing comments; there is no "population" taxonomy that selects between them. (2) The documented rationale for the fail-fast pool is deadlock avoidance under shared pool inheritance (README:55), not an "ambient children" rule — and that rationale is a DOC, i.e. THEIRS CLAIM, UNVERIFIED beyond the throw itself. (3) The error message documents recovery, not a choice: it states the limit and two next actions, never mentions queueing, and presents no alternative being weighed. The only code comment on ActivationPool (line 40) describes pool scope, not policy. The real queue-vs-fail-fast split in workflow-ptc runs along a different axis (concurrency vs total cap) on the SAME population, which further undercuts "per population".
evidence: 1) QUOTED MESSAGE EXISTS VERBATIM — but is pure fail-fast, no queue.
packages/subagent/subagent/src/continuation-activation.ts:41-57, class ActivationPool:
  reserve(capacity: number): () => void {
    if (this.slots.size >= capacity) {
      throw new SubagentError(
        `subagent limit reached (active child limit: ${capacity}); wait for an existing child to finish `
        + 'or complete this work with the current agents', 'ACTIVATION_LIMIT_REACHED')
    }
    const slot = Symbol(); this.slots.add(slot)
    return () => { this.slots.delete(slot) }
  }
No waiter array, no awaiting, no FIFO. `pool.reserve()` has exactly ONE call site: continuation-activation.ts:489 inside `materialize()`, which returns a release closure synchronously. Verified by grep: only `pool.reserve` hit in src is line 489.

2) A QUEUING SEMAPHORE DOES EXIST — but in an unrelated subsystem.
packages/workflow/workflow-ptc/src/runtime.ts:142-152:
  /** Acquire one concurrency slot in FIFO order. */
  private acquireSlot(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.activeSlots < this.limits.maxConcurrentAgents) { this.activeSlots += 1; return Promise.resolve() }
    return new Promise<void>((resolve) => { this.slotWaiters.push(() => { this.activeSlots += 1; resolve() }) })
  }
  private releaseSlot(): void { this.activeSlots -= 1; const next = this.slotWaiters.shift(); if (next) next() }
Used at runtime.ts:179 by `agent()`. Grep confirms `slotWaiters` appears ONLY at runtime.ts:60,149,158.

WHY THE PAIR IS NOT A POLICY DECISION:
- Different packages: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow-ptc` (VM `agent()` call concurrency inside one script run) vs `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent` (host-process continuable child Agent residency). Different resources, different lifecycles, no shared code/constant/comment linking them.
- The only per-"population" thing in the subagent pool is WHICH POOL a child draws from, not which POLICY: continuation-activation.ts:488 `const pool = this.resident.get(inputs.parent.id)?.pool ?? this.rootPool(inputs.parent)` (rootPool at 604-612). Both branches then call the IDENTICAL fail-fast `reserve()`. Pool partitioning ≠ queue-vs-fail-fast.

3) THE ACTUAL QUEUE/FAIL-FAST SPLIT IS A DIFFERENT AXIS, ON ONE POPULATION.
Same file, same `agent()` call: `acquireSlot()` queues (runtime.ts:179) while AGENT_CAP fails fast (runtime.ts:166-172):
  if (this.started >= this.limits.maxTotalAgents) throw new WorkflowError(
    `this run reached its total agent cap (${this.limits.maxTotalAgents}) — a runaway-loop backstop; ...`, 'AGENT_CAP')
Code itself calls the total cap "a runaway-loop backstop" — a different concern (runaway loop), not a different population. The concurrency-vs-total-cap axis is what varies, not caller-waits vs ambient.

4) THE DOCUMENTED RATIONALE IS DEADLOCK AVOIDANCE, NOT A POPULATION RULE.
packages/subagent/subagent/README.md:55 — THEIRS CLAIM, UNVERIFIED (vendor doc; code corroborates only the throw, not the why):
  "Admission does not queue, because a parent waiting for descendants must not wait for its own occupied slot."
The code comment on the class (line 40) says only: "Process-local slots shared through uninterrupted continuable parent links." — scope, not policy. No rationale in code anywhere.

5) THE ERROR MESSAGE DOCUMENTS RECOVERY, NOT A CHOICE.
Text is: `subagent limit reached (active child limit: N); wait for an existing child to finish or complete this work with the current agents`. It reports the limit and two recovery actions. It never mentions queueing, never names the alternative it declined, and states no rationale. Note the browser/remote path deliberately DISCARDS it: control.ts:88-96 maps ACTIVATION_LIMIT_REACHED to RemoteError 'subagent/delivery-unavailable' with the generic message "subagent follow-up is temporarily unavailable" — so the quoted text does not even reach every consumer.

6) SCALE (measured, non-test .ts):
- packages/subagent/ src = 10,857 LOC
- packages/workflow/ src = 3,105 LOC (excluding bundled guest-source.ts)
- Repo-wide, only THREE pool/limiter/gate classes exist in src: CompressionLimiter (attachment-local/src/compression-limiter.ts:15, FIFO, image compression), ResponseCapacityGate (session-query/session-log-export/src/archive.ts:416, single-waiter backpressure), ActivationPool (subagent, fail-fast). None is a sibling semaphore to ActivationPool. "Semaphore" in this repo otherwise means the Win32 kernel semaphore in packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/win32.ts (unrelated file lock).

7) FAIL-FAST IS THE TESTED CONTRACT, not incidental. packages/subagent/subagent/tests/continuation.spec.ts:315-331 asserts startContinuable REJECTS with ACTIVATION_LIMIT_REACHED at capacity, including after lowering the cap — never that it waits.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED on portability: the pattern is TRUE and load-bearing in dsh, but the port is a regression, not a net win.

CLAIM IS TRUE IN dsh (verified in code, not docs). `goal-round-driver/src/index.ts:142-150` is exactly the described block: `if (state.needsCheckpoint) { ... try { await ctx.sessions.flush(agent.session) } catch { logger.warn(...); disarm(state); return } }`. `disarm` is at :117-124 and is called from **12 sites** (:148,222,228,238,248,276,330,337,371,415,431,440). It is test-covered twice by name: `tests/goal-round-driver.spec.ts:543` "disarms without dispatch when a durability checkpoint fails" and `:554` "disarms instead of reserving another round when the round checkpoint fails". Scale: 456-line index.ts + invariant.ts (86) + prompt.ts (26) = 568 LOC.

Why it does not survive the port — four independent blockers:

(1) THE BARRIER DOES NOT EXIST IN omp. The pattern's entire logic rests on "flush is the crash-durability barrier." In dsh that premise is documented and true — `packages/session/session-persistence/src/handle.ts:90` "only a resolved flush promises it survives a crash"; `index.ts:122` "append persists best-effort". In omp, `SessionStorageWriter.flush()` is `packages/coding-agent/src/session/session-storage.ts:46-47` — literally `/** Resolve once all queued appends complete. No fsync. */`. And `append` at :31-33: "File and memory storage apply the line synchronously before the returned promise settles, so a software crash after append returns ... still sees the entry on disk." omp has no durability barrier that can fail. Porting "disarm on flush failure" matches a homonym: an omp flush rejection means "a queued write errored", not "this round will never be recorded."

(2) THE TRIGGER SEMANTICS ARE INVERTED, so dsh's response would be wrong in omp. dsh's barrier failure is terminal. omp's persistence failure is explicitly retry-by-design — `packages/coding-agent/src/modes/persistence-failure.ts:5-9`: "The store keeps the unlanded entries in memory and retries the whole transcript on the next write, so this reports a retryable condition and claims nothing about durability — the write may still land." Reinforced at `session-manager.ts:1321-1325`: "The failed entry and any later entries remain in memory. A full replacement is the writability probe and restores all of them once transient storage pressure clears." Disarming on a transient ENOSPC blip would permanently kill an autonomous goal loop over a condition omp is engineered to ride out. dsh can afford fail-closed; omp cannot.

(3) THE DELIVERY MECHANISM DOES NOT EXIST. dsh's driver owns the checkpoint and can `await` it in a try/catch. omp's `GoalRuntimeHost.persist` is `persist(mode, state?): void` (`goals/runtime.ts:13`), implemented at `agent-session.ts:1954-1959` as a bare `appendModeChange(...)` — no await, no try/catch, no failure channel. `#commitState` (`goals/runtime.ts:169-180`) structurally cannot observe a persist failure. You would have to build the barrier and the failure channel before you could copy the reaction.

(4) THERE IS NO GOAL-ROUND DRIVER TO DISARM. `GoalRuntime.buildContinuationPrompt()` (`goals/runtime.ts:506-511`) is a pure string builder. The scheduler is `InteractiveMode.#scheduleGoalContinuation` (`modes/interactive-mode.ts:2313-2356`), an 800ms debounce timer. I read its full guard list — 15+ guards (loopModeEnabled, onInputCallback, cfgGoalContinuationModes, planModeEnabled/Paused, goalModeEnabled/Paused, #goalSuppressNextContinuation, #goalOpenWorkAllBlocked, #pendingSubmittedInput, editor text, pendingImages, enabled+active ×2, #isAutoSubmitBlocked) — and **not one consults persistence state**. The single `sessionManager.flush()` in interactive-mode.ts is at :3471 and belongs to TODO-HUD dismissal, not goals.

WHY omp IS NOT SIMPLY "MISSING IT" — it has a better version, elsewhere. omp latches `#diskFailure` (`session-manager.ts:767`) and exposes `onPersistenceError` (:2680) with replay-of-already-latched-failure for late subscribers. All three production subscribers are notice-only by deliberate, documented choice: `interactive-mode.ts:1788-1795` → `showWarning`; `rpc-mode.ts:748-752` → `notice` frame + stderr; `print-mode.ts:219` → shutdown message. omp consciously chose "surface, don't stop."

And the "halt autonomous authority on substrate failure, require human re-arm" pattern ALREADY EXISTS in omp — just not on the goal loop. `advisor/runtime.ts:534-548` (`#noteDroppedBacklog`): sets `#halted = true`, clears pending work, logs "advisor halted after repeated failures; use /advisor or reload config to re-enable", and only `reset()` (:591) clears it. That is structurally dsh's disarm. Crucially, its trigger policy is **strictly better than the one being proposed**: it requires `#droppedBacklogs >= 3` OR a classified permanent error (`isPermanentAdvisorError`, defined :103) — see the guard at :538-539. dsh disarms on the FIRST failure. Copying dsh's version would replace omp's classify-permanent-vs-transient + repetition-threshold policy with an unconditional trip on the first blip. That is a measurable downgrade in trigger quality.

TIERS:
- DO-NOT-COPY — the disarm-on-checkpoint-failure pattern as written. No barrier to fail, inverted retry semantics, no failure channel, no driver to disarm; and its trigger policy is worse than the incumbent one.
- BORROW — the `disarm` primitive itself (dsh `goal/src/index.ts:285-294`, "Remove process-local continuation authority without changing durable goal phase or revision"). This is genuinely missing in omp: `state.enabled` is *persisted* (`goals/runtime.ts:451` → `appendModeChange("goal_paused", …)`), so omp has no cheap, transcript-mutating-free way to stop auto-continuation. A process-local, non-persisted authority latch is a real gap. If you build it, wire it to the advisor's trigger policy, not dsh's.
- REFERENCE — dsh's `session-checkpoint-policy` (`packages/session/session-checkpoint-policy/src/index.ts`) is the better document to read: it states the fail-closed philosophy explicitly ("Checkpoint failures are fail-closed at the model and tool side-effect boundaries"), which makes clear the whole dsh design rests on a real barrier that omp does not have.

## [v2]

reason: The pattern is real in its home repo, but omp already implements the invariant in a strictly more general form, and the primitive being ported is a linear-seq-range narrowing that omp deliberately retired in session format v2. The downstream payoffs the claim names (derived FTS, crash repair, shadow pricing) are either absent in omp or solved by unrelated mechanisms, so the port buys nothing and costs a user-facing on-disk format migration.

(1) omp ALREADY surface-replaces compaction. `CompactionEntry` carries `firstKeptEntryId` (session-entries.ts:120-146) and `buildSessionContext` emits only the summary plus entries from that id onward (session-context.ts:210-330). The transcript branch's own comment: "Compactions do not erase prior history here — each renders inline (as a divider in the TUI) at the point it fired" (session-context.ts:399-405). `ResetBoundaryEntry` (session-entries.ts:157-159) gives `/clear` the same property. The invariant "shadowed events stay in the log, only the replay surface is replaced" is omp's current behavior, not a missing feature.

(2) The primitive is structurally incompatible. deepseek's `surfaceOp: {op:'replace', startSeq, endSeq}` is a range over a linear `SessionSeq` on one append-only log. omp's session is a TREE — `SessionIndex` with `#children`, `leafId()`, `pathTo()`, `childrenOf()` (session-manager.ts:466-510, 687). On a root-to-leaf path a compaction shadows an ancestor SUBPATH, not a seq interval; there is no `endSeq` to point at. Decisively, `migrateV1ToV2` (session-migrations.ts:14-35) already performed this exact migration — converting `firstKeptEntryIndex` (linear-index-shaped) to `firstKeptEntryId` (tree-node-shaped) "to add id/parentId tree structure." omp paid this cost once and resolved toward the tree. Re-porting the linear primitive re-runs a retired migration across a v3 on-disk format (CURRENT_SESSION_VERSION = 3) plus foreign/claude/codex session stores and collab readers.

(3) The FTS payoff is unavailable — there is no index to unlock. omp's only FTS5 is `history_fts` over the `history` table (history-storage.ts:60,103) indexing user PROMPT history (`prompt, session_id, cwd, use_count`), not messages. `session-index.ts` DDL holds only `session_titles` + `session_recaps`. Building the deepseek analog is a new ~6,200-line package (`packages/session-query/`) that would work unmodified against omp's already-retaining tree with zero change to compaction.

(4) omp's "what did it originally say?" affordance already exists, differently: `history://current/full` (internal-urls/history-protocol.ts:59-140) serializes the entire branch as markdown with full tool-call arguments, and its own comment notes server-side search results "can hold the only copy of research from before the rollover."

(5) omp's real durability gap is destructive REWRITES of retained entries, which `surfaceOp` is orthogonal to. `rewriteEntries()` → `#rewriteAtomically()` is called at session-maintenance.ts:680, 698, 726, 777, 855, 971, 1810. `shake({mode:"thinking"})` mutates `message.content` in place and drops thinking blocks (session-maintenance.ts:834-846); `pruneToolOutputs`/`dropImages` do the same, with `elide` substituting `artifact://` recovery links. That is a content rewrite, not a surface cut — surface-replace would not prevent it. Same for `truncateForPersistence` / `TRUNCATION_NOTICE` (session-persistence.ts:13, 96-184). If the concern is original content, the target is `rewriteEntries`, not the compaction cut.

(6) "Crash repair" and "shadow pricing" are misattributed. deepseek's repair.ts (211 lines) is TOOL-CALL LIFECYCLE repair (TOOL_NOT_STARTED / TOOL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN), not log truncation — and omp's turn-recovery.ts is 2,988 lines, ~14x larger, already covering that ground. There is zero "shadow" concept in omp's session/compaction layer (grep for shadow/shadowed across packages/coding-agent/src/session/ and packages/agent/src/ returns only unrelated tool-alias and speculative-execution hits). omp's pricing is a per-call `ModelUsageEntry` ledger with an explicit `purpose` field (session-entries.ts:76-91), consumed by session-stats.ts:75 — usage is recorded at the call site with its purpose, never folded from a surface, so it has no need for this primitive.

VERDICT: DO-NOT-COPY the primitive (narrowing + migration cost). BORROW nothing from this claim directly. The genuinely separable, net-positive idea is deepseek's log-derived session full-text index with a `surface` label column — but that is a separate ~6k-line bet on a read model omp does not have, and it depends on nothing omp is currently missing.

- The counter is credited as *the* mechanism, but two co-equal guards do real work: the retry budget (index.ts:199-200) and the prune-before-summary ordering (index.ts:294-301). And the counter is a proxy for reduction, not a measurement of it — it counts any committed positional replace, not net token drop.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED as stated — the "streaming" architecture does not survive the port, and the claim misstates the blast radius by ~40x. The two properties it names are real gaps in omp (I proved one empirically), but the mechanism offered to close them is the wrong shape for omp on both counts.

CITATION ERROR: the cited paths are not at repo root. Real paths are packages/session/session-format/src/chain.ts and packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/generation.ts.

SCALE CORRECTION: the claim cites 2 files / ~145 lines. The real unit is session-format = 8 files / 945 lines plus session-persistence-jsonl = 13 files / 4,963 lines (6 of which mention migration) = ~5,900 lines across 21 files.

(1) "STREAMING" DOES NOT SURVIVE — structural impedance mismatch. dsh's SessionFormatMigrationStage is a one-way push transform (chain.ts:172-199: transformEvent/transformRun/finish) with no random access and no retraction. omp's ONLY real migration, migrateV1ToV2 (session-migrations.ts:28-37), requires exactly what a one-way stage forbids: `const targetEntry = entries[comp.firstKeptEntryIndex];` — an arbitrary-index lookup used to rewrite a compaction entry's firstKeptEntryIndex into firstKeptEntryId. Under a streaming stage that entry may already be emitted downstream and cannot be retracted. omp's own streaming reader agrees: visitEntriesFromFileStream (session-loader.ts:109-113) exposes a forward-only `visit: (entry) => void | boolean`. Porting dsh's chain forces rewriting v1→v2 as a two-pass algorithm, erasing the exact benefit the word "streaming" is selling.

(2) "VERIFIED ATOMIC WRITE-BACK" IS ARCHITECTURALLY BLOCKED. dsh's verification is file-only and assumes concepts omp lacks: exclusive temp open 'wx' 0o600, sha256 digest, and zstd compression (createZstdCompress(ZSTD_CHECKSUM_OPTIONS), generation.ts:757). omp's writeTextAtomic (session-storage.ts:707) sits on the SessionStorage INTERFACE with three production backends — FileSessionStorage (session-storage.ts:397), MemorySessionStorage (session-storage.ts:1127), IndexedSessionStorage (indexed-session-storage.ts:118, driving Redis + SQL). grep for zstd|gzip|compress in session-storage.ts returns ZERO hits; omp sessions are uncompressed JSONL with a fixed-width title slot. Digest-verified publish is a per-backend concern in omp's design; hoisting it to the interface contract would break indexed backends that publish remotely over no filesystem to hash.

(3) omp IS ALREADY BETTER ON CONCURRENCY — DO NOT COPY dsh's publish. omp runs commitGuard() and #assertExpectedSize inside #withPublishLock with NO await between check and renameSync (session-storage.ts:718-731, with an explicit comment on that invariant), plus an epoch fence (#atomicRewriteFenceEpoch) and a `do…while(#atomicRewriteDirty)` loop re-capturing appends landing mid-rewrite. dsh's equivalent is a single stat identity comparison. Copying it would be a regression.

BUT THE COMPLETENESS GAP IS REAL AND I PROVED IT (BORROW, in reduced form). omp has CURRENT_SESSION_VERSION = 3 (session-entries.ts:13) and a hand-written ladder `if (version < 2)…; if (version < 3)…` (session-migrations.ts:68-69) with nothing tying the ladder to the constant. I copied the real module to /tmp, bumped the constant to 4 without adding a v3→v4 step, and ran it against a real v3 session array: migrateToCurrentVersion returned true while header.version stayed 3. The caller at session-manager.ts:1882 (`#rewriteRequired = migrated || loaded.malformedRecords > 0`) then fires a full file rewrite, and the next load does the same — a silent, non-converging rewrite loop with no error thrown. dsh's constructor makes that state unrepresentable.

Porting the 200-line registry means first building a DI container, against omp's class-instantiation style. That alone is a regression.

2. omp's event path structurally CANNOT reject. `AgentSession.#emit` (agent-session.ts:2805-2825) wraps every listener call in try/catch and downgrades a throw to `logger.warn("AgentSession listener threw")` (line 2821). The session-event analogue `#emitSessionEvent` (agent-session.ts:2925-2962) fans out to `#emit` FIRST, then awaits `#emitExtensionEvent`. There is no pre-publication veto seam — dsh's `fail(): never` has nowhere to land.

3. The persistence path is non-throwing BY CONTRACT. `appendMessage` (session-manager.ts:2777) → `#recordEntry` (1581) → `#appendToSessionFile` (1313). The comment at session-manager.ts:1386 states it: "Callers stay non-throwing here — the core turn loop invokes appendMessage/appendCustomEntry without try/catch." A throw-based invariant here would kill the turn loop instead of rejecting the entry — the exact opposite of "reject before the event exists."

4. dsh's pre-commit trick is a SIDE EFFECT, not a contract. In vendor/cordis/src/events.ts, `dispatch()` calls `this.emit('internal/dispatch', ...)` and `emit()` is `this.dispatch('emit', args).map(cb => cb(...args))` — unguarded, so a throw skips the real listeners. That is why it works. But the framework's own JSDoc calls `internal/dispatch` "event-bus diagnostics before public events are delivered" (events.ts:326) and types it `void` — no veto semantics. Under `ctx.parallel(...)` (events.ts:186-191) listeners are wrapped in `Promise.allSettled`, so the throw becomes an AggregateError AFTER every listener already ran and the event is delivered anyway. The pattern only rejects on the `ctx.emit` path. Porting it copies a coupling to a framework's missing error handling.

5. Scale does not transfer. Measured 39 src companions = 3,676 LOC + 34 test files = 4,768 LOC = 8,444 LOC. omp has 14 packages, and its seams are not cordis fibers, so there is nothing to hang a child installer off.

6. The claim also overstates its own scope: only 25 of the 39 companions do pre-commit (`internal/dispatch`); 14 are detect-only — validating after the event exists, which the claim calls "the part that does not matter." So "pre-commit is the part" is true for a majority, not the mechanism.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED on portability. The quote is faithful to dsh, but porting it into omp is a net-negative regression: omp already enforces the same invariant by a strictly better mechanism, and the two designs are not even measuring the same quantity.

1) The `min()` conjunction is already covered elsewhere, better. dsh conjuces the output reservation into the *compaction threshold*. omp does not — measured: `percent=80` and `percent=80 + reserveTokens=16384` both return 160000 on a 200k window; the reserve is a dead knob once a percent is set. But omp enforces the identical invariant at *request* time in `fitOutputTokensToContextWindow` (output-budget.ts:58-73), which shrinks `maxTokens` to actual remaining room. That is strictly superior to compacting earlier: it also covers side turns (`/btw`, recaps) and mid-turn requests, which a threshold structurally cannot (the docstring at :46-47 admits the residual gap: "a prompt that fills the whole window still overflows and is left to the caller's compaction"). Porting dsh's min() would make omp compact strictly earlier for zero safety gain and double-count the reservation.

2) The two "reserves" are different quantities. dsh's `reservedCompletionTokens` is an *output* reservation; `headroomTokens` is a safety margin. omp's `reserveTokens` is "tokens reserved below the context window for the next prompt + response" (compaction.ts:195-196) and it is simultaneously the summary budget: `floor(0.8*reserveTokens)` capped at MAX_SUMMARY_TOKENS=16384 (compaction.ts:214-224, :868). Folding dsh's headroom into that knob would silently shrink summary budgets as a side effect. omp's default threshold is also not a ratio at all — it is `window - max(0.15*W, reserveTokens)`.

3) The rejection messages guard branches omp makes unreachable, and that is already a defended contract. dsh throws on `pressureBudgetTokens <= 0` (config.ts:182-190). omp *recovers* instead — `resolveBudgetReserveTokens` (compaction.ts:349-358) substitutes the 15% proportional reserve — and `compaction-reserve-provenance.test.ts:59-75` asserts `resolveThresholdTokens(cw) < cw` for cw=1..10. Recover-don't-throw is the better form and it is already regression-tested. Likewise dsh's `retainTokens >= thresholdTokens` (config.ts:198-204) has no omp analogue: omp's `keepRecentTokens` is a backward-scan cut budget (compaction.ts:539-547), not an absolute retention floor, so the inversion is not even expressible.

4) Throwing is the wrong control flow in omp. dsh resolves the spec once at load against a fixed, fully-known window, so throwing is correct. omp recomputes on every `shouldCompact` — 6 live call sites (session-advisors.ts:1995,2005; session-maintenance.ts:2507,2639,3205,5317) plus the TUI render path (context-usage.ts:124,465). A throw there is a per-turn crash in a hot path, not a config diagnostic. omp places the actionable message at the layer a user can act on: compaction-threshold.ts:26-29 names the accepted forms and what was received.

The only marginally portable piece is dsh's warn-once-per-target suppression (index.ts:167-170, a `Set<targetKey>` so the throw cannot spam every pre-step). That is a *symptom* of dsh's design, not a feature — omp has no repeated throw to suppress, so it would be dead code.

Tier: DO-NOT-COPY. Not BORROW, not REFERENCE.

Scope honesty: the dsh quote is verified; the omo repo was also checked (grepped repo-wide for thresholdRatio/thresholdTokens/headroom) and has no counterpart — the claim is genuinely dsh-only. I did not find a second threshold implementation in omp; that rests on a repo-wide grep over `packages/`, not a proof.

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED on portability: the claim is factually accurate about dsh, but omp ALREADY has a strictly richer version of the same concern, and the "session projection" primitive the claim depends on does not exist in omp and cannot be ported as a pattern — it is a framework.

1) omp already does "retry intent persisted before the cancellable wait," with MORE payload than dsh. turn-recovery.ts:2656 awaits #recordPendingRetryError (which persists the failed assistant turn into the session JSONL and resolves a durable persistenceKey), :2658-2665 emits auto_retry_start {attempt, maxAttempts, delayMs, errorMessage, errorId}, and only then :2687 does `await sleepLong(delayMs, retryAbortController.signal)`. Identical ordering to dsh index.ts:188-190, richer record. The second half of the claim is already satisfied.

2) omp already has log-derived retry-state recovery by a cheaper mechanism. #markPendingRetryErrors (turn-recovery.ts:792-855) re-locates the failed entry by entryId and, when that id goes stale after a session rebuild, falls back to a reverse branch scan on sessionMessagePersistenceKey (:805-813), writes entry.message.retryRecovery, and calls sessionManager.rewriteEntries() to persist (:843, :852). On load, session-context.ts:386 reads retryRecovery back during replay. That is content-keyed recovery of retry state from the log, done in ~60 lines — the functional benefit a projection would buy, without the framework.

3) "Session projection" is a FRAMEWORK in dsh, not a pattern. It lives in packages/session/session-projection (714 LOC src/index.ts + 24 types.ts) and session-projection-cache (471 + 108), with 24 non-test registration sites spread across 109 referencing files. In omp, grep -rn "projection" over packages/ returns only unrelated senses (tool-schema projection, OAuth projection, header/body projection) — no sessionProjections service, no stateVersion, no reducer registry. omp's log is also a CLOSED union: SessionEntry is 15 fixed entry types (session-entries.ts:300-317), not a free-form event stream. There is an appendCustomEntry(customType, data) escape hatch (session-manager.ts:2951) but no reducer consumer for it.

4) The durability window is too narrow to justify anything, and omp's counter semantics are deliberate. dsh's own reducer resets to {} on step/start and turn/end (index.ts:131), so its projection survives only WITHIN one step — a window during which an in-memory map behaves identically. omp's #retryAttempt (turn-recovery.ts:293) is a per-prompt() budget: incremented once at :2281, reset at ~8 terminal points (:513, :521, :918, :2559, :2586, :2611, :2644, :2730, :2772, :2938). On --resume omp builds a fresh AgentSession, so a user returning hours later correctly gets a fresh retry budget.

5) One narrow real gap, not worth a framework. omp writes the retryRecovery annotation at saga CLOSE, not schedule time — so a crash DURING the backoff sleep leaves the failed turn in the log with no auto-retry marker. Closing that is a ~5-line change (call the existing appendCustomEntry at :2656), not a 738-LOC port. And omp already handles the adjacent "a context rebuild invalidated my handle mid-saga" failure (:2751-2761 #stripFailedAssistantTail, re-checked at :2699-2710 for issue #5382) — the same hazard a projection would paper over.

6) Copying dsh's keying would be a REGRESSION, not a port. dsh keys the counter by [provider, policyKey] (index.ts:133, :219-225) so each provider/policy gets its own bucket. omp deliberately does NOT: :2566 `if (switchedModel) this.#retryAttempt = 1;` grants a fallback model a fresh budget while credential rotation keeps the cumulative count (documented at :2563-2565). Adopting dsh's keying would silently change omp's fallback budget semantics.

TIERS — BORROW: the ordering discipline only (durable intent recorded before the cancellable wait); omp already complies. REFERENCE: the crash-during-sleep marker gap and the appendCustomEntry fix. DO-NOT-COPY: the session-projection framework port (no substrate, 24-site blast radius) and dsh's per-provider counter keying (breaks intentional fallback semantics).
evidence: DSH CLAIM SOURCE (accurate): packages/llm/llm-retry/src/index.ts:125-138 = ctx.sessionProjections.register({key:'llmRetry', stateVersion:1, stateSchema, init, apply}); :131 resets to {} on step/start|turn/end; :188-190 = agent.session.append('llm/retry', eventData) -> await cancellableDelay(delayMs, fusedSignal) -> append('llm/retry-started'). Counters read back at :220-222 via ctx.sessionProjections.stateOf(). Keying at :133/:219-225 = retryStateKey(provider, policyKey).

FRAMEWORK SCALE IN DSH: packages/session/session-projection/src/index.ts = 714 LOC (3 ts files, 738 total); session-projection-cache/src/index.ts = 471 + spec.ts 108 (4 files, 579 total). 24 non-test `sessionProjections.register(` call sites (llm-retry, goal, token-meter, time-context, tmux-context, agent-loop turnBoundary+inbox, agent-team, permission-presets, session-controller list/imageLimits/modelSelection, ...); 109 files reference the service. So the mechanism is load-bearing infrastructure, not a local idiom.

No `sessionProjections` service, no stateVersion, no reducer registry. omp's log is a closed union: packages/coding-agent/src/session/session-entries.ts:300-317 (SessionMessageEntry | ModelUsageEntry | ThinkingLevelChangeEntry | ModelChangeEntry | ServiceTierEntry | CompactionEntry | BranchSummaryEntry | CustomEntry | CustomMessageEntry | LabelEntry | TitleChangeEntry | TtsrInjectionEntry | SessionInitEntry | ModeChangeEntry | CredentialPinEntry | ResetBoundaryEntry).   :2658-2665  await emitSessionEvent({type:"auto_retry_start", attempt: this.#retryAttempt, maxAttempts: maxRetries, delayMs, errorMessage, errorId: message.errorId});

  UI consumption: modes/controllers/event-controller.ts:2397 component.applyRetryRecovery(retryError.retryRecovery).
  Persistence field: packages/ai/src/types.ts:1108 retryRecovery?: AssistantRetryRecovery.

Sibling counters :305-307 (#emptyStopRetryCount, #unexpectedStopRetryCount, #malformedFunctionCallRetryCount), reset together at :438-440. Budget check :1300 and :2300.

SEMANTIC CONFLICT: turn-recovery.ts:2563-2566 "A fallback model gets a fresh retry budget. Credential rotation instead keeps the cumulative attempt count" then `if (switchedModel) this.#retryAttempt = 1;`. dsh's per-[provider,policyKey] keying (index.ts:133, :219-225) would give each provider its own bucket and erase this distinction.

No retry logic exists in omp's extensibility surface: `grep -ril retry packages/coding-agent/src/extensibility` matches only custom-tools/types.ts, extensions/types.ts, hooks/types.ts, legacy-pi-ai-shim.ts, shared-events.ts (event type declarations only, no counters).

## [v2]

reason: REFUTED — the pattern solves a problem omp does not have, by adding a problem omp would suffer.

(1) The source claim is only half-true, and the load-bearing half is dead. The type is genuinely merge-extensible, but ZERO dsh extensions merge into it. dsh's own code admits a plugin variant "cannot be listed", making the extensibility a liability rather than a feature. All 7 variants are core-emitted.

(2) omp has no TurnEndReason and needs none. omp's `stopReason` is a closed provider-wire normal form written by 20 provider adapters with 566 non-test consumers. Widening it to a merge-extensible sum would force a `default` defense on every consumer — importing dsh's proven tax without dsh's plugin ecosystem to amortize it.

(3) omp's plugin surface is architecturally incompatible. `turn_end` is a void observer hook with no reason field; only `*_before_*` hooks carry typed Results and can block. There is no mechanism by which a plugin could author a terminal reason, so the extension point would have zero producers on day one.

(4) omp's existing design is strictly better on the same axis. Plugin influence flows through OPEN channels (open-string `reason`, boolean `willContinue`) and blocking hooks with typed Results, not through a widened closed union. omp's two non-union stop literals (DAP `breakpoint`, ACP `cancelled`) prove the idiom is deliberate per-boundary closed vocabularies.

Verdict: DO-NOT-COPY the merge-extensibility pattern. The only borrowable idea is inverted — dsh's unreachable `default` branch is the exact maintenance tax omp's closed `stopReason` already avoids.

reason: Both cited line ranges are exact and both described behaviors are what the code actually does; I could not find a reading under which the claim is overstated or narrow.

HALF 1 (fail-soft, index.ts:127-130): the catch returns `undefined` and both call sites honor that sentinel — :141 `if (retained === undefined) return decision` and :154 `... ?? content` — so the untouched original is returned. `ctx.logger.warn` at :128 includes `String(error)`, so "logs why" is literal. "Any error in the size-reduction path" holds structurally, not just for the tested cases: the try opens at :95 and every throwing call inside `bound` lies within it (pricing :66/:68, fullText :85, saveText :103, cap guard :113, retainContent :114); the only code outside the try is `retainable()` at :94, which cannot throw.

HALF 2 (budgeting, index.ts:112-113): `reserved = price(GAP) + price('\n\n' + worstNotice.text)`; the guard throws when `price(worstNotice) > maxTokens`; :114 gives retention `maxTokens - reserved` floored at 0. The worst case is a genuine upper bound, not a heuristic: `worstNotice` is built from `totalBytes` (:107) and `images.length`, while the emitted footer uses `retained.omittedBytes`/`retained.omittedImages` (retention.ts:101-102), and both are provably <= the worst case since head/tail are substrings of `content`.

CAVEATS THE CLAIM IS SILENT ON (material, but they do not falsify either stated behavior):
1. Orphaned spill artifact. `saveText` at :103 runs BEFORE the cap guard throws at :113. Measured: cap=4 with a 400-char body gives `spill.saves.length === 1` while the full inline content is kept and the notice is never emitted — a persisted file nothing references. The existing tests at spill-policy.spec.ts:183 and :590 destructure only `{ ctx }` and never assert `spill.saves`, so this is uncovered. Bounded, not permanent: spill-local reclaims it via a startup sweep (default `cleanupPeriodDays: 30`, spill-local/src/index.ts:40) — but with `cleanupPeriodDays: 0` it is never reclaimed.
2. Merged-adjacent-text token accounting is an approximation; the code says so at :119.
3. The catch assumes `ctx.logger` exists; a throw there would escape `bound`.

TIER: BORROW. The shape worth taking is (a) one `try` boundary wrapping the entire reduction so fail-soft is structural rather than per-call-site, and (b) reserve-then-emit budgeting that prices the notice at its worst case BEFORE allocating content. DO-NOT-COPY the ordering in (3) above: write the spill artifact only after the cap is known satisfiable.

Scale (honest): spill-policy is 4 source files / 442 lines (index.ts 156, notice.ts 59, retention.ts 104, types.ts 31) and 5 spec files / 1176 lines. The claim covers one 41-line function in a 156-line file.

1. omp already has the split, and a wider one. `packages/agent/src/agent.ts:412-413` declares `#steeringQueue` and `#followUpQueue`; `steer()` at :1223 ("Delivered after current tool execution, skips remaining tools") and `followUp()` at :1232 ("Delivered only when agent has no more tool calls or steering messages") are dsh's `steer`/`followup` verbatim. The user surface is `streamingBehavior?: "steer" | "followUp" | "aside"` (`packages/coding-agent/src/session/agent-session-types.ts:374`) — THREE buckets vs dsh's two. dsh's only non-waking entry point, `inject()`, shares the same next-step list as `steer()` and is therefore not a distinct queue; omp's `aside` is a genuinely separate non-interrupting queue (consumed at `agent-loop.ts:1725-1726` and `:1753`).

2. omp's turn-end condition is the same check, done more carefully. `agent-loop.ts:1720-1732` drains steering at the stop boundary; then `:1752` RE-POLLS, with a comment naming the exact race that dsh's single check leaves open: "a steer can land between the stop-boundary dequeue above and this yield point (e.g. queued while onBeforeYield ran). Without this poll it would strand in the queue until the next manual prompt." The re-poll→break at :1755-1762 has no await between check and break, so omp's exit is race-free. dsh's `:359`→`:363` window contains only the `agent/turn-stopping` dispatch.

3. omp does what dsh structurally cannot: mid-tool-batch steering. dsh's inbox is claimed at exactly ONE site — `preStep`, `agent.ts:271` — so a steer arriving during a tool batch waits for the entire batch. omp has an event-driven steering watch (`agent-loop.ts:3546-3576`) that interrupts a running tool batch, with subscribe-before-check to close the edge race (:3549-3552), plus hard-vs-soft cooperative interrupts (`checkSteering` at :3166-3195, `steeringSoftController` at :3163) and a 250 ms poll fallback (:179, :3580-3586).

4. omp has live steering dsh's design cannot express. `packages/agent/src/live-steering.ts` (89 LOC) implements OpenAI Responses `response.steer` — the provider pulls queued steering INTO the in-flight response, with accepted/deferred bookkeeping so the transcript matches what the model saw. dsh's inbox is only ever consulted at a step boundary; there is no mid-response injection point in that architecture.

5. The extension point maps onto omp unchanged. dsh's `agent/turn-stopping` (agent.ts:360; typed `runtime-types.ts:381`) is a pre-break notification. omp's `turn_end` is pushed and awaited at `agent-loop.ts:1687` → `emitTurnEnd` (:737-759, `await config.onTurnEnd?.()` at :752), which runs BEFORE the drains at :1720/:1752, and is exposed as both hook and extension event (`extensibility/hooks/types.ts:400,492`; `extensibility/extensions/types.ts:1341`). An extension calling `pi.steer()` inside `turn_end` is consumed by the very next drain — same observable effect.

THE ONE REAL GAP (a DIFFERENT claim, BORROW-able separately): dsh's inbox is a durable session projection folded from `agent/inbox/spliced` events (`packages/core/agent-loop/src/inbox.ts:27-65`), so pending input survives process restart and is reconstructible by any client (71 non-test files repo-wide reference the inbox). omp's queues are plain in-memory arrays — grepping `steeringQueue|followUpQueue|queuedMessages` across `packages/coding-agent/src/session/` returns only `#pendingNextTurnMessages` (advisor cards, agent-session.ts:748), and `session/queued-messages.ts` (95 LOC) is editor-restoration only (feeds `input-controller.ts:1751 restoreQueuedMessagesToEditor`), not persistence. If omp ever wants restart-durable pending input, THAT is the idea worth taking — and it would be layered onto omp's existing queues, not replace them.

The claim fails as a port for four reasons.

(1) THE SEAM DOES NOT EXIST IN omp. Measured across all of packages/ and crates/: bwrap 0, bubblewrap 0, landlock 0, seatbelt 0, sandbox-exec 0, AppContainer 0, ConfinedArgv 0. No sandbox/security/permission package exists in `ls packages/`. ConfinedArgv would have no producer and no consumer — a type describing a boundary never established.

(2) EACH FIELD ANSWERS A QUESTION ONLY A WRAPPING BACKEND CREATES. `enforcement` grades how completely the thing that wrapped omp's argv enforced policy; omp's only "sandbox" (task/worktree.ts under ~/.omp/wt/, per isolation-ownership.ts:1-6) is a subagent STATE directory, not a file-effect boundary — nothing to grade. `denialSignatures` describes the stderr dialect of a specific backend; omp never parses child stderr to infer a denial, it SYNTHESIZES denials first-party: `throw new ToolError("Tool call rejected by user (bash)")` (session-tools.ts:~993) and `denyError(resolved, this.tool.name)` (extensions/wrapper.ts:236, 293). A synthesized error has no dialect. `runnerFailureRules` covers the case where the runner died before the command ran; omp has no runner.

(3) THE "PARTIAL HONESTY" DIFFERENTIATOR HAS NO REFERENT. windows-acl's holes (Low label revokes the write authority it conferred; NTFS hard links alias a granted workspace file outside the root; reads stay unconfined; the AppContainer-ACL'd tree is unreadable) describe a Windows ACL backend's own limits. With no backend the enum ships as 'full' on one hardcoded value forever — dead vocabulary that reads as a safety guarantee it cannot back.

(4) omp ALREADY HAS A BETTER VERSION OF THE UNDERLYING CONCERN, and the 'partial' honesty is not the differentiator it appears to be. Where omp actually meets this problem — file-write-fallback.ts:214 — it uses a UNION: `const PERMISSION_DENIED_CODES: Record<string, true> = { EPERM: true, EACCES: true, EROFS: true }` plus `PERMISSION_DENIED_MESSAGE = /\b(EPERM|EACCES|EROFS)\b/` (:215), driving classifyWriteFailure (:381) which re-runs mkdir to recover the real errno that Bun.write's mkdir hid behind ENOENT. Same question ("permission boundary or ordinary failure?"), answered with structured errno instead of stderr text. Critically, the union is correct there BECAUSE of the exact ambiguity dsh's per-backend split exists to avoid: omp is the one making the syscall, so the kernel hands it a structured errno — one speaker, no dialect needed. dsh must split per-backend only because it reads a DIFFERENT process's prose. The comment at :377 even names the threat omp is robust to ("it sees kernel-level denials (Seatbelt, LSM)") — omp already knows it may run under an external sandbox; it reads the errno, not the child's prose.

Additionally, omp already carries the axis the claim is really reaching for — decision provenance — under a different name: resolveApproval (tools/approval.ts:203) returns `source: "tool" | "user" | "mode"` beside policy/tier/override/policyKey/reason. That is "which authority spoke and how binding is it" on the axis omp actually has (authority), not dsh's (kernel backend).

reason: OVERSTATED on the causal clause; the structural description and line citations are all exactly right. (1) CITATION RESOLVES: the repo has two agent.ts — packages/api/session-controller/src/agent.ts (536 lines, 0 "inbox" hits) and packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts (688 lines). The claim can only mean the core one. (2) SPLIT CONFIRMED: inbox.ts:22-24 declares two distinct durable lists ('next-turn', 'next-step'), init at :30, getters nextTurn/:nextStep at :82/:87. (3) agent.ts:163-173 CONFIRMED LITERALLY: followup->'next-turn'+wake, steer->'next-step'+wake, inject->'next-step' no-wake. (4) agent.ts:359-363 CONFIRMED LITERALLY: the turn-end condition consults this.inbox.nextStep.length === 0 twice — once gating the agent/turn-stopping dispatch (359-362), once the break (363). (5) REFUTED — "which is what makes mid-turn steering actually work" is false as a general attribution. The gate is guarded by `turnEnds &&`, and step() returns null on tool-call steps (agent.ts:533 `if (toolCalls.length === 0) return {kind:'completed'}`, :538 `return concluded ? {kind:'completed'} : null`), so on any tool-call step turnEnds is null and lines 359-363 are SKIPPED ENTIRELY. I instrumented the branch and measured it (then reverted via git checkout; git status clean, lines 359-363 byte-identical to HEAD). In the tool-loop steering test (contract-regressions.spec.ts:525) the probe read {"steps":3,"turnEndsSet":1,"gateEval":1,"gateBreak":1} — two mid-turn steers were delivered with the gate firing ZERO times on their steps. The real general delivery path is ReactLoopInbox.claim() at inbox.ts:109-114, which drains next-step UNCONDITIONALLY on every step boundary (line 110) regardless of `target`, and only additionally consumes one next-turn item when target==='next-turn' (line 111); it is called from preStep at agent.ts:271. Contrast the case where the gate IS load-bearing: contract-regressions.spec.ts:330 ("steer() from an agent/turn-stopping listener continues the same turn") probed {"steps":2,"turnEndsSet":2,"gateEval":2,"gateBreak":1} — the re-check at 363 is precisely what stops a late steer from being stranded, because the first check at 359 saw an empty next-step, then the listener steered during the serial dispatch. So there are TWO independent, co-necessary mechanisms, and the claim names only one. Practical consequence for anyone borrowing this into omp: copying only the turn-end gate would silently break mid-turn steering during tool loops, since that path is carried entirely by the claim() drain.

reason: REFUTED on all three of portability, cost, and redundancy. (1) NO PORT: omp has no process-confinement layer for the contract to govern. Measured grep for SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE|seatbelt|landlock|seccomp|bwrap|confine( across all of packages/ + crates/ returns zero hits except two incidental `seccomp` prose mentions (cli.ts:414 pidfd_open fallback; input-controller.ts:1439 SIGSTOP refused by the host). omp's `sandbox` is a WRITE-SCOPE ENUM meaning "session scratch space" (internal-urls/types.ts:75 `type SchemeWriteScope = "workspace" | "sandbox" | "coordination" | "device"`), not confinement; the other hits are a git worktree (worktree-cli.ts:328) and comments. A `SandboxProvider` with zero implementations and zero callers is a vacuous abstraction — precisely the shape AGENTS.md forbids ("Two implementations of the same thing is a bug"; "If you cannot name the contract, do not add the test"). (2) NOT CHEAP: the error-code half is a cross-cutting refactor of the agent-core result contract, not a drop-in. omp's `AgentToolResult` (packages/agent/src/types.ts:960-971) has content/details/isError?/providerMetadata?/useless? — NO code field; `isError` is a bare boolean. omp has NO HarnessError equivalent: ~20 ad-hoc `class X extends Error` (AgentBusyError, ToolCallBlockedError, CliUsageError, ConfigError, …) and not one carries a `code`; ToolCallBlockedError (run-collector.ts:619-623) has only `name`. omp's tools layer FLATTENS errors to message strings (agent-loop.ts:3417, :3454 `text: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`) — the exact "parse the message" antipattern dsh's own HarnessError doc forbids ("route on this, never by parsing message"). The only structured `code:` in omp is telemetry span codes (agent/src/telemetry.ts:549+), which is observability, not a tool-result channel. Porting it means a new error base + ~20 retrofits + a new AgentToolResult field + a tools-layer propagation point — multi-package churn across every tool and renderer, to serve a sandbox that does not exist. dsh's 182-line contract also sits on 12,485 lines of machinery, so "cheap" does not survive contact with the home repo either. (3) omp ALREADY HAS A STRONGER VERSION where it matters. omp's real seam is the approval gate (tools/approval.ts, 387 lines), already fail-closed: approval.ts:57 "fail-closed: `always-ask` with an empty policy map — no user grant"; approval.ts:220-222 "only `deny`/`prompt` carry over … so a stale `allow` cannot mask a `deny`"; and extensions/wrapper.ts:349-351 "Provider safety checks fail closed without an interactive prompt. Unlike ordinary tier approval, no setting or yolo mode may bypass this gate." That is STRONGER than dsh's, because a dsh provider is bypassed by any caller who forgets to consult it, whereas omp's gate sits on the tool path and yolo cannot bypass it. Separately, where omp deliberately fails OPEN it documents why (plugins/loader.ts:71-75: "rethrowing aborts plugin tool-path collection, which fails agent and subagent startup outright, and no plugin is worth that") — importing a blanket "fail closed everywhere" would regress a considered decision. TIERS: the fail-closed ETHOS = DO-NOT-COPY (omp's approval posture is deliberately different and already stronger on the live path); the abstract-provider + error-code MECHANISM = REFERENCE at best; BORROW = nothing net-positive. HONEST CAVEAT: if omp ever adds real confinement (bwrap/landlock/seatbelt), the SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE vocabulary becomes worth borrowing — but as one piece of that larger build, never as a standalone cheap contract.

## [v1]

reason: The mechanism claim is CONFIRMED from code, with a real implementation, not just a docblock. Two things are wrong with the claim as written, and one of them is the actionable part.

(1) THE CITATION IS WRONG. `credentials/src/index.ts:256-262` — the only evidence the claim offers — contains `deleteRecord`'s docblock ("Remove one record; removing an absent record is a no-op") and the opening of `notifyUpdated`'s docblock. It contains no token-refresh text. The actual justification is at `packages/credentials/credentials/src/index.ts:166-168` and `:236-250`. The claim is off by ~80 lines. The substance is still in the same file, so this is a citation defect, not a fabrication.

(2) "ONLY WRITE PATH" IS OVERSTATED. The claim quotes the code's own phrasing, but the code's phrasing is itself loose. `CredentialProvider` also declares `set` (index.ts:201), `unset` (:209) and `deleteRecord` (:256) — all real write paths. In `LocalCredentialProvider` there are FOUR `writeFileAtomic` call sites (:691 modifyRecord, :712 deleteRecord, :764 ref write, :834 migration). `modifyRecord` is the only path that MUTATES a record's value; it is not the only path that writes the document. "Exclusion holds across processes **where the backing store supports it**" (:240) is a hedge the claim drops — the interface does not guarantee it, only one production impl does. And `withFileLock` is cross-PROCESS, not cross-host: its own docblock (atomic-write/src/index.ts:226-229) states "writers on other hosts or in other PID namespaces sharing the file are unsupported and could both hold the lock."

(3) THE NORMATIVE TAIL IS REFUTED. "omp has refresh tokens" is true (`packages/ai/src/auth/refresh.ts`, 575 lines), but the inference "the one-write-path rule is right" is unsupported and points the wrong way. omp's substrate is NOT a single text document — it is SQLite (`packages/ai/src/auth/sqlite-credential-store.ts`, 2043 lines) — and omp ALREADY has the direct equivalent of what dsh's file lock buys, implemented more precisely: a fenced lease table `auth_credential_refresh_leases` with acquire/renew/release, owner fencing and expiry (sqlite-credential-store.ts:377-379, 480-497), plus CAS-guarded `updateIfMatchesWithLease`/`deleteIfMatchesWithLease` (:419, :434), plus in-flight dedup and explicit peer-rotation detection ("OAuth refresh race detected; another process rotated token first", refresh.ts:327) with a dedicated test `packages/ai/test/auth-storage-oauth-refresh-race.test.ts`. Adopting a file-lock read-decide-replace over that would be a regression.

(4) AN OMITTED COST. dsh pays for this design: because the decision includes a network round trip, the lock wait is inflated to 30s (`DOCUMENT_LOCK_WAIT_MS = 30_000`, credentials-local/src/index.ts:112), and because refs and records share one file and one lock, "every writer of this document — reference writes and record deletes included — waits this long, not only the mutation that holds it." omp's lease-renewal design exists precisely to avoid holding an exclusive lock across a network call.

TIER: the read-decide-replace discipline is BORROW-worthy as a principle. The specific file-lock mechanism is REFERENCE for a text-document store, DO-NOT-COPY for omp's SQLite store.
